text: raw meat is best from christmas day until lent, and is commonly used for special occasions at no other time. bacon, beef, and mutton are good at all times, but the worst time for mutton is from easter to midsummer. a fat young pig is never out of season. goose is worst at midsummer and best in stubble time, but they are best of all when they are young, green geese. veal is good at all times, but best in january and february. kid and young lamb are best between christmas and lent, and good from easter to whit sunday, but kid is ever good. hens are good at all times, but best from all hallowtide to lent. fat capons are ever good. peacocks are ever in season, but when they are young and of a good stature, they are as good as pheasants, and so are young grouse. snipes are best between hallowe en day and lent. a mallard

title: To boyle Mutton with Mallowes or Turneps.
text: take a neck of mutton, cut it into ribs, and put it in a pot with a good quantity of beef broth. bring to a boil. then, take turnips or mallows and cut them into pieces about the size of the mutton. add a little pepper to the pot and let everything stew until tender. remove the vegetables and serve them on toasted bread.

title: To boyle Mutton with Spinage.
text: take a neck of mutton and cut it into pieces, placing it in a pot with a generous amount of mutton broth. bring to a boil. add pieces of sweet bacon, about the size of your finger and of a reasonable length, using six or seven pieces. next, take three handfuls of spinach, wash it thoroughly, wring out the water, and chop it finely. add it to the pot, along with a little pepper and salt. ensure you have just enough broth to cover the meat. let it simmer gently until the meat is tender, then serve it on toasted bread.

title: To boyl mutton with Carrets.
text: take a piece of mutton, about the size of your thumb, and put it into an earthenware pot with fresh water, and bring it to a boil. then take carrots, peel them clean, and cut them to the size of your mutton, and let them boil. add half a handful of stripped thyme, as much savory and hyssop, and a little salt and pepper. let them simmer until the mutton and carrots are very tender, then serve them on toasted bread.

title: To boyle Mutton with Colworts.
text: take a neck of fat mutton and cut out the ribs. broil them on a spit until they are half cooked, then place them in a large earthenware pot with a generous amount of beef broth and bring to a boil. add two handfuls of chopped kale, washed clean. add a ladleful of beef broth fat, a little pepper, and salt. let it stew until the meat is very tender, and serve on bread. do not add salt until the meat is ready to be served.

title: To boyle a legge of Mutton with a pudding.
text: first, with a knife raise the skin around the leg until you reach the joints. when you have boiled the meat, shred it finely with suet or marrow, parsley, marjoram, and pine kernels. then season it with pepper and salt, cloves, mace, and cinnamon, and take the yolks of nine or ten eggs, and mix them with your meat, a good handful of currants, and a few minced dates. put the meat into the skin of the leg of mutton and close it with pricks, and then boil it in the broth you boiled a capon in, for the space of two hours.

title: To boyle a leg of Mutton with Lemmons.
text: when your mutton is half boiled, take it up, cut it into small pieces put it into a small pot, cover it closely, and add the best of the broth, as much as will cover the mutton, your lemons being sliced very thin and quartered, and currants. add coarsely beaten pepper, and let them boil together. when they are well boiled, season with a little verjuice, sugar, coarsely beaten pepper, and a little sandalwood. lay it in fine dishes on croutons. it will make three servings for the table.

title:
To boyle Mutton with Endiue, Borage, or Lettice, or any kinde
of hearbes that may serue thereunto.
text: when your mutton is well boiled, take the best of the broth and put it in a small pot. add a handful of endive, borage, or any herbs you like, and a few currants. let them boil well, then add a piece of the upper crust of white bread. season with coarsely beaten pepper, a little verjuice, and a little sugar, and then pour it over your meat.

title: To boyle Mutton for a sicke bodie.
text: put mutton into a pot, boil it, and skim it clean. add a crust of bread, fennel roots, parsley roots, carrots, large raisins, and herbs, according to the patient's condition. if they are cold, use warming herbs if they are hot, use cooling herbs such as endive, cinnamon, violet leaves, and some sorrel. let them boil together. then add prunes and a very little salt. this is broth for a sick person.

title: To make balles of Mutton.
text: take your mutton and mince it very fine with suet. then season it with sugar, cinnamon, ginger, cloves, and mace, salt, and raw eggs, making it into round balls. let your broth simmer before you put them in. make your broth with currants, dates quartered, whole mace, and salt. thicken it with egg yolks and verjuice, and serve it upon soppes.

title: To boyle a Capon with Oranges after Mistres Duffelds way.
text: take a capon and boil it with ale, or a marrow bone, or whatever you prefer. then take a good amount of that broth and put it in an earthenware pot, adding a generous handful of currants, as many prunes, and a few whole maces, along with some marjoram. add a good quantity of white wine or claret to this broth and let them simmer gently together. next, take your oranges and with a knife scrape off all the outer pith. cut them in half and squeeze the juice from three or four of them, adding the juice to your broth with the rest of the ingredients. then slice the oranges thinly and have a skillet of boiling water ready. put the sliced oranges into the water, and when that water becomes bitter, have more ready, and change them repeatedly as long as you can detect the bitterness, which will be six or seven times, or more if needed. once the bitterness is gone, remove the oranges from the water and rinse them

title: To boyle a Capon in white broth.
text: boil your capon in clear broth, and cover it to keep it white, but do not boil any other meat with it. take the best of the broth, and as much verjuice as of the broth, if your verjuice is not too sour, and add whole mace, whole pepper, and a good handful of endive, lettuce, or borage, whichever you prefer, small raisins, dates, marrow from marrow bones, a small stick of cinnamon, and the peel of an orange. then add a good piece of sugar, and boil them well together. then take two or three yolks of hard-boiled eggs, strain them, and thicken the broth with them, and boil your prunes by themselves, and lay them upon your capon. pour your broth upon your capon. thus may you boil anything in white broth.

title: Another way to boyle a Capon in white broth.
text: take marrow bones, break them, and boil them, then remove the marrow. next, simmer your capon in the same liquid. take the best of the liquid in a small pot to make broth. then take currants, dates, and prunes, and boil them in a pot until they are plump. take them out and add them to your broth, then add whole mace, a generous amount of ground ginger, and some salt. add the marrow you removed from the bones, and strain egg yolks with vinegar, adding them to the broth with a good piece of sugar, but do not let it boil after this. take bread and cut thin slices, laying them in the bottom of a dish. sprinkle sugar around the sides of the dish, then place the capon and fruit on top, and serve.

title: To boyle a Capon in brewes.
text: boil your capon with fatty meat, then take the best of the broth and put it in a small pot. add whole mace, whole pepper, some red currants, about half as much white wine as broth, a generous amount of marrow, and dates. skim the broth thoroughly to keep it clear, and season it with verjuice and sugar. lay finely cut parsley over the capon and pour the broth over it.

title: To boyle a Capon with Orenges or Lemmons.
text: take your capon and boil it until tender. then, take some of the broth and place it in a small pot with mace and a generous amount of sugar. peel three oranges, remove all the pith, and add them to the pot. boil them gently in the broth, then thicken with wine and egg yolks, a generous amount of sugar, and a pinch of salt. do not let the broth boil, as it will curdle, and serve it without croutons.

title: To make Sops for a Capon.
text: take slices of bread, butter, claret wine, and slices of oranges, and lay them upon the toast. sprinkle with cinnamon, sugar, and ginger.

title: To make Sops for Chickens.
text: first, take butter and melt it in a chafing dish with coal. lay thin slices of toasted bread in the dish, and make a sorrel sauce with parsley and gooseberries. simmer them with a little parsley and lay them upon the bread.

title: To boyle a Mallard with Cabage.
text: clean and wash the cabbage, then parboil it in clear water. drain the cabbage in a colander and place it in a pot. add enough beef broth to cover the cabbage and the marrow from three bones. take a duck and make a slit along each side of the breast. remove the duck meat and add it to the cabbage, along with its drippings. the duck should be roasted halfway and the drippings saved. let the mixture stew for about an hour. season with pepper and a little salt, then serve the duck on toasted bread, with the cabbage around it and some of the broth ladled over the top.

title: To boyle a Mallard with Onions.
text: take a duck, roast it about halfway, and save the drippings. then put the duck into a large pot along with its drippings. stuff its belly with six or seven whole onions and a spoonful of whole peppercorns. around the duck in the pot, add enough beef or mutton broth to cover it, half a dish of sweet butter, and two spoonfuls of verjuice. let it boil for an hour. then add salt to taste, remove the pot from the heat, and place the duck on toast. arrange the onions around it, and pour the broth over the top.

title: To boyle a Ducke.
text: cook duck with marrow bones or mutton, and reserve the best broth. add cloves and a generous amount of sliced onions, and simmer until the onions are tender. season the broth with verjuice and a little crushed pepper. remove the duck and place it on toasted bread. serve two slices of duck breast, studded with cloves, and pour the broth over it.

title: To boyle Stockdoues.
text: simmer them with beef or mutton. take the best of the broth and place it in a small pot. add finely minced onions and a few carrots, and boil until very tender. season with herbs and a little sweet butter, and pour over your stockdoughs when they are laid on your toast.

title: To boyle a Conie with a Pudding in his bellie.
text: prepare a rabbit, skin it, leaving the ears on, and wash it thoroughly. then, combine grated bread, finely minced suet, currants, and finely chopped herbs parsley, spinach, or beets, sweet marjoram, pennyroyal, and winter savory. season with cloves, mace, sugar, a little cream, salt, and egg yolks, along with finely minced dates. mix all ingredients together and stuff the rabbit's belly, sewing it closed with thread. for the broth, use mutton broth and once it has simmered a bit, add gooseberries or grapes, currants, sweet butter, verjuice, salt, grated bread, and a touch of sugar. when the broth is boiled, serve it in a dish with crusty bread.

title: To boyle Chickens or Capons.
text: first, boil them in fair water until they are tender. then take bread and steep it in the broth, and with the yolks of four or five eggs, and verjuice or white wine, strain it, and therewith season your broth and your capon in it. then take butter, parsley, and other small herbs, and chop them into it. and so serve them forth upon soppes of bread.

title: To boyle Chickens with a Cawdel.
text: take chickens when they are scalded, and trussed and stuffed with parsley in their bellies. put them in a pot with fair water and a little salt, and add twenty prunes, half a handful of carrots and raisins. let them boil altogether until the chickens are tender. then, take six yolks and a pint of vinegar and strain them together. add a quarter of sugar, or as you think best, and let it boil, but you must stir it still, else it will curdle. when it boils, take it from the fire. take your chickens and put them in a colander, that the broth may go clean away, and then put your chickens and the fruit into the sauce. make toasts, lay them on your chickens and the fruit, and pour on the sauce.

title: To seeth Chickens in Lettice.
text: spiced apple cake first, cream together 1 pound of butter and 1 pound of sugar until light and fluffy. then, beat in 4 eggs, one at a time. sift together 1 1 2 pounds of flour, 2 teaspoons of baking powder, 1 teaspoon of ground cinnamon, 1 2 teaspoon of ground nutmeg, and a pinch of salt. gradually add the dry ingredients to the butter mixture, alternating with 1 cup of milk, beginning and ending with the dry ingredients. stir in 6 peeled, cored, and chopped medium apples. pour the batter into a greased and floured 9-inch round cake pan. bake in a moderate oven for 50-60 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted into the center comes out clean. let cool in the pan for 10 minutes before inverting onto a wire rack to cool completely.

title: Wie man schwartze Karpffen seud.
text: to prepare a dish for both young and old, take a clean earthenware pot and put in a spoonful of wine, then add the blood of the bee-loaves. but you must not cut the bee-loaves' throats, as common cooks do, otherwise all the flavor will run away it should be a small slit near the ear, where they weld together vigorously when you hit it right, and they will die quickly. now, make sure everything comes together and doesn't settle retain it. afterwards, add the bee-loaves with wine, and a little rosewater if it curdles or foams. heat some lard, burn a spoonful of grated or ground bread until it is brown without burning, and stir it into the pot. when it is almost at its final stage of boiling, add well and sufficiently ground cloves, ginger, and pepper. let it simmer completely, then take the blood, strain it through a sieve to remove any small clots that may be present.

title: Salmen zu braten.
text: to prepare a salmon steak for frying wash it with vinegar or good strong wine, as much as the other. let it lie for half an hour, then take pepper, a little nutmeg and muscatel, all finely ground, and mix with salt, not too much. sprinkle the steak well all over. prepare it on the grill, let it dry gradually. then, in the same, prepare a sauce heat some schmaltz, add the aforementioned spices, a little hard bread, half wine and vinegar, finely chopped savory and parsley. let it simmer well together. it should be like a thin pepper sauce. moisten and brush the steak with a little sprig of savory until it is sufficiently roasted. they are almost quickly roasted. if you want to serve it warm, pour the warm sauce over it. if you want to serve it cold, moisten it with the sauce so that the sauce has a fine skin and is well colored. it will remain beautifully

title: Ein Aal zu braten/ fast herrlich vnd gut.
text: prepare the eel, removing the skin and preparing it as it should be. then, place the pieces in a good vinegar, pepper, and salt for about an hour, so they become almost bright and beautifully blue. afterwards, take a small bird's skewer, and thread one piece along its length, and the other across it, and sprinkle savory between them, or bay leaves if you have them, with a little salt and pepper. place the skewer near the embers, and roast it like a bird. set a roasting pan underneath, heat some rendered fat, prepare a broth as before, but without bread or cloves. put it in the roasting pan, basting it constantly, and when it is roasted to its liking, take fresh butter and sprinkle it well with a hot, frothy cream. have ready a bowl of white sugar and finely grated bread, well mixed with cinnamon and sugar. then sprinkle it

title: Wie man ein Aal auffs beste seud.
text: skin the eel and prepare it as it should be. then, place it in a beautiful pot with three supports. add wine and water, equal in amount to the fish. set the pot over embers and, when it begins to simmer, add a little salt. simmer it like other fish. afterward, cover it again and let it simmer over the heat for an hour or an hour and a half, depending on the size of the eel. underneath, make a little melted lard hot. take a small piece of onion, about the size of a bone, and do not cut it, but chop it finely, like a mash. when the lard is hot, add the onion to the pot and stir it in. add a little dried bread, as you always have in the kitchen. take a handful of beautiful sorrel, wash it well, drain the water from it, hold the stems in your hand, cut away the ends, and chop the leaves as finely as you

title: Ein Pasteten von Aalen vnnd Lampreten.
text: skin the eels and cut them into pieces. take vinegar, plenty of pepper, and lay the pieces in it. you may also take a fairly strong wine, malmsey or a strong muscatel the stronger, the better. if it covers them well for three or four hours, then sprinkle the pieces generously with pepper and sweet wormwood. chop some herbs quite finely, as mentioned above, along with parsley and a little crumbled bread. spread this on the bottom of a pie crust. sprinkle it well with the previous wormwood, also saffron and a little may butter, according to how rich the fish is. place the pieces neatly in it, and then small pieces of butter on top. sprinkle with spices. some people add wine as well, as in the boiled dishes i, however, prefer lemon, entirely, and leave it at that. bake in a water bath for an hour and a half. you may also take the wine in which they lay and

title: Ein Pasteten von Salmen.
text: choose the best pieces of salmon, such as the head, the haunch, and whatever other parts are most flavorful. soak them for an hour in good wine. then, one piece at a time, spread them with pepper and finely chopped parsley at the bottom, a little coarsely crushed muscatel and whole cloves. place a piece next to another, baste them with the wine, and sprinkle with a little of the previous spices. alternatively, insert two cloves into each piece. then, add a slice on top and prepare it in this way. bake in a very hot oven for an hour or three-quarters of an hour they will bake quickly. do not add any liquid they should be served hot on the table, due to their richness, but they are also good cold. do not salt them.

title: Ein andere Forme.
text: prepare the salmon by pulling it from the back, so you can form a piece like a large pike. take the tail and the front together, or just the tail, as you wish. tear the tail end a little, as you prefer for fried fish. place it in a mixture of half-strong wine and vinegar for about three or four hours it won't hurt if it's overnight. then take ginger and pepper, more pepper, and salt as needed. fill the incisions with butter and cover it well with dough, according to the shape you desire. sprinkle it generously, as far as the fish extends, with mace and finely ground cloves and nutmeg, and finely chopped savory. then place the salmon in a beautiful mold shaped like a bent fish, sprinkling it with the previous spices, parsley, and savory. place small pieces of fat on top, and sprinkle it well with the wine and vinegar in which it lay. cover it with the remaining dough, smoothing and shaping it

title: Fohren in einer Pasteten.
text: to fry fish well and to the best, take them beforehand, especially eel and roach, which are usually served cold, and leave the backs whole. remove the roe and nearly all the innards, then seek out the gall and leave that inside. put them in vinegar as long as you have time. before that, cut from the backs to the half of the belly neatly, on both sides, cutting into them according to how thick the fish are, but not all the way through. when they have been in vinegar long enough, make pepper and ginger, and according to how each person likes to season the fish when boiling, that also serves for frying. for example, carp like pepper, ginger, and cloves that is best for frying with the most pepper. when frying, use prussian carp, roach, perch, eel, dace, and the like. take muscat buds and cloves, and also sage behind the ears, inside the belly, having already seasoned

title:
Ein Pasteten von einem Karpffen warm
zu geben.
text: to prepare a good, plump carp, cut it open. before you boil it, remove the entrails and wash out the inside thoroughly, but retain the liquid. next, boil the carp and cut it into pieces as you desire. place it in wine for half an hour, then turn each piece carefully in the liquid. prepare beforehand pepper, quite sweet herbs, and good cloves, salt it as seems right, and season each piece one after another. have a pastry ready, as if you were preparing chicken or something similar. place clean wineberries on the bottom, then add the seasoned pieces, cover with the skin, and top with more wineberries. sprinkle generously with herbs and a little sweet fat. the fish should then be very tender, as it should be. cut lemon slices in between, if you have them, but the broth should be yellow, not black. add angelica root and herbs, then cover and bake for an hour and a half or two hours, depending on

title: Plateißlein oder Halbfisch.
text: once you have prepared it beautifully and cleaned it, put it in water, then take it out and lay it nicely on cabbage leaves, sprinkle it well with ginger, and drizzle with hot melted lard. if you wish, make hot lard, throw in a small onion as with the eel, with toasted bread, or leave out the onion, add plenty of ginger, finely chopped parsley, and a little broth from the dumplings in which they were boiled, as much wine as broth. let it simmer well together, drizzle over, and let it cook on the embers.

title: Anderst.
text: roll out the dough and place it in a bowl, taking it up gently. prepare the broth in it, as much as you need. add rendered goose fat, chopped parsley, and ground nutmeg. salt is right in everything, season well, and let it cook over the charcoal or a grate.

title: Ein ander Form.
text: prepare it as before, then take crab and sorrel, or juice of cranberries, and a piece of celery. let peter sit with it, put him into the half-fish with goose fat and plenty of pepper. let it cook together in the cabbage pan. sprinkle it all over with ginger it is helpful and good, also beneficial for the sick.

title: Anderst.
text: to prepare it, take a pan or cauldron. remove from the water in which it was cooked, and add a good amount of breadcrumbs, hot or melted butter, as needed, along with a little flour, as it seems appropriate, and a crushed muscat grape, and thyme. let it simmer well. if you wish, add parsley. if a sick person cannot eat spices, use only thyme with a little salt, and perhaps muscat grapes. in this way, also cook the noble walnuts and other noble fish.

title: Ein Pastet von den Schnecken.
text: prepare the snails as they should be take them from the water, toss them like a salad in a clean cloth, then place them in a dish or bowl. add pepper generously, also a little nutmeg, mix well together. when the harbor is ready, add salt and fresh butter. as soon as the harbor hardens, prepare underneath it a fresh breadcrumb mixture with plenty of finely chopped parsley. add well-sweetened butter to it. if the snails are not sufficiently peppered, add more to the mixture when it simmers, sprinkle as always over the harbor, let it bake for half an hour. they are otherwise no way better prepared than this, and filled or mashed into the shells, placed in a deep pan, and covered with broth. prepare a breadcrumb mixture as mentioned before and let it simmer, then splash it over again so it's not too hot, and stir it in and let it simmer until the egg yolks are firm. there is not much of use

title: Ein herrlich Essen von einem gefu:elten Hechtdarm.
text: if you have a nearly large pike, take its intestines, wash them thoroughly, and blanch them with a little egg so that they become even larger. then take a good piece of pike, as much as you think you need, and soak it in vinegar. next, add as much bacon as you like, chop it well with a little salt or not, depending on whether the bacon is salted, and a good amount of sweet marjoram and coarsely ground cloves. stuff the intestines with this mixture, sew them up, and put the pike in a pot with a little wine and water. cover and simmer until the intestines can be cut easily it makes a very fine broth, which you can improve with ginger and vinegar. when the pike is cooked, pour the broth over the fillets. cut the intestines like lemons or radishes, place them in the broth, and over the pike. you can also prepare stuffed or fried pig intestines in this way. if you have leftover fish that is no

title: Wu:erst fu:er vnessige Leut.
text: beat the gingerbread on a grater almost clean take a portion of the flour with a frothy honey, then add more flour and work it as a dough for small tarts, making long, round strips as thick as a sausage, cut them as long as you wish, curl them, and bake them in hot lard. if you want, make a gingerbread broth with it, such as boiled bacon and fish roe, pounded well and alternately layered, season the roe well, and stuff them into casings, then quickly fry them on the grate or bake them in the lard as you wish. they are not suitable for the sick, they burden the stomach, all roe is indigestible.

title: Ein Soß oder Su:eltzen von einem Lebkuchen.
text: grind a nearly good gingerbread into very fine flour. add as much as you need to a sauce or jelly, or to a breadcrumb mush, like bread mush. you may also well add bread underneath. heat the schmaltz, not too much, and roast it well within. also add good wine to it. cinnamon and enough sugar, let it cook. sprinkle it well with sugar it serves well with fish.

title: Strauben auß Fischrogen.
text: prepare the roe of a pike, removing it and pressing it in a bowl until it separates. grind it with a mortar, make a dough with it as you would a strudel dough, add wine, salt, a little ginger, and saffron. bake it like other strudels. you can also make this with carp roe, but pound it in a mortar and mix it with more wine than you used for the pike roe. add pepper and cloves. this pastry is not suitable for the sick it is only for those who enjoy unusual things.

title: Suppen von einem Hecht.
text: to prepare the best pieces of a pike, wash them well and let them sit in salt for an hour or four. hang them up so that a day or three passes through the smoke, but not so they become black, only nicely dried. when you want to cook them, wash them again in lukewarm water, simmer them in half wine and water, a bit more wine. while they are simmering, cut a quince, two or three, one as large as might be enough. cut them small, as for a soup. cook them in the fat, making them nicely yellow. when the pike is half cooked, pour the broth off into a clean dish. add a clear sorrel broth to it, and some of the broth in which the pike was cooked, as is proper, and the half quince, and the sweat. then add nicely browned white bread slices, but not burnt. when the pike is cooked, place the slices in a sheet, and pour the pike broth over

title: Auff ein ander Form gesaltzen Hecht.
text: season the pike well and soak it in quite warm water. then, skin it. put it in a pan with a little of the best broth. if the pike is almost salted, add wine with fresh water and a cup of good, strong wine, chopped parsley, well-ground muscatel grapes, and pepper. return it to the heat. make a hot fat, and when the fish starts to simmer, pour it into the pot. when it is properly stewed, add enough sweet butter. as soon as a bubble appears, season it and serve hot.

title: Mehr ein Polnischen Hecht.
text: to make a good dish of pike, take onions and soak them in water until they are soft. then, from the water, take a slice or two of white bread, as needed, and put it in good wine. when the onions are boiled, strain the water through a sieve. mix the strained liquid with the bread and wine well. then prepare the pike and boil it with vinegar as usual. afterwards, add the same broth and add the strained onions, with enough wine as needed, chopped parsley, very sweet mace, well-ground muscatel, raisins, galangal and such spices that it almost turns red, and each has a good flavor. add well-chopped lemons that have been salted, if you have them if not, take them as they are. also add hot lard or sweet butter, a little sugar. let it simmer until it reaches its consistency. and in this way, one can also boil carp, which is boiled in wine. when it

title: Weiter von den Schnecken.
text: to begin, put the snails into a pot, while their shells are still firmly closed. add water and boil them until the shells open. then, remove them with a knife, discard the insides, and cleanse them as thoroughly as a calf's head with warm water, gradually increasing the temperature until the snails are well cleaned. place them in a pan with water covering the shells, make a good broth, and keep it in fresh spring water until you are ready to use them. carefully and thoroughly clean the shells. then, take the snails from the water, dry them slightly with a cloth, salt them well, and season with plenty of pepper and a few cloves, finely chopped parsley. mix everything together well. prepare a meat broth, and add a little wine or vinegar to it, just enough to barely taste it, so they don t become tough. add a spoonful or half a spoonful of the broth to each shell, and place a snail inside, along with a generous piece of

title: Von den Fro:eschen fu:er die Lungsichtigen.
text: roast frogs, which i have cooked well, though i have never actually seen them alive i only know they are found in weyher. they appear to be somewhat greenish and a bit larger than tree frogs the large black ones are poisonous. now, cut them apart like hares, separating the hindquarters from the forequarters, and remove the skin, soaking it briefly in fresh water. afterwards, dry them with a white cloth, then sprinkle them with good vinegar and salt, as with other fish, and bake. then simmer them in wine with a little water until done. the broth should then be made from this, and the frogs placed in a dish or platter, with plenty of pepper and sweet butter, and covered and cooked in a cabbage pot until the fat is clear. they will become as white as chickens. if one has a portion remaining, cut the meat from the bones after they have been boiled, and prepare them in a pastry shell, like crabs. they can also

title: Ein gut Muß von Fischrogen.
text: take some fish roe, more or less, and soak them in half wine and water. then pound them well in a mortar with white bread, not too brown, softened in broth or otherwise good, strong wine. mix everything together into a puree, pour it into hot rendered fat. season it well with sweet mustard and saffron, do not salt it. cook it over the fire it shouldn't cook for too long.

title: Folget von den Krebsen.
text: to prepare a beloved crab dish, first remove the flesh from the crab, carefully picking out the hair and other parts. add a little more inside as well. then, grind everything together in a mortar. add slices of white bread and soak them in good red wine, if you desire. mix the ground crab and bread thoroughly, including a bit of the liquid they were cooked in, making it quite thick, like a child's porridge. in a heated earthen pot, melt some lard and pour it in. cook until hard-boiled eggs are done. add marjoram with sweet marjoram, and sprinkle it generously with cinnamon. this is almost beneficial for those with lung ailments, but the marjoram should not be too strong.

title: Gebachene Krebs.
text: once the crabs are boiled, take as many as you want, and cut off their noses or shells. leave the gills and tails behind, clean them of their hair, and remove the insides, making sure you don t break the gills and tails. then, take from other crabs what is in the gills and tails that is the best. chop this up with a little bacon. if you want to prepare it for a sick person, leave it as it is, and also chop in some parsley, the doctor recommends it with pepper, which is especially good for those with fever and those with much bile, and for older people too. add a few raisins, and nutmeg if you like. then, crack in an egg or two, especially if there is no bacon. however, it depends on who will eat it, as a cook can recognize what suits the sick or the healthy. otherwise, as mentioned, much will be spoiled. sprinkle a little vinegar over it. when it is well

title: Ein ander Form.
text: boil the crabs. then remove their claws and noses cleanly, and cut off their feet. shell them completely, including the tips. also prepare sweetbreads or shanks, moisten them with vinegar and milk, and bake them quickly. make a filled white bread from a portion of the crabs, as you have done before, or another kind as you find suitable. layer it three times in leaves, with the crabs on top, and insert a sprig among them so that the others are visible. the filled ones are also pleasing to have alongside, so that the others are not seen. if you wish, prepare a pie from the chopped crabs, using whatever you have left over, or a cake with bread and almonds. then garnish it with a small broth. everything from the crabs is almost delightful, and it serves those with poor eyesight.

title: Ein anders.
text: boil the crabs alive, or if you can't, pour boiling water over them until they turn red. then prepare the noses and gills, just as you did with the first ones, with other crab meat and bacon. the bacon should always be previously simmered well. leave out eggs and wine. make a boiling vinegar and water mixture, salt it, put the crabs in, cover, and let them simmer as you would other crabs. afterwards, serve them hot as usual, sprinkling them generously with parsley, pepper, ginger, and vinegar. it is quite pleasant and good, but requires quite a few crabs.

title: Ein Pasteten von Krebsen.
text: to begin, select crabs shell the claws and bodies. alternatively, use crayfish, but nothing else will do. the crabs should be soaked in half wine and half water. prepare a pastry crust, large or small, as you prefer. place the crabs inside, cut into small pieces. add parsley if you wish, plenty of pepper, and salt to taste. use a generous amount of sweet fat. as soon as the crust is hardened, make a small slit as you know how, and pour some of the broth into it, allowing it to simmer. do not bake for long, about a quarter of an hour that is sufficient. when it is opened, the fat and broth should be even. in this way, you can prepare it in any small pastry crust, using leftover or fresh ingredients. if you happen to have weak crabs and do not need them, you can boil them and then prepare them in this way, or cook them in a dish or pan over the embers, alone

title: Ein Salat von einer Fischbru:eh.
text: boil the eggs hard, as one would for a salad, but after peeling, carefully remove the white around the yolk so that you can separate them nicely, leaving the yolk whole. place them in a small dish or similar container, add a good fish broth it should be salmon broth that is nearly good, meaning almost fully cooked, or broth from other fish that have been well seasoned, especially herring. let it stand for an hour so that the broth soaks into the eggs. place it in a leaf, sprinkle some parsley on top, so that the eggs are covered. if you wish, cut the white like flakes and place them between the eggs. if you wish, you can make a bread crust as you know how, fill it and bake it, as you find it fitting. there is a special dish for both the sick and the healthy, as follows.

title: Ein anders.
text: to make a fine dish of eggs, take some meat from a fowl, or a calf, and season it well. if it's somewhat cold, cut off the outer part, if it's black, and chop the meat and the eggs separately, the meat as finely as you can, the eggs reasonably. then mix them alternately, as much meat as you want eggs. if you want more eggs, add them so that you have some yolk and some white. after that, arrange each color beautifully on a plate, color by color roses, stars, patterns, whatever you can. if you have leftover chicken, boiled or roasted, or cold roast, veal, take the breast from the chicken, and the inner part from the roast, which is beautifully white, chop it equally white, mix a portion with the white and another with the yolk, or put the white into the red, make a circle with the red, roses or whatever you wish. then, with the other colors

title: Plateiß oder Halbfisch zubereiten.
text: boil some peterlein root in water until it is half cooked. add the half fish and let it cook further. prepare some green herbs for the broth, as you would otherwise use them. fry it in a pan with its own water. spread it nicely on a bowl or platter, drizzle with hot melted lard, salt it well. if you wish, add a little vinegar and pepper to the lard. let it simmer and drizzle over the fish. place the peterlein root on top, drizzle again with lard, and sprinkle with ginger.

title:
Wie man den Peterlein zu den Fischen/ wie
auch zu dem Fleisch bereiten solle.
text: to prepare a fine root clean and scrub it thoroughly. bind it with a thread. place it in a pot, then set another pot behind it, of the same height, filled with cold water so that the root simmers, keeping the herbs always in the cold water this will keep them a lovely green. when you take the root out, dry the herbs on a white cloth and place them with the meat. if you prefer it with fish, blanch it in salted water and add it to the fish. if you have time, let the root lie in a fish basket for an hour, which is good with cold fish, as it should contain a lot of parsley.

title: Folgen etliche Essen von Erbsen.
