text: to prepare almond milk, grind almonds and soak them in water. then add finely chopped parsley. next, add one-third of the almond milk, stirring in sugar well it will turn green. then add the remaining two-thirds, also stirring in sugar well, and let it simmer in a pan. simmer one-third white in a pan, and another third, making it yellow. put the green portion in a pan as well, and let it stand. you will then have three colors. lift it up and plunge it into hot water, then spread it onto a beautiful board or bench. cut it into pieces and arrange them on a dish, alternating white, yellow, and green, until the dish is full. serve.

title: Ayrenschmaltz von Mandel.
text: grind a handful of almonds and a little white bread. mix this into an egg and make a thin batter. spread it on a hot surface, and in a pan with oil, bake it until it is quickly fried in the fat, or make fritters from it. cut these into strips, and fry them on the surface where the tarts will lie. place in a bowl as usual. for the topping, use good wine or rhenish wine, and a little muscatel. cut a small green sprig and place it on top, and serve.

title: Bachen Wu:erst in der Fasten.
text: mix the apples and almonds together. add a little white salt and wineberries. work them between your hands on a smooth board, shaping them into sausages. enclose the sausages in an apple dough, bake them, and place them on green herbs.

title: Ein geweichts in der Fasten.
text: take shelled almonds and chopped meat, grate half. add saffron and put it separately into a bowl. add wineberries separately to another bowl. take all sorts of fish but not herring pound them in a mortar, grind them on a flat stone, and bake in an oven. they will be good to eat.

title: Ein Mandelschotten zumachen.
text: grind almonds as you wish, well in a mortar. take them in a linen cloth and rub until it forms a ball when squeezed between your hands. while you rub, add water to make them like dried apples but if you don t have a linen cloth, do it in a mortar as thick as a cook. take the almond and put it in a pan with water in which sorrel leaves have been boiled, and much sugar. simmer it as long as two hard eggs. then take them out and let them cool. beat them in a tin bowl finely, high like a scotsman. it stands. add a thin almond milk to it, some boilings over, some not but i boiled it over and let it cool again, and sweetened it with sugar. i have also seen that in the almond boiling, a half-measure of reinfall was added on the table. don t use sorrel leaves this boiling can also be made in the shape

title: Marcipan.
text: sixteenth. to make almond paste, whether whole or ground very fine, so that it tastes of rosewater, add sugar to it, about as much as the almonds. take the oblate and lay it on a paper, and if you want to make the marzipan large, take the oblate, moisten it with water, and lay another oblate on top they will stick together. otherwise, a single oblate is too small for a large marzipan. then take a ring, whether of wood or iron, about the size of a little finger, and place it on the joined oblates. cut around the ring, over and over, so that it is even. but before you cut it off, put the almonds in the ring, as high as the ring itself, and press them firmly on. then lift the ring away and see how the marzipan looks. bake the marzipan coriander seeds on a baking sheet, which

title: Ein fast gu:ots gemu:eß zumachen.
text: take wineberries, almonds, and cubes of bread, about the same quantity of each. wash the wineberries, shell the almonds, and cut the bread cubes into small grains. then chop them together, as you would a loaf of gingerbread. take some stale bread, crumble it, and roast it in fat. add the chopped mixture, sprinkle with a bit of salt, season with good linden spices and sugar. let it simmer for a good while until it thickens, then adjust the seasoning. it will be quite pleasing.

title:
Jtem gesultzte Mandel/ der farben

hat wie vil du wilt.
text: to make it white, use almonds as they are, or yellow them with saffron to make them green, use parsley to make them red, obtain coloring from the apothecary. this coloring should be boiled, so that the water becomes red. with this, you may temper the almonds, but houseleek leaves must be boiled along with them, and well mixed with sugar, like turkish delight. to make them brown, do this take ground almonds and add sour cherries. this will turn the almonds brown-black. then take a small nail, chop it, and add water that has been boiled with houseleek leaves. add seakale and strain the seakale through a cloth sweeten it with sugar, and it will become black.

title: Rote farb zumachen.
text: boil houseleeks in water. this makes it sweet and soft. strain it through a cloth. then take red dye from a sworn apothecary. let the water cool. stir the dye into it. sweeten it as desired, and shape it as you like.

title:
Ein Mandelzüger zumachen/ der farb

hat wie vil du wilt.
text: mix the prescribed color into a cup, let it stand about a finger's thickness, then add more color on top, not hot, just cold, or let it flow into the other. mix the color in as much as you like until the cup is full. once it has been boiled and stood, place the cup in hot water and then quickly remove it. set the cup over a bowl, and you will have all the color. then chop a blanched almond into strips, so you can see the color unfold.

title: Gossen Blu:omen.
text: to prepare a tinted blue glaze, use either blue flowers or elderberries. place white almonds with elder leaves in a bowl. once they have steeped, cut the flowers or greenery into the mixture, replacing them with another color as needed.

title: Gegossen Wappen.
text: prepare a molded crest, using the color of the field. afterward, cut out the helmet and color it accordingly. also, for lent, do this have a wooden or other model made, consisting of two joined parts, like a mold in which to make marzipan, rubbed with almond or hazelnut oil, studded with almonds and violet leaves so that it remains yellow and sweet, or let it stand this is the yolk. to the almond paste, take afterward the yolk from the model, when it has stood well. then take an almond as large as the yolk, place the yolk in the model, along with the studded almonds in the same model, where the yolk is. let it stand again, so that the yellow surrounds the white give it the hardness of an almond. add a quince for the vinegar, sugar for the salt.

title:
Ein getheilt Mu:oß in ein Schüssel zumachen/

von vier oder sechß farben.
text: make also a tinned support, which you assemble into four or six parts, so that it fits properly into the bowl. if you wish to divide it, set the same support in the bowl so that it rests on the bottom of the bowl and stands against it in all places. take the seasonings red, white, brown, black, and blue, and put each in a special place. place the support in the bowl. mix the seasonings all together in a thick layer, and use one as high as the other in the bowl. afterwards, remove the inserted support from the seasonings.

title: [C1a||5a] Ein schwartzen Jgel von Weinbern.
text: combine a pound of wineberries wash and clean them well. gently heat them in a pan until they cool and are dry, then pound them finely. add ginger, nutmeg, sugar, and salt. mix everything together and form it into a ball. when ready, garnish with a small piece of nutmeg. add a golden muscat to the mouth it is then ready.

title: Ein roten Jgel.
text: take a pound of figs, and grind the meal from them, so that it becomes dry, and chop them finely, pound them with spices. add nutmeg, and then add honest sugar. when it is finely ground, add it in, then beat it together. make a cake from it, and decorate with nutmeg for the first ones, and put a fig in the mouth.

title: Ein Feygen Sultzen.
text: roast six figs on a spit, or as many as you like, and place them in a pot or cauldron. add wine and water. then, take bread and grated cheese, add them to the broth, along with honey and vinegar from the figs. season with spices and herbs, mix well, and strain through a cloth. when serving, place in a clean bowl, sprinkle with wine berries, and serve chilled.

title: Ein Reindel von Weinbeern.
text: to make almond milk, take a quarter or half a pound, as much as you want. strain it, then grind it. if you have a stone, it s better ground, as it yields more, and the milk will be fine and thick. then strain it through a sieve or cloth, and on the thickest part, grate some semolina. add this to the milk, and then take some raisins, pick them finely, and wash them. add them to the almond milk and grated bread. make it as thick as a cook does, placing it in a small pan, salt and sugar to taste. set the pan over a heat, being careful not to burn it. place a hot cinder on top, so it browns nicely, and serve warm.

title: Mandel formm macht man also.
text: to form almonds first, break the almonds, but grind them in a mortar. then take into a linen cloth, as thick as a dough. you must add water little by little, rub it until it comes together. keep balls, such balls you may keep for eight days for almond soup. then take those ground almonds, rub them with water and strain them, making a milk. but if you want to make almond milk into a form, rub it with water in which borage leaves have been boiled. strain it through a cloth. you must take four lots of borage leaves to a half pound of almonds. then, after you have strained it, add the borage leaf water to the almond milk and boil it for a long time, adding much sugar. you must boil it for a long time. when it is boiled, put it into a cauldron on the hearth, let it cool well. i have seen it. then see that you have a model

title: Gebachen schnitten von gestossem Mandel.
text: quick almond cookies so they don't become oily, beat them in a little water, whisk until it becomes a thick milk, make a dough with flour as one usually makes gingerbread, and bake a small bread roll in it, and bake it. if you like, you can sprinkle it with sugar.

title: Ein Torten von Mandel.
text: grind almonds finely, almost as fine as grated apples, and mix them with water to form a dough. then, add as much grated almonds and raisins as you like, beating them together until the mixture becomes thick like a kneaded dough. add plenty of sugar. make a pastry of water and flour. roll it out thinly and lay one layer over another, pressing them together with a rolling pin. spread the almond filling over the pastry. bake it in a pie dish or in an oven until it is set but not overbaked. when it appears dry and firm, it is done.

title: Weinbersuppen zumachen.
text: to make wine cordial crush beautiful plums in a mortar. when it is all cooked, add a piece of gingerbread. then add wine that is sweet, afterward spice with gentle spices, such as nutmeg, mace, and muscat. add water to the wine as you strain it, so it is not so strong for the sick.

title: Weinber mu:eßlin.
text: finely chop thirty-three wineberries, pound them in a mortar. pound also thirty-two pieces of bread, pound them very thoroughly. when they are pounded very long, beat them through and through. then add honest sugar. serve cold, but for sick people, it should be served warm. you must also add sugar to the wineberry soup.

title:
Die Weinbersuppen magst vber ku:echlein

vnd anders geben.
text: for the cake, take half a pound of almonds, finely ground, with rosewater. then, take bird s beak, with 5 eggs, and let it drain very well. add a lot of sugar and beat it together in a bowl. next, add a bit of lard or butter, and more rosewater. make a batter from one egg and semolina. spread it over the mixture. decorate with raisins all around. then take an egg white, beat it well with sugar, and spread it over the top of the cake. bake it until it browns on top. serve it warm. if you prefer it cold, don t use much lard. you must also beat two eggs with the bird s beak and ground almonds it is then ready.

title:
Von Erbes suppen/ vnd sonst
Etlich suppen.
text: to make a hearty herb soup, take fresh herbs and finely chop a small amount. add a little lard. add a few musk grapes and some bread, but omit the crust. fry some lard, and if you make it thick, stir it a little through the herbs. roast a small amount of finely chopped herbs, lard, and musk grapes. you may stir it as you wish, gently.

title: Auff ein andere weiß.
text: boil the beans until soft, then stir them a little so they are not too thick. take only the bean broth, no water. if you want them good and white, take a generous amount of honest sweet cream, but don t add too much cream if you want them white it will be as good as almond soup.

title: Ein andere suppen von Zisserel.
text: boil long green beans, quite white, and south-facing. also, drive them through with your own soup, generously, and set them aside. then add bread and wineberries on top.

title: Linsen suppen.
text: boil lentils finely until tender, then roast a few in it. add vinegar, pepper, and raisins. sprinkle on a piece of buttered bread and serve as a supper.

title: Weinsuppen.
text: to make wine soup, take a measure of wine. beat two eggs, break the eggs, and add a little water to the eggs. pour the wine over them into a pan. let the fat be very good, about a third part. this soup is beneficial for children, if you cook it properly.

title: Ayersuppen zumachen.
text: to make a lemon soup, take only the yolks. add water to them, and either cook them or strain them together. fry in a little rendered fat, and add a little vinegar it will immediately turn yellow. this soup is good for women after childbirth who have a fever, as wine soup is harmful to them.

title: Hadersuppen.
text: make a soup. grind finely. add a walnut shell full of water underneath. to the water, add some rendered fat, and simmer it. if you wish, add a piece of ginger or quince. pound it and add water to it, and a little salt. it will then taste good with a few poppy seeds. serve on a plate, or anything else. a child's porridge is good too.

title:
Ein andere Erbessuppen den Kindbetterin
zumachen.
text: to make a good pea soup, let it boil over. do not let it be too hot add one or two, or three egg yolks, as much as you like to make it. beat or whisk it like a wine soup. add butter and bread crumbs. add water and melted schmaltz alternately. even a delicate child can eat it.

title: Ein dünstel suppen.
text: cut a roll into pieces and place it over a pot in that pot, simmer some herbs, and enrich the pot with broth. let it simmer thus, then place it on a bowl. then, add water, and make a herb soup. thereupon, melt some schmaltz over it, and add a spoonful. herb soup and sliced bread are made in this way. to make a cubed soup, also do this cut a roll into cubes, ensuring the inner crust is completely exposed. add water or herb soup to it, and melt some schmaltz over it.

title: Weinsuppen mit raum.
text: 113. take a lemon, sweeten it with wine, and simmer. sweet lemon soup take water under the lemon, if you wish, you may also add honey to such a soup.

title: Schmaltz suppen.
text: four hundred thirty-two. wine soup, sweet soup, or cider soup a burnt soup. brown some flour in fat. pour it into boiling water, stirring with a spoon. let it simmer. serve it on bread.

title: Saur suppen.
text: one hundred and sixty-five. brew a soup well, season it. or burn some meal in it.

title: Hoecht suppen.
text: make a large pot of broth. take a piece of beef from it, and season it with salt until it is sufficiently cooked. if it is too salty, add salt as needed until it is properly cooked. lower the broth. add butter to it and stir well until it simmers. season with ginger and cinnamon. if you wish to add a little pepper, you may. afterward, peel the beef finely and season the broth with butter. let it simmer for as long as two hours, then season the broth and serve it on toasted bread slices. arrange pieces of beef on top and season. it is now ready.

title: Staubsuppen zumachen.
text: beat three egg yolks with salt until well combined. then take the foam that rises on top and let it overflow. add the foam to the egg yolks, as much as possible, like a wine soup. if the foam becomes too sour, add a little water underneath. if it's still too sour, add a spoonful of sugar. a generous amount of egg is good they are also not bad, as they cleanse the stomach.

title: Wie man den staub am ersten anmacht.
text: make a nice, sticky dough. knead it well and beat it a little, then form a dumpling with the prepared dough. let it stand overnight. this will make it sour. if it becomes very sour, add fresh water to it, stir often, and it will become finely sour. the dough must not be too wet, but rather floury. from this flour, you make the flour soup, as mentioned before.

title: Geißlitz zumachen.
text: grind the oats finely. then take half, making it soft like for a bread. afterwards, make a thick cake. when it appears slightly gray, add water and stir well together. knead it out with your hands so it remains thin in the water. then keep it beautiful and cold this is now the geißlitz. if you want to cook one, press it to the bottom or stir it through. melt lard in a pan until it is thick, then place it on a bowl and let it stand so it forms a skin. remove the skin and cut it into thin slices, and roast them in lard, not too little. then cook the boiled geißlitz and roast it as well. place it on a few embers, cover with a lid with embers on top, and roast pieces on top of it. add currants and figs, and also almond kernels. it can also be cooked in a small pot.

title: Habermuoß zumachen.
text: boil in hot fat, stirring constantly, and add water, meat broth, or pea soup. you may also make it with pea flour.

title: Pfann brey zumachen.
text: make the dough very fine and boil it in milk in a pan. put the brains in it. when it is done, add a knob of rendered fat. set it so it glows underneath and above. then it will brown, and give it.

title: Reyßkoch.
text: boil john and cook john in good boiling milk. also, beat in honey, then rub a loaf of bread not hard, but cooked in boiling milk, and add sugar. boil milk. boil groats. boil prunes. boil plums.

title: Erbes zumachen.
text: prepare the lovely white nimb herbs in a cauldron. rub them between your hands, allowing the skins to fall off, then wash them. squeeze them dry. if you wish to make a purée, add a piece of pork to the broth with the herbs, let it simmer until tender, and then press it through a sieve. alternatively, if you have a lot of herbs, chop them into slices and cook until completely softened, then mix with pork broth, as thick as when cooking a brain. place in a beautiful dish. when serving, dice some good bacon, roast it lightly, and add it to the pea purée. place a slice of bread in the center, and top with a piece of pork. to accompany, a little milk is a good addition.

title:
Ein einbrennts Erbeßmuoß/
macht
man also.
text: to make fine oat flour, put it into a good milk in a pot over the fire, and brown some oat flour in lard. add it to simmering milk, stirring well until it thickens. add sugar, and salt if you like it. when serving, you may put some pork fat or bacon on top, and serve with greens. this is suitable for feasts or gatherings. also, boil white oats whole in pork broth, not boiling, and serve with greens, the broth being on the side.

title:
[O1b||49b]
Gruen Erbes in schaelfen
text: to make green herbs in broth, you can also use them for cabbage when it is honestly large. in the broth, and yet not yellow, add some parsley, also in pork. season the herbs with it, but do not boil them too quickly. also take some bacon, cut it small, roast it until it doesn't dry out.

title: I. DE LEONE
text: i have described three natures and their forms, which i, christ, have written to you in verse thrice repeated. the other animals of the divine book recall, concerning which i have set forth, and again mystically know, if i could write of them in diverse meters and with an added penny, they fill our number together. for the lion standing strong upon the high peaks of a mountain, wherever the valley descends to the depths, if he smells the scent known to the hunter, he licks his whole tail, and fixes his footsteps, so that he cannot seek his lost quarry from there. he does not wake until the sun has turned for the third time, but the roaring of his father awakens him. then he revives, then he grasps the five senses, and whenever he sleeps, he never closes his eyes. thus, to you who dwell on the high peak of heaven,

title: II. DE AQUILA
text: they say the eagle is the first of all birds, and is renewed just as old age weighs her down. she seeks a spring, one that never ceases to rise there, she is close to heaven and near to god. then she kindles her wings with both the sun's ardent fire and lessens and alleviates great burdens. then also, the mist is consumed by nearby fire, which restores her ancient sight. soon she plunges and submerges herself in the liquid springs, and as she falls to her nest, she is renewed suddenly. she has a beak, with which she gathers food, that is curved she can scarcely take a few morsels of food from anything but striking a rock or biting, as she is wont, she brings down food obliquely thus she captures food from it. a man is with sins, which are from the origin of his mother, just as the eagle is

title: III. DE SERPENTE
text: the old snake delights to be new. and fasting, it shudders with dread its withered skin trembles only the bones remain. it seeks a narrow opening in the rock, barely moving, and finally coming forth, then passes through and strips away the old skin. repeating any streams of water, so that it may quench its thirst, it vomits forth poison therefore, in the waters i will fear this one less, without venom. if it beholds any man without clothing, the snake retreats far from the fire but seeing him who bears a garment, it rises upon him. whom a man conquers and follows closely, he abandons the body, makes it a shield but he holds care of the head always, lest he should die. from the spring once renewed, you sin again, you are startled, stony one therefore, be always an imit

title: IV. DE FORMICA
text: let the ant be an example to us of labor, when it carries its food in its mouth and in its actions, it demonstrates a spiritual quality, which because the jew does not love, he is guilty. to be secure in the future, it must be warmed, meanwhile, it does not rest and we too, brothers, must labor while we have time, to be secure in the time of judgment. it examines the grain if it finds wheat, it rejects it it gathers a new law, not an old one. but so that it may not sprout when sprinkled with rain, or perish, to be something that cannot come from this, the prudent ant divides the grain in two this is that which has two laws, two paths, which sounds earthly at the same time and points to heavenly things, now nourishing the mind and now feeding the body. may it fill us, so that hunger

title: V. DE VULPE
text: the fox is widely known in the city for her cunning. she is not loved by the farmer, because she steals his poultry. but she has hunger, because she lacks food, and finds a way to seize squawking birds. she lies flat on the cracked ground, and as if she were dead, she does not stir a flame. the crow or black raven thinks it is a carcass he sits down to eat it, scraping it with his beak. she suddenly rises and swiftly snatches the bird, and, eating, makes his fate a sorry one. then she holds a double form, which it is useful to know, sometimes resembling zabulus, even a bit like a man. he is truly dead, who made death seem to have him, and hides it, pretending he does no wrong whose flesh is eaten by the one who makes everything empty wh

title: VI. DE CERVO
text: the stag has two natures and forms. it is said by the physician, when he teaches this, listen. for though snakes draw out great things with their nostrils, from caves of the earth, or from stones, which they devour and quickly swell with a terrible venom, they are made to pass through liquid springs of water. when they happen to drink these, full of poison they conquer, and make themselves young, when they cast off their antlers. we also, when overcome by the serpent s deceit, contract poison, are burned and with torches, we must run to the living spring, christ, who, when he wets us, drives away the poison taken. and we are made young, having cast off these, and become proud, which are like antlers, when they

title: VII. DE ARANEO
text: a small spider, 1 spin diligently with many threads, and strive to weave skillfully. these are webs, so that the fly, you, while flying, may be caught there, a sweet and useful food for him. this delicate work pleases him, but it is worthless to him as it is fragile any breeze draws it open it breaks and falls into nothing. man follows these little worms, deceiving his companions, he eats them, making them miserable and he delights greatly when he can harm another. yet he does evil things, when he dies, he falls like a web, as he, the spider, just described, does.

title: VIII. DE CETO
text: it is superior to every beast that lives in the sea, a whale, a large monster that rises above the waters. looking at it, one would think it is a maritime mountain, or an island in the ocean in the middle. if ever it desires to alleviate hunger, which it often carries in great measure, it opens its clever mouth, from which it emits a blast of scents, like flowers, to draw small fish to itself only small ones, for it cannot grasp a large one perfectly, nor press it in its mouth. the fish swallows the fish, glues them together, and those too not so, not so did that one swallow jonah. if there is a storm, when it goes or comes, and stirs up all its depths, it continuously raises itself to the waves it is possible to see a considerable headland. the sailors hasten to secure the ship swiftly for the storm, and

title: IX. DE SIRENIS
text: sirens are sea monsters with a great sound, forming songs with many voices and tones, to which sailors most unguardedly come, and they induce sleep with the sweetness of their voices, and sometimes shipwreck, and sometimes mortal peril. those who have fled them have described them as such from the navel down they are like the most beautiful of maidens, but below that, they are birds.

title: X. DE HONOCENTAURIS
text: just as the centaur is in nature double-formed, so too are some men, with an ass mixed into the human body. many men are in this way double-faced, saying one thing, and doing another to you soon after, who appear splendid outwardly, but do not work well within. indeed, there are many who speak of virtue but indulge themselves with their buttocks how brightly they shine in the crowd.

title: XI. DE ELEPHANTE
text: among the indians, there are elephants of such great size, as to be equal to mountains in strength. they walk together like sheep when they seek pasture they come together, averse, when they meet. and they bear young but once, though they live for so long a time,, and never produce twins. bearing but one, and carrying it for two periods, when she gives birth, in a large pool, so it does not fall. it cannot rise, because it never bends its legs if it happens to rush, the mother fears it. when she wants to rest or refresh herself with sleep, she leans against a small tree trunk, which the hunter marks and conceals with a hindrance, and quietly sits, while she seeks rest. he, as if once safe under the tree s shade, when he comes, leans, and with a rushing sound falls.

title: XII. DE TURTURE
text: a dove does not know how to love, for once married to a single husband, she always approaches with him alone, remaining joined both night and day, no one will see her without her husband but if widowed, deprived of him, she will not marry again, even a friend she will fly alone, sit alone, and hold him as if alive in her heart, remaining chaste while waiting. thus is the soul, and each faithful one, made blessed by a male fragrance, for her husband is christ, filling her with his own heart and living well, she will always remain devoted, seeking no foreign friend, however fierce the underworld he may have taken. she believes him to survive in heaven, looking forward to seeing him again, so that he may judge all things.

title: XIII. DE PANTERE
text: a four-footed panther, no other more beautiful, who, white, is sprinkled with black. fed on various hunts and sated, he retreats and lies stretched in a cave after three days he rises, then truly roars. a scent emerges from his throat, so sweet, that with its power surpasses all fragrances to whom quickly comes what hears the beast s voice, and is seized by him, filled with excessive sweetness. thus do all only panthers are dragons, when he sounds, they flee or become sluggish in body and hide in caves, not obeying at the appointed time. but christ is called a panther through mystic speech, who, above, is offered to all in human form. and he was sated, for he takes as many as he wills, and fell asleep when he redeemed us by dying. he sent a roar after he recovered from death, ascending to the

title:
Epistola Theodori philosophi ad imperatorem
Fridericum.

Vorrede.

title:
THE VERTUES OF
CHOCOLATE
text: this pleasing drink preserves health, diverts sickness, cures consumption and coughs of the lungs, expels poison, cleanses the teeth, and sweetens the breath. it provokes urine, cures kidney stones and difficulty urinating, promotes weight gain and a plump physique, enhances beauty, and treats ailments of the kidneys, along with many other serious diseases. it also aids conception, as described in these verses. it is impossible to list all the new and admirable effects experienced daily by those who drink it, so i leave the judgment of its merits to those who continually test it.

title:
THE PROPERTIES OF 
CAVEE
text: egyptian drink. it perfectly cures consumption, gout, spleen, dropsy, sore eyes, and all those troubled with rheumatism. it immediately relieves headaches, promotes appetite, and aids digestion. for students or others who must stay up late or all night, drinking two or three pennyworths around their usual bedtime, or when they begin to feel sleepy, will cheer and comfort their spirits, making them lively and ready for their work, without any drowsiness throughout the night. it is incomparable for those troubled with melancholy and excellent for preventing miscarriage in women, as well as beneficial for those who have never borne children. it is also excellent for eliminating worms in young or old, drying all types of tetters or ringworm, and curing other skin ailments. the stem is good for dim, watery, or bloodshot eyes. it would be too tedious to list every benefit, so i will refrain.

title: [1r] Aqua Juniperi.
text: a small book on medicinal remedies concerning juniper berry water and the ailments for which one may use and apply it.

title: [2r] An den Leser.
text: by god's grace, dear and friendly reader, now that you know that a small book of medicine has come from the juniper berry oil, within which are many valuable and good ingredients, which have been used by many people, therefore i have not delayed showing it to you, and also have had printed the water of the juniper berry or its oil, through the request and desire of many people. as how it should be used and applied, for what ailment, and how many drams one should take at a time, you will kindly accept this small instruction from me. it will be increased and improved at another time, so that it may be done by god's grace..

title: [2v] Zum Ersten.
text: for the virtue and power of juniper water, if a person has discomfort in the loins, kidneys, or bladder, one should administer juniper water to them in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, each time 3 measures. it truly helps with such ailments and is effective.

title: Zum Andern.
text: whoever is weak and cannot pass water or relieve himself, let him take water three times, and each time three measures thus he will relieve himself.

title: Zum Dritten.
text: whoever has a cold or chills should drink two or three times a day, each time three spoonfuls, which will dispel the chills and cold.

title: [3r] Zum Vierden.
text: a woman experiencing a difficult birth should take three spoonfuls of juniper berry water and drink it to expel the difficult birth.

title: Zum Fünfften.
text: a woman who does not have her period, or what is called the menstrual flow, should use water, drinking three lots three times a day, and this will bring on the menstrual flow.

title: Zum Sechsten.
text: anyone with sores or open wounds on their body should take juniper berry water and apply it three times over. wash the evil, heavy, and open wounds with it, healing them from the root and making them clean.

title: [3v] Zum Siebenden.
text: whoever is poisoned, or has received, eaten, or drunk poison, let them drink water it is good for all poisons.

title: Zum Achten.
text: whoever has been bitten by a venomous animal should drink water several times and apply it to the bite this will help him.

title: Zum Neunden.
text: whoever has drunk harmful and impure water should take some of the aforementioned water several times, which will draw out and cleanse the impure water from their body.

title: [4r] Zum zehenden.
text: whoever feels pain externally on the body, wash with this water several times and lay a linen cloth upon it it helps also.

title: Zum Eilfften.
text: whoever has a heavy chest or short breath, let them drink this water in the evenings and mornings it will certainly help them and is worthy. printed in zwickau by wolfgang meyerpeck.

title: Gummihandschuhe in der chirurgischen Praxis.

title:
To boyle a Capon Larded with Lemons, 
on the French fashion.
text: scald your capon, and use a little oatmeal to help it boil white. then add two or three ladlefuls of mutton broth, a bundle of sweet herbs, two or three dates cut into strips, a few pre-boiled currants, a little whole pepper, a piece of whole mace, and one nutmeg. thicken it with almonds. season it with verjuice, sugar, and a little sweet butter. then remove your capon and lard it thickly with preserved lemon. place the capon in a deep dish for boiled meats, and pour the broth over it. garnish your dish with candied fruits and preserved barberries.

title: To sowce a Pigge.
text: scald a large pig, cut off its head and split it down the middle, removing the bones and washing it in two or three warm waters. then shape it like a headcheese and sew the casing in a fine cloth. boil them very gently in clear water, then remove and plunge them into clear water and salt until they are cold, as this will make the skin white. take a gallon of the water the pig was boiled in, and a gallon of white wine, along with a piece of sliced ginger, two quartered nutmegs, a spoonful of whole peppercorns, and five or six bay leaves. simmer all together when it's cold, place the pig into the sauce, and you can keep it for half a year, but use the head.

title: To sowce Oysters.
text: take the meat from the largest oysters, saving the liquid they release and straining it into an earthenware pot. add half a pint of white wine and half a pint of white wine vinegar. include some whole peppercorns and sliced ginger. boil these ingredients together with two or three cloves. once it has boiled for a short time, add the oysters and let them boil for two or three minutes, but not too long. remove the oysters and allow the syrup to cool. then, return the oysters to the syrup, and you can preserve them for the entire year.

title:
To sowce a Pike, Carpe, or
Breame.
text: draw your fish, but do not scale it. save the liver and the trimmings of it. slice the trimmings and wash them. then take a gallon of clear water, a quart of white wine, and a bundle of sweet herbs. as soon as you see your wine boil, put in your fish with the scales on, and when you see your fish boil, pour in a little vinegar, and it will make your fish crisp. then take up your fish and put it in a dish. then put into the liquid some whole pepper, a little whole ginger, and when it is boiled together well with a little salt, and cold, put your fish into an earthenware pan. when you serve it, serve jelly in small plates, with a little fine ginger around the plates edges, and fennel on your fish.

title:
To boyle Flounders, or Goodgeons, on
the French fashion.
text: boil a pint of white wine and a pint of water, with a few sweet herbs, tips of young thyme, sweet marjoram, winter savory, tips of rosemary, a piece of whole mace, and a little parsley, finely chopped. when all is well boiled together, add your fish and skim it well. then add a small crust of manchet bread and a quarter pound of sweet butter. season with pepper and verjuice, and serve.

title:
To boyle a Gurnet on the French
fashion.
text: draw your turbot, and wash it clean. boil it in water and salt, with a bundle of sweet herbs. then take it up, and pour upon it verjuice, nutmeg, butter, and pepper. thicken it with the yolks of two freshly laid eggs. once this is poured over your fish, garnish your dish with preserved barberries or a sliced orange.

title:
To boyle a legge of Mutton on the
French fashion.
text: cut off all the meat at the lower end, leaving the bone intact. grind it finely with beef suet and marrow. then take sweet cream, egg yolks, a few raisins, two or three minced dates, and a little grated bread. season it with pepper, salt, and nutmeg then work it stiff, like a pudding, and stuff it back inside. then stew it in a pot with a marrow bone and a knuckle of veal. serve the leg by itself, and your veal knuckle in a stewed broth, and your marrow bones on toast, with carrots and pepper.

title:
To hash a Legge of Mutton on the
French fashion.
text: boil your leg of meat, and take it up, removing some thin slices. prick the leg through and let the gravy flow over the slices. then crush sweet herbs with the back of a ladle, and add a piece of sweet butter. season it with verjuice and pepper. when the mutton is boiled, pour the gravy over it and serve it to the table.

title:
To roast a Legge of Mutton on
the French Fashion.
text: prepare the skin as thinly as you are able. layer it with sweet lard, and stud it with about a dozen cloves. when it is half-roasted, cut off three or four thin pieces and mince them finely, with a few sweet herbs and a little grated ginger. add a ladleful of claret wine, a piece of sweet butter, two or three spoonfuls of verjuice, a little pepper, and a few blanched capers. when all of this is boiled together, chop the yolk of a hard-boiled egg into it. then coat your leg with flour and serve it with this sauce.

title:
To roast a Neates tongue, on the
French fashion.
text: chop sweet herbs finely, with a piece of a raw apple. season it with pepper, ginger, and the yolk of a newly laid egg, chopped small to mix among it. then stuff it well with that farcing and roast it. the sauce for it is verjuice, butter, and the juice of a lemon, and a little nutmeg. let the tongue lie in the sauce when it goes to the table. garnish your dish as you think fittest, or as you are furnished.

title:
To boyle Pidgeons with Rice, on
the French fashion.
text: cook them until tender, and stuff into their bodies sweet herbs, such as parsley and young thyme. then place them in a small pot with enough mutton broth to cover them, a piece of whole mace, and a little whole pepper. boil all together until the pigeons are tender. remove from the fire and skim the fat cleanly from the broth with a spoon, otherwise it will make it taste stale. add a piece of sweet butter, season it with verjuice, nutmeg, and a little sugar, and thicken it with rice boiled in sweet cream. garnish your dish with preserved barberries and skirret roots, boiled with verjuice and butter.

title:
To boyle a Rabbet with Hearbes
on the French fashion.
text: prepare your rabbit for boiling, and simmer it with a little mutton broth, white wine, and a piece of whole mace. then take lettuce, spinach, parsley, winter savory, sweet marjoram all these being picked and washed clean, crush them with the back of a ladle. thicken it with a crust of bread, soaked in some of the broth, and a little sweet butter mixed in. season it with verjuice and pepper, and serve it to the table on small pieces of bread. garnish your dish with barberries.

title: To boyle Chickens in white broth.
text: prepare your chickens for boiling, as previously demonstrated with rabbits. chop two or three dates into small pieces. take a small piece of whole mace. thicken your broth with almonds. season it with verjuice and a little pepper. garnish the sides of your dish with sweet fruit preserve and sugar, after you have seasoned your broth. you may boil a capon in a similar manner, but then add marrow to your white broth. if you dislike mutton broth, boil it separately in clear water until it turns as white as curdled milk. however, the french prefer the other method, and that is the better way.

title:
To boyle a Teale, or Widgeon, on
the French fashion.
text: boil either of these fowl, and put them into a pot of clear water. then roast them halfway, and take them off the fire, putting sweet herbs in their bellies. lace them down the breast, and stud them with two or three whole cloves in the breasts with your knife, as many in each. then put them into a small pot, with two or three ladlefuls of strong mutton broth, a piece of whole mace, and two or three small onions minced finely. thicken it with a piece of toasted bread. put in a piece of sweet butter, as big as a walnut. season it with pepper and verjuice.

title:
To smoore an old Coney, Ducke,
or Mallard, on the French
fashion.
text: boil any of these partially, and then half roast them. cut slits down the breast with your knife and stud them with two or three cloves. then place them in a small pot with half a pound of sweet butter, a little white wine, a piece of whole mace, a little beaten ginger, and pepper. next, finely chop two onions with a piece of apple, and let them simmer gently, covered, for about two hours, stirring occasionally. serve them on toasted bread.

title:
Another way to boyle Chickens, or
Pidgeons, with Gooseberryes,
or Grapes.
text: boil them with mutton broth and white wine, adding a piece of whole mace. stuff the bellies with sweet herbs. when tender, thicken with a piece of manchet bread and two hard egg yolks, strained with some of the broth. then, put some of the broth into a dish with verjuice, butter, and sugar, and boil your grapes or gooseberries in the dish, covered, until tender. pour this over the top of your dish.

title:
To boyle a Chyne of Mutton, or Veale,
in sharpe broth, on the French fashion.
text: cover your meat with fresh water and a little white wine, a piece of whole mace, a quartered nutmeg, a handful of clean, picked herbs bruised with the back of a ladle, young lettuce, spinach, parsley, and tops of young thyme. when all is boiled well together, thicken it with a crust of manchet bread and the yolk of a hard-boiled egg, steeped in some of the same broth, and draw it through a strainer, then thicken your broth with it. season it with a little verjuice and pepper.

title: To boyle Larkes or Sparrowes.
text: prepare the meat for boiling and place it in a small pot with a ladleful of mutton broth, a piece of mace, a quarter of a nutmeg, a bundle of sweet herbs, and a little fresh parsley, finely chopped and cleaned. add the parsley to the broth, and season with verjuice, pepper, and sugar. thicken the broth with the yolks of two fresh eggs, hard-boiled, and a piece of bread soaked in some of the broth until softened. garnish the dish as desired.

title: A made Dish of Conyes Liuers.
text: boil three or four of them, and chop them finely with sweet herbs, the yolks of two hard eggs. season it with cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg, and pepper put in a few parboiled currants, and a little melted butter, and so make it up into small pasties. fry them in a frying pan, sprinkle with sugar, and serve them to the table.

title: A made Dish of a sweet-Bread.
text: boil or roast your sweetbreads, and add a few lightly cooked chives, a minced date, the yolks of two fresh eggs, and a piece of breadcrumbs finely grated. season with a little pepper, salt, nutmeg, and sugar, squeeze in the juice of an orange or lemon, and enclose it between two sheets of puff pastry or another good pastry. bake or fry as you prefer.

title: A made Dish of Sheepes tongues.
text: boil them until tender, and slice them into thin pieces. then season them with cinnamon, ginger, and a little pepper, and place them in a crust made of fine pastry, with sweet butter and a few finely chopped sweet herbs. bake them in an oven. next, take a little nutmeg, vinegar, butter, sugar, the yolk of a fresh egg, one spoonful of sherry, and the juice of a lemon. boil all these ingredients together over a low heat, and pour it into your pie. stir it well and serve it at the table.

title:
A Florentine of a Cony, the wing
of a Capon, or the Kidney,
of a Veale.
text: mince these ingredients with sweet herbs, parboiled currants, a date or two minced small, a piece of preserved orange or lemon, minced as small as your date. season with ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, and sugar. then take the yolks of two fresh eggs, a spoonful of sweet cream, a piece of shortcake grated, and marrow cut in short pieces. bake this in a dish between two leaves of puff pastry, adding a little rosewater before closing the pastry. when baked, sprinkle with sugar.

title:
A Fridayes Pye, without eyther Flesh
or Fish.
text: wash the green beets clean, remove the central string, and chop them finely with two or three well-flavored ripe apples. season it with pepper, salt, and ginger. then take a generous handful of raisins, and put all into a crust of fine pastry, with a piece of sweet butter, and bake it. but before you serve it, cut it into pieces, and squeeze in the juice of an orange, and sugar.

title: A Chewet of Stockefish.
text: boil flaked codfish until cooked through. once it is cold, take the whitest parts of the fish and mince them finely. add parboiled carrots and raisins. season with nutmeg, pepper, salt, and a piece of sweet butter. bake it, and before serving, cut it into pieces and squeeze in the juice of an orange.

title: A quarter Tart of Pippins.
text: quarter them and place between two sheets of pastry. add a piece of whole cinnamon, two or three crushed cloves, a little sliced ginger, orange zest, or just the yellow outside of an orange, a bit of sweet butter about the size of an egg, a generous amount of sugar, and sprinkle with a little rosewater. then close your tart and bake it. cool it before serving. this tart can be made with puff pastry or shortcrust pastry that won t rise. if you bake it in either of these kinds of pastry, first boil your apples in claret wine and sugar, otherwise the apples will be hard when the crust is burnt and dried out. furthermore, the wine gives them a pleasant color and a good taste too. though you boil the apples gently, be careful not to break the quarters, but bake them whole.

title: A Gooseberry Tart.
text: pick the stems of your gooseberries, and the seeds from the tops. put them in good paste, with a little green ginger, sliced. add a generous amount of sugar and rosewater, and then seal them.

title: A Cherry Tart.
text: bruise a pound of cherries and stamp them. boil the syrup with sugar. then remove the stones from two pounds, bake them in a small, deep dish, ice them, and serve them hot to the table.

title: To make an Oyster Pye.
text: take the liquid from your largest oysters, season them with pepper and ginger, and place them into a pie crust. add a minced onion, a few raisins, and a generous piece of butter. then pour in your syrup, and seal the pie. when baked, cut the pie and add a spoonful of vinegar and melted butter. stir well, and return it to the oven for a short while. take it out and serve.

title: A made Dish of Mussels and Cockles.
text: boil them, and remove the meat, washing it very clean in the water it was boiled in and a little white wine. chop the meat finely with two or three yolks of fresh eggs. season with pepper, salt, and a little nutmeg. then squeeze in the juice of an orange, and place them between two sheets of pastry. bake, freeze, and use as desired you may also fry them.

title:
To bake a Neates tongue to be
eaten hot.
text: boil it until tender, and peel off the skin, taking the flesh out from the bottom end. mince it finely with ox-tail and marrow. season it with pepper, salt, nutmeg, parboiled currants, and a minced date cut into pieces. take the yolks of two freshly laid eggs, and a spoonful of sweet cream, and mix all together with a silver spoon in a dish, adding a little powder from a dried orange peel. sprinkle a little verjuice over it, and sprinkle with sugar. then press it in as tightly as you can. bake it on a dish in the oven, basting it with sweet butter so that it doesn't dry out on the outside. when ready to eat, serve it with a sauce of vinegar and butter, nutmeg, sugar, and the juice of an orange.

title: A delicate Chewit.
text: boil a piece of veal leg, and once cold, mince it with beef, marrow, and an apple or two pear-plums. when you have minced it finely, add a few parboiled currants, six minced dates, a piece of candied orange peel minced, marrow cut into small square pieces. season all of this with pepper, salt, nutmeg, and a little sugar. then put it into your pastry shells, and bake it. before you close the pie, sprinkle on a little rosewater, and when they are baked, shave on a little sugar, and serve it to the table.

title:
To make an Vmble Pye, or for want of
Vmbles to doe it with a Lambes
head and Purtenance.
text: boil your meat until tender, then remove the flesh from the bone. finely mince it with beef suet and marrow, along with the liver, lungs, and heart. add a few sweet herbs and currants. season with pepper, salt, and nutmeg. bake it in a pastry crust shaped like a small pie, and it will taste very much like real umbles, so much so that you will hardly be able to tell the difference.

title: To bake a Calues Chaldron.
text: boil it, and cool it, and remove the kernels, then cut it into small pieces. season with pepper, salt, and nutmeg. add a few chopped sweet herbs, a piece of sweet butter, sprinkle with verjuice, and then seal it. when serving, add a little sauce made with nutmeg, vinegar, butter, sugar, the yolks of two fresh eggs, a spoonful of sack, and the juice of an orange.

title: To bake a Carpe.
text: scale, wash, and clean a fine large carp. season it with pepper, salt, and nutmeg, and place it in a baking dish with a generous amount of sweet butter. add large raisins and the juice of two oranges, ensuring the butter is on top to keep everything moist. sprinkle a little vinegar over it before covering, and then bake it.

title:
To bake a Tench with a Pudding in
her belly.
text: let the fish bleed from the tail, then scald and scrub it. wash it clean and dry it with a cloth. then take grated bread, sweet cream, the yolks of two or three fresh eggs, a few part-boiled currants, and a few sweet herbs, finely chopped. season it with nutmeg and pepper, and make it into a stiff pudding, and put it into the tench s belly. season your fish on the outside with a little pepper, salt, and nutmeg, and then put him in a deep dish, with a piece of sweet butter, and close your pie. bake it. then take it out of the oven and open it, and add a piece of preserved orange rind. then take vinegar, nutmeg, butter, sugar, and the yolk of a fresh egg, and boil it over a dish of embers, always stirring it to keep it from curdling. then pour it into your pie, mix it well together, and serve it in.

title: To bake Eeles.
text: cut your eels about the length of your finger. season them with pepper, salt, and ginger, and then place them into a dish with a generous piece of sweet butter. add to your pie large raisins and a finely minced onion, then seal it and bake it.

title: To bake Chickins with Grapes.
text: truss and scald your chickens, season them well with pepper, salt, and nutmeg, and place them in your pie with a generous piece of butter. bake it, then cut it open and place on the breasts of your chickens grapes boiled in vinegar, butter, nutmeg, and sugar, with the juice of an orange.

title:
To bake a Steake-Pye with a French
Pudding in the Pye.
text: season your steaks with pepper, salt, and nutmeg, and let them stand in a tray for an hour. then, take a piece of the leanest meat from a leg of mutton and mince it finely with ox suit, a few sweet herbs, tips of young thyme, a sprig of pennyroyal, two or three leaves of red sage, grated bread, egg yolks, sweet cream, and raisins. mix all together like a pudding with your hands until stiff, then roll it into balls and place them in the steaks within a deep dish. add a generous piece of sweet butter, sprinkle with verjuice, and bake. once baked, cut it up, roll sage leaves in butter, and fry them, sticking them upright around the dish. serve the pie uncovered, with the juice of an orange or lemon.

title: To make a good Quince Pye.
text: peel and core the quinces, taking care to remove as little of the fruit as possible since the best part is near the skin. fill them with sugar, then with as much sugar as they weigh. place the quinces with slices of ginger in a pie dish, sprinkle with a little rosewater before covering. bake until fully cooked, allowing them to soak in the oven for a long time. cool and serve.

title: To make a Pippin Pye.
text: take their weight in sugar, and stick a whole clove in every piece of them, and put in pieces of whole cinnamon. then put in all your sugar, with a slice or two of whole ginger. sprinkle rosewater on them before you close your pie bake them, and serve them in.

title: To bake a Pigge.
text: scald it, and split it in the middle, flay it, and take out the bones. season it with pepper, salt, cloves, mace, and nutmeg. chop sweet herbs finely, with the hard yolks of two or three newly laid eggs, and parboiled currants. then lay one half of your pig into your pie, and herbs on it. then put on the other half with more herbs on top of it, and a good piece of sweet butter on top of all. it is a good dish both hot and cold.

title:
To bake Fallow-Deere in the best
manner.
text: bake it first in its own blood, only wipe it clean, but do not wash it, bone it, and skin it, and season it with pepper and salt. then bake it in fine pastry afterward, puff-pastry or shortcrust pastry.

title: To bake redde Deere.
text: boil it, and press it, and let it sit overnight in red wine and vinegar. then lard it generously, and season it with pepper, salt, cloves, mace, nutmeg, and ginger. bake it in a deep crust of rye dough, with plenty of butter. let it soak well. leave a vent in your pie, and when you take it out of the oven, add melted butter, vinegar, nutmeg, ginger, and a little sugar. shake it together very well and put it back in the oven, and let it stand for at least three or four hours to soak thoroughly. when the oven is cool, take it out and seal the hole with butter.

title: To bake wilde Boare.
text: take the haunch of a smoked ham, and the tender fillets. partially boil it, then mince it finely and pound it in a mortar until it forms a paste, all in one mass. then lard it, and treat it like venison. beef fillets will also serve very well if needed.

title: To bake a Swan.
text: scald it, and remove the bones. then partially boil it, and season it well with pepper, salt, and ginger. then lard it, and place it in a deep crust of rye dough with plenty of butter. let it soak well when you take it out of the oven, put in more melted butter through the vent hole.

title: To bake a Turkey, or a Capon.
text: bone the turkey, but not the capon. part-boil them and stud cloves in their breasts. lard them and season them well with pepper and salt, and put them in a deep dish with the breast facing down, and plenty of butter. when it is baked, pour in more butter, and when it is cold, seal the vent hole with more butter.

title: To bake a Hare on the French fashion.
text: boil two hares, and take the meat from the bones, mincing it small and beating it into a coarse mixture. then sauce it with wine and vinegar, as you would red deer, and season it similarly. wrap all this meat around the backbone of one hare, so it appears as a single hare. lard it well, and place it in a baking dish with plenty of butter, and then bake it. remove it from the oven, and add a little melted butter, nutmeg, ginger, and sugar, then return it to the oven to absorb the mixture. when it is cold, seal the hole with butter.

title:
To bake a wilde Goose or
Mallard.
text: boil them, and break the breast bone of a large goose, or remove it entirely along with all the other bones, except those of a mallard. season them, and lard them, then place them in deep pastry shells with plenty of butter. when you take them from the oven, add more butter, and proceed as described.

title: To bake a Curlew or Hearneshoe.
text: dress them and partially boil them on one side. season them with pepper, salt, and ginger. place them in deep dishes, with plenty of butter, and let the heads stick out for display.

title:
To bake Woodcockes or
Blacke-Birds.
text: truss, parboil, and season them with pepper and salt. your woodcock may be larded proceed as with others.

title: Larkes, or Sparrowes.
text: serve them as previously described, as with woodcocks and blackbirds.

title: Fritters on the Court fashion.
text: take the curds of a sack posset, the yolks of six newly laid eggs, and the whites of two of them, fine flour, and make a thick batter cut a quince in small pieces season it with nutmeg, and a little pepper, put in a little strong ale, warm milk mix all together and put them into lard, neither too hot nor too cold. if your butter swim, it is good temper.

title:
To make Pancakes so crispe that you
may set them vpright.
text: make a dozen, or a score of them in a small frying pan, no bigger than a saucer, and then boil them in lard, and they will look as yellow as gold, besides the taste.

title:
A Sallet of Rose-buds, and cloue
Gilly-slowers. [=Gilly-flowers.]
text: pick rosebuds and put them into a small earthenware pot with white wine vinegar and sugar. you may also use cowslips, violets, or rosemary flowers in the same way.

title:
To keepe greene Cucumbers all
the yeere.
text: cut six cucumbers into pieces, boil them in spring water, sugar, and oil for a short while. take them up and let your pickle stand until it is cold.

title: To keepe Brome Capers.
text: boil the largest and firmest buds of the broccoli in wine vinegar and bay salt skim it clean. when it is cool, you may add raw buds as well, each separately. put a piece of lead on the raw buds all that float will turn black, and the others that are pressed down will be as green as any leek. the boiled buds will change color.

title: Purslaine stalkes.
text: gather them when they are fully grown, but not too old. parboil them, and keep them in white wine vinegar and sugar.

title:
To make Caper rowlers of
Radish cods.
text: take them when they are hard, and not overly ripe boil them gently in clear water, white wine vinegar, and bay salt together, and keep them in it.

title: Diuers Sallets boyled.
text: boil spinach and chop it finely, using the edges of two hard trenchers on a board or the backs of two chopping knives. then place them on a warming dish with butter and vinegar. season with cinnamon, ginger, sugar, and a few boiled currants. cut hard-boiled eggs into quarters to garnish, and serve on small toasted bread slices. you may also prepare borage, bugloss, endive, chicory, cauliflower, sorrel, marigold leaves, watercress, boiled leeks, onions, asparagus, rocket, and alexanders in the same way. boil them and season them all alike, whether with oil and vinegar or butter and vinegar, cinnamon, ginger, sugar, and butter. eggs are necessary, or at least very good for all boiled salads.

title: Buds of Hoppes.
text: simmer them with a little of the tender stalk in clear water, and place them in a dish over hot coals with butter, and serve them at the table.

title: A Sallet of Mallowes.
text: pluck the leaves from the tender stalks, keeping the tops. soak them in water and cook until tender, then place them in a dish over hot coals with butter and vinegar. let them sit for a while, then sprinkle grated bread and sugar between each layer.

title: A Sallet of Burdock rootes.
text: peel the fruit and soak it in water for at least an hour. when done, boil until tender. then place them on hot coals with butter and vinegar, and let them stand for a while. next, add grated bread and sugar, layering them between the fruit, and serve.

title:
To make blauncht Maunchet in
a Frying-pan.
text: take six eggs, half a pint of sweet cream, a small loaf of bread grated, a nutmeg grated, two spoonfuls of rosewater, and two ounces of sugar. beat all together until stiff, like a pudding. then fry it like a fritter in a very small frying pan, so that it may be thick. fry until browned, and turn it out onto a plate. cut it into quarters and serve it like a pudding, sprinkling with sugar.

title: A fierced Pudding.
text: mince a leg of mutton with sweet herbs. sift grated bread through a sieve, mince dates, currants, and raisins, add a little orange peel or preserved lemon, coriander seeds, nutmeg, ginger, and pepper. mix all together with milk and eggs, beaten raw like a paste. wrap the meat in a casing of mutton or veal, and then either boil or bake it. if you bake it, beat egg yolks with rosewater, sugar, and cinnamon. when it is almost baked, draw it out and stud it with cinnamon and rosemary.

title: A Pudding of Veale.
text: finely mince raw veal, and cut some lard into small diamond shapes. mince sweet marjoram, wild mint, chamomile, winter savory, nutmeg, pepper, ginger, and salt, heating them gently. prepare the intestines of a fat mutton hog, cutting them about an inch long. combine them with plenty of cinnamon and sugar, and sliced barberries and blanched almonds, along with half a pound of finely minced beef. stuff this mixture into the prepared casings. simmer them in a small pot of claret wine, with whole mace, a sliced lemon, and barberries tied in knots, or grapes. this is a delicate pudding.

title: A Fregesey of Egges.
text: beat a dozen eggs with cream, sugar, nutmeg, mace, and rosewater, and a pomewater cut crosswise in slices. put them into the frying pan with sweet butter, and the apples first. when they are almost done, take them up and clean your pan. put in sweet butter and make it hot. put in half the eggs and cream at one time. stir it with a saucer, or something similar. take it out and put it in a dish. put in the rest of the eggs and cream, like the first time, and then put in your apples all around the batter. then flip it over on top and keep it from burning with sweet butter. when it is fried on both sides enough, squeeze on the juice of an orange, and serve it.

title: A Cambridge Pudding.
text: sift grated bread through a sieve, mince it with flour, dates, raisins, nutmeg, cinnamon, and pepper, mix well. add sweet milk, warm, fine sugar, and eggs remove some of the whites, and combine all ingredients thoroughly. take half of the pudding and place it on one side, and the other half on the other side, forming it into a loaf shape. then, place butter in the center of the pudding, and top with the remaining half. boil your liquid, and place the pudding, tied in a clean cloth, into the boiling liquid. once boiled through, cut it in the middle, and serve.

title: A Swanne or Goose Pudding.
text: stir the blood of a swan or goose, steep fine oatmeal in milk, nutmeg, pepper, sweet herbs, and a little salt. mix all together with rosewater and lemon peel, finely minced. add a small quantity of coriander seeds. this method applies to grated bread pudding or any other pudding served with swan or goose.

title:
A Liueridge or Hogges
Pudding.
text: boil a pig's liver well, let it be completely cold. then grate it like bread. grate bread, take fresh milk, the pig's fat rendered very finely, and put it with the bread and the liver the more fat, the better. divide the mixture into two parts. take a generous amount of dried herbs, minced very finely, and put them into one part, along with nutmeg, mace, pepper, anise seeds, rosewater, cream, and eggs. wash the animal casings, and then fill them up, and let them boil until done. to the other mixture, add barberries, sliced dates, currants, fresh milk, and eggs, and work them as the first.

title: A Chiueridge Pudding.
text: prepare the fattest intestines of your hog in cold water and salt to clean them. take the longest and fattest intestine, beginning in the middle, and stuff it with nutmeg, sugar, ginger, pepper, and sliced dates. boil it and serve to the table.

title: A Ryce Pudding.
text: soak it in clear water overnight. then boil it in fresh milk, and drain the milk through a strainer. mince beef finely, but not too small, and add it to the rice, along with partially cooked currants, egg yolks from newly laid eggs, nutmeg, cinnamon, sugar, and barberries. mix everything together. wash your cleaned hog casings, and stuff them with the mixture. partially boil them, and let them cool.

title: A Florentine of Veale.
text: finely grind cold veal, then take grated bread, raisins, dates, sugar, nutmeg, and pepper. add two or three eggs and rosewater, mixing all together well. place the mixture on a chafing dish over hot coals, stirring until warmed. then, put some between two sheets of puff pastry and bake it. spread the remaining mixture on slices of white bread and fry in a frying pan that has been wiped with egg yolk. serve with cinnamon and ginger as a second course.

title: A Marrow toast.
text: boil minced veal and very finely chopped sweet herbs separately, then mix them together with sugar, nutmeg, cinnamon, rosewater, grated bread, and the yolks of two or three fresh eggs. open the minced meat and cover it with marrow. then put your toast into a small pot with some rich broth. let it boil with whole mace, a bundle of sweet herbs, skimming it very clean, and let it simmer until almost dry. then add boiled potatoes, chestnuts, skirrots, or almonds boiled in white wine if you don't have wine, use verjuice and sugar.

title: Another in a Frying-pan.
text: take the marrow whole out of the bone as near as you can. ten oysters are a suitable proportion for that marrow, after it has been partially boiled, trimmed, and cut into small pieces. add a little young thyme and parsley, finely minced. mix all together like batter. then roll the marrow within that mixture, and season it with pepper, salt, and nutmeg. next, form it into small patties with fine pastry, shaped like pea pods. fry them, sprinkle with sugar, and serve.

title:
A Pudding stued betweene two
Dishes.
text: take the yolks of three eggs, and the white of one, half a dozen spoonfuls of sweet cream, a nutmeg grated, a few cloves and mace, a quarter of a pound of beef suet minced, a quarter of a pound of currants, temper it like a pudding with grated bread, and a spoonful of rosewater. then take a coil of veal, cut it in square pieces like trenchers, lay three spoonfuls of the batter upon one side, then roll it up in the veal pin one side over the other with two small pricks, and tie each end with a thread. you may put two, three, or four of them in a dish, then take half a pint of strong mutton broth, and half a dozen spoonfuls of vinegar, three or four blades of mace, and an ounce of sugar. make this broth to boil upon a chafing dish of coals, and then put in your pudding when it boils, cover it with another

title:
To make French puffes with greene
Hearbes.
text: take spinach, parsley, endive, and a sprig or two of savory. mince them very finely, season them with nutmeg, ginger, and sugar. moisten them with eggs, according to the quantity of the herbs, more or less. then take the zest of a lemon, cut it in thin round slices. put one spoonful of this mixture on each slice of lemon. fry it with sweet lard in a frying pan, as you fry eggs, and serve them with toasted bread or without. sprinkle them either with white wine or sack, or any other wine, except rhine wine. serve them either at dinner or supper.

title: Dropt Razins.
text: take the finest raisins, slit them on one side, and lay them open as round and as broad as you can. then take of the aforementioned herbs, minced and seasoned, and lay between two raisins as many as you can close between them. take half a spoonful of the same stuff that you fried your lemons with, and fry them brown.

title: A fond Pudding.
text: take either mutton, veal, or lamb, roasted or raw, but raw is better. grind it finely with beef suet, then take spinach, parsley, marigold, endive, a sprig of thyme, and a sprig of savory. chop these finely and season them with nutmeg, sugar, and minced dates. add currants and grated bread, the yolks of three or four fresh eggs, a spoonful or two of rosewater, and as much verjuice. mix them well, shaping them into the forms of birds, beasts, fish, pears, or whatever you desire. fry or bake them and serve on toasted bread, with verjuice or white wine, butter, and sugar. serve them at either dinner or supper.

title:
To make Puffes, on the English
fashion.
text: take fresh milk curds, press out all the whey. take the yolks of three eggs and the white of one, and mix fine wheat flour among the curds. season with nutmeg, sugar, and rosewater, mixing all together. butter a clean white paper, place a spoonful at a time on it, and set them in a warm oven, not too hot. when they rise as high as a half-penny loaf, brush with rosewater and butter. sprinkle with sugar and return them to the oven until the tops are dried like ice. then take them out and serve on a plate, either at dinner or supper.

title:
To make a Pudding in a 
Frying-panne.
text: take four eggs, two spoonfuls of rosewater, nutmeg grated, sugar, and grated bread the quantity of a penny loaf. also, half a pound of beef suet, minced fine. work these ingredients together as firmly as you would a pudding with your hands, and place the mixture in a frying pan with sweet butter. fry until browned, then cut into quarters and serve hot, either at dinner or supper. if it is a fasting day, leave out the suet and currants, and add two or three pomewaters minced small, or any other soft apple that has a good flavor.

title: To make Apple pufs.
text: take a pear or any other apple that is not hard or harsh in taste mince it finely with a dozen or twenty raisins. moisten the apples with two eggs, beating them all together with the back of a knife or a spoon. season them with nutmeg, rosewater, sugar, and ginger drop them into a frying pan with a spoon, and fry them like eggs. squeeze in the juice of an orange or lemon, and serve.

title: To make Kicks-Hawes.
text: take the kidney of a veal, or lamb, or if you have neither, then take the ear of a mutton, fat and all. boil it and mince it finely, seasoning it with nutmeg, pepper, and salt. then take two or three eggs, a spoonful of rosewater, two or three spoonfuls of sack, and as much grated bread as will bind them like lithpaste. then flour your molds and fill them with that paste. then roll a thin sheet of paste, wet it and cover it over. fry them and turn them into small dishes, keeping them warm in the oven, to serve at dinner or supper. if you wish to bake them, you may turn them into the dish raw, out of your molds, and glaze them with rosewater and sugar, and set them in the oven when your pies are half-baked.

title:
To make some Kickshawes in Paste, to
Frye or Bake, in what forme
you please.
text: make some puff pastry, roll it thinly. if you have any molds, you may shape it over them, filling with the pulp of apples, seasoned with cinnamon, ginger, sugar, and rosewater. seal them up and bake or fry them. alternatively, fill them with gooseberries, seasoned with sugar, cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg. roll them up in egg yolks, and this will prevent the marrow from melting when boiled. or, fill them with curds boiled with egg whites and cream, or colored yellow with egg yolks and cream, creating a tender curd. season the curd with a few parboiled currants, three or four sliced dates, or six pieces of marrow about the size of a half walnut. add small pieces of almond paste, sugar, rosewater, and nutmeg. this filling will work for any of these pastries, either baked or as a florentine in puff pastry. you may fry or bake any of these for dinner or supper.

title: To make an Italian Pudding.
text: take a white loaf, remove the crust, and cut it into square pieces like large dice. mince a pound of beef very finely. take half a pound of raisins, remove the stones, and mix them together. season them with sugar, rosewater, and nutmeg. moisten these ingredients with four eggs and stir them very gently to soak the bread. then place it in a dish, and add three or four pieces of marrow and some sliced dates. bake in a moderately hot oven. if the oven is too hot, it will burn if too cold, it will be heavy. when baked, sprinkle with sugar and serve hot at dinner, but not at supper.

title:
To boyle a Rack of Veale on the
French fashion.
text: cut it into steaks, cut a carrot or turnip into pieces, like diamonds, and put them into a small pot with a pint of white wine, parsley tied in a bundle, a little rosemary, and ground mace, and a cinnamon stick. peel a lemon or orange, and add a little coarse pepper, half a pound of butter. boil all together until tender. when done, add a little sugar and verjuice. garnish your dish as you like.

title:
To fearce a Legge of Lambe, on
the French fashion.
text: take the meat from inside the casing and leave the skin whole. finely chop it with suet. add grated bread, finely minced orange zest, sliced nutmeg, coriander seeds, picked barberries, and a little pepper. mix all together with egg yolks, like a pudding, and return it to the casing. if you wish to seal it with a mutton broth, take the yolk of an egg and spread it over the top, and it will hold it securely. then place it in a dish and set it upright, adding a little butter to the dish. place the dish in the oven. add sugar, currants, and sliced dates, salt, and verjuice. when serving, sprinkle it with egg yolks and parsley, either separately or together.

title:
To hash Deere, Sheepe, or Calues
tongues, on the French
fashion.
text: boil, blanch, and lard them, stick them with cloves and rosemary, and put them on a spit until they are half roasted. then put them into a small pot with claret wine, cinnamon, ginger, sugar, sliced lemon, a few caraway seeds, and large mace. boil all together and serve them with fried toast.

title: To boyle a Capon.
text: take a rich broth made from marrow bones or any other flavorful broth. place the marrow in a small pot with salt. boil the capon in the pot, skimming it clean before removing it. add salt. use a pint of white wine for each capon increase the wine if you have more capon. add half a pound of sugar, a quarter of a pound of sliced dates, boiled and blanched potatoes, and generous amounts of mace and sliced nutmeg. if you lack potatoes, use jerusalem artichokes, and if you have neither, boil and blanch skirrets instead. boil all these ingredients together with a quarter pint of verjuice and egg yolks. strain the mixture, stir it well, and add it to the capon and the rich broth.

title: To garnish your Dishes.
text: garnish your dishes with fine sugar, using orange slices dipped among biscuits and caraway seeds. take a pomegranate and garnish the side of your dish with it. use currants and prunes, wrapping them in fine sugar after they have been gently boiled in clear water. add lemon slices to your dish, along with large mace steeped or boiled, or preserved barberries. any of these are suitable for garnishing. remove the capon from the broth and place it in a dish with toasted bread cubes, surrounded by these garnishes.

title: To boyle a Capon another way.
text: boil a knuckle of veal until it makes a strong broth. then take your capon and boil it in clean water and salt, and when it is almost boiled, take it and put it in a small pot, and strain your broth into the capon. then wash and scrape parsley, and clean fennel roots, remove the core, and slice them lengthwise. boil them in a skillet of water, and when they are half boiled, take them from the fire and put them in a strainer, and then in a clean small pot. then take a little rosewater and a quarter of a pound of fine sugar until it is as clear as glass. then take a little ground mace, a bundle of sweet herbs, a small lemon with the peel removed, and boil a few raisins in the sun with it. but first, take out your capon and strain the broth. put the capon into a dish very finely garnished, then pour the broth over the capon. then take parsley

title: To boyle a Capon in Rice.
text: boil a capon in salt and water. if you like it, you may put into a fine cloth a handful of oatmeal. then take a quarter of a pound of rice and soak it in clean water, and then half boil it. strain the rice through a colander. then boil the rice in a small pot with a quart of milk. add half an ounce of mace and half a pound of sugar. boil it well, but not too thick. add a little rosewater. blanch half a pound of almonds and beat them in a mortar with a little cream and rosewater. beat them fine and strain them into a small pot by itself. then take up your capon and set your almonds near the fire. garnish your dish as you think fit, and lay in your capon, and put your rice neatly upon the capon, and then the broth upon the rice.

title:
To boyle a Capon with Oysters, and
pickled Lemmons.
text: partly boil the chicken until almost cooked, with fresh water and salt. then strain some of the broth into a quart of sparkling wine. add a few sweet herbs, muddled with a pickled lemon or orange, and put everything into a small pot and let it simmer. next, prepare the oysters, removing any tough bits, and blanch them briefly. transfer them from the broth to a strainer, then into the small pot. add a few raisins and, if you like, the juice of an onion first boil some onions separately, strain them, and then add them to the pot. serve with any garnish you have.

title: To boyle a Capon with Pippins.
text: boil it as before, then put two marrow bones into a small pot, or rather the marrow of two or three bones into a small pot, with a quart of white wine, a little sliced nutmeg, and half a dozen dates. when you have done so, add a quarter of a pound of sugar. then peel your apples, and cut them into quarters, and put them into a small pot, covering them with a little rosewater and sugar, and boil them. then take crumbs of biscuit, and if you do not have that, use other bread. next, boil seven or eight hard eggs, remove the yolks and put them in a strainer. then take a little lemon juice, and strong broth from where the capon is boiling, strain it, and put it in a small pot, and stir all together with the apples and muscat. add the muscat when the apples are cold.

title:
To boyle Chickins in
White-broth.
