text: to make ravioli with herbs or another filling, clean and wash the herbs well. then let them sit a bit, drain them thoroughly, and chop them finely with a knife. afterwards, in a mortar, combine with fresh, strained cheese, eggs, and sweet and strong spices, mixing well to form a paste. then make the dough thinly, like lasagna, take a small piece, and shape the ravioli. when they are ready, cook them and, when cooked through, sprinkle with spices and season with good salt. they are delicious.

title:
LXIV. Rafioli per altro modo
e chiamasse licaproprii. (?)
text: take fresh, very sweet cheese and drain it well, then press it. add egg white and gently mix in a little flour. have clarified goose fat ready and form the liche with well-floured hands, making them large and round like apples, that is, pears. fry them over low heat when cooked, remove them from the fat and generously dust with sugar. serve hot.

title: LXV. Rapa armata.
text: to make a dressed turnip, cook the turnip in the fire once cooked, peel it and then cut it into thin slices. with sweet cheese, cut thin slices and between each slice of turnip place a slice of cheese and leave it like this to blend together well. if you wish, you can put a hot plate on top and it will be done then sprinkle with powdered sugar, etc.

title: LXVI. Rosto in cisame bono e perfetto optimo.
text: to make roast in sauce, you need a pork loin and roast it, then add raw and cooked eggs and pound them together. add good white wine and vinegar, bring to a boil in a pan, and add pieces of the roast, letting them boil with it. add finely chopped parsley, pine nuts, and washed black currants, and spices when cooked, remove from the heat and it will be good.

title: LXVII. Savore rinforzato perfetto.
text: to make a strong flavoring, take cloves, cinnamon, ginger, and a little garden thyme, and roast them over hot embers. add a little ground bread and sugar pound these ingredients together a bit, then mix with vinegar. this is a good flavoring with any roast.

title: LXVIII. Savore a caponi.
text: to flavor capons, use lean meat and roast it. then, use chicken livers and roast them as well, pounding them and grinding them with cloves. add nutmeg and ginger, and then, if desired, dilute with vinegar, white wine, and water. if you wish, add some of the hot fat from the roast and cook it with this flavoring, mitigating the sweetness as much as possible.

title:
LXIX. Savor de zenzevro biancho
a caponi.
text: to make a white sauce of ginger, take white ginger and parsley, well cleaned, and some spinach and sage, also well cleaned. combine these ingredients and add as much sugar as needed, blending this flavor with verjuice and white vinegar. this sauce is best served raw with roast chickens and capons.

title: LXX. Savore aranzato.
text: to make a flavorful orange preserve to last the whole year, and to serve with any roast or create any flavor you desire take a large quantity of oranges and wash them well with good wine, along with a certain amount of salt. when they are well washed, add four parts of sugar. use the best wine you can find, a large barrel s worth, and pour it over the oranges. quarter them and add a generous amount of salt. keep it well-maintained so it doesn t mold it will be perfectly good, truly excellent.

title:
LXXI. Sambugado zoè lacte
con fior de sambuco.
text: to make sambuco cordial, you need clear sheep s milk, elderflower blossoms, and blend them together in the milk. let it blend for a while, then strain it. for a quarter of milk, use twelve eggs and beat them together. add them to boil and stir constantly.

title:
LXXII. Sambugado per dare in schudelli
perfettissimo e vantazato.
text: to make sambuco for serving in bowls, for twelve people, you will need a pot of fresh sheep s or goat s milk, one pound of rice, one and a half pounds of lard, three ounces of sugar, and the elderflower blossoms, fully ripe, and some milk that you have strained. bring the milk to a boil, and when it has boiled, the first thing you add is the pounded rice, the second is the elderflower blossoms, the third is the shredded lard, and the fourth is the sugar. add a pinch of saffron, tempered. this dish should be hot, thick, sweet, and flavorful with elderflower.

title: LXXIII. Specie fine a tute cosse.
text: take one ounce of pepper and one of cinnamon, one of ginger and half a quarter of cloves, and a quarter of saffron.

title:
LXXIV. Specie dolce per assay cosse
bone e fine.
text: to make the best sweet ending, whether for lamprey in crust or other good freshwater fish cooked in crust, and also for a good broth and flavor, take a quarter of cloves and an ounce of good ginger, and take an ounce of ground cinnamon, and take as much nutmeg as you like. grind all these spices together as you please, and if you want to make more, use the same proportions, and it will be wonderfully good.

title: LXXV. Specie negre e forte per assay savore.
text: a strong and flavorful spice blend half a quarter of cloves and eleven of pepper. and a good amount of long pepper and a pinch of nutmeg, making a blend of all spices.

title: LXXVI. Stuffà molto breve perfettissima.
text: to make a very quick stew, take six quail and brown them in lard. remove any excess lard add almond milk tempered with verjuice, some ginger chopped finely, and dates, sliced into quarters. color this dish with saffron and make sure it is well salted.

title: LXXVII. Spalle de castron implite.
text: to make castron shoulders filling for two or four, lift the castron shoulders with all the shanks. if it s for 20 people, use 3 for 40 people, use 6. if it s for more or fewer people, use the same proportion. take four castron nets, 4 pints of castron broth, 6 pounds of pork loin, one large pork liver, and its net, 20 fresh mushrooms, the best you can find, 37 eggs, 1 pound of raisins, ½ pound of sugar, ½ ounce of cinnamon, ½ ounce of fresh ginger, ½ quarter of cloves, and have ½ pound of fine, warm sweet spice made, and ½ pound of strong spice. take the shoulders and shanks to boil whole and cook them well, but not so much that the bones separate. take them out and remove as much meat as possible, beat it well, and add plenty of parsley, sage,

title: LXXVIII. Salamura de anguille optima.
text: roast the eels and place them under a pan with water in which all the fat will simmer as they roast when they are cooked, add strong spices and salt, and put them in this water and fat, shredding the eels and mixing them with the marinade. if you wish to add a little cooked wine, it will give them a good flavor.

title: LXXIX. Savore a çiascuna carne.
text: to flavor the aforementioned grated dish, with or without meat, using beaten eggs and almond milk, slightly sour. others add bread and rose water, broth, and loosen everything together, especially sweetening it, and boil everything together, adding a little saffron or beet juice, frequently.

title: LXXX. Savore de pesse.
text: to make a dish with a delightful flavor called sabeto, fry some small pasta in good oil, add dried grapes and mash it with verjuice and vinegar. add onion and cook it, then chop it with a knife. fry it with that flavor and add spices, but no saffron, and plenty of galangal. make sure it's slightly acidic, but not too much.

title:
LXXXI. Salza verde a capreto
e ad altre carne alesse.
text: rub with pepper, ginger, cloves, and cinnamon, and a little salt, and sugar. combine everything together and mix with good vinegar make sure it's well blended and doesn't separate, or it will spoil.

title:
LXXXII. Salsa bona a carne de castron
o de capreto.
text: the best sauce you can make for this meat, whether it's roasted or grilled. it's made with lean meat, well-cooked and well-beaten, pounded in a mortar with plenty of parsley, mint, sage, rosemary, and other good herbs that you may have, seasoned with nutmeg, cinnamon, cloves, and pepper. thin this sauce with the finest vinegar you have.

title: LXXXIII. Savore de ruga overo Rochetta.
text: grind the seeds of arugula and almonds. then add cooked sugar and ginger and walnuts, mashed together and seasoned with everything. temper with good vinegar and it is good with any meat, excellent.

title: LXXXIV. Savore tartaresco perfettissimo.
text: boil the almonds in water. add lemon zest, ginger, cloves, sugar, and cooked egg yolks. mix everything together and temper with vinegar. this has a good flavor, similar to roast pork or other meats.

title: LXXXV. Savore a carne alessa overo arosto.
text: to make seasoned salmon, grind basil and almonds, ginger, and nutmeg with sugar and marzipan, combining all ingredients and mixing with vinegar. this has a good flavor with castrated lamb, veal, or roast.

title: LXXXVI. Savore confetto, etc.
text: to make a sweet confection of bread and roast pork and mussels soaked in vinegar with cloves and candied ginger, cinnamon, nutmeg, and cardamom, sugar, and marzipan, combine all ingredients and mix with saffron and good wine, and it is done.

title: LXXXVII. Savore de gambari.
text: shrimp chowder. listen. take shrimp and boil them, then remove the peeled tails. grind the rest well, adding a little water, then strain it. add a little good herbs and red saffron, and almonds or breadcrumbs, pounded very finely in a mortar and thinned with verjuice add a little water so it s not too acidic, and add sweet and strong spices and oil. add the shrimp tails and put them in that flavor you ve made, and boil when it suits you.

title: LXXXVIII. Salsa sarasinesca.
text: to make a sarasinesque sauce with almonds, raisins, ginger, cinnamon, and cloves, and apples, marzipan, galangal, and nutmeg mix everything together and thin with verjuice this is good flavor.

title: LXXXIX. Savore a tute carne grossa.
text: to make good, rich gravy, start with meat and simmer it. then add parsley and fry it in pork fat. add the meat in small pieces and fry well with the parsley. next, add almond milk, egg yolks, saffron, lemon zest, and sweet spices, and beat them together. pour this mixture over the meat. this is good with any other meat.

title: XC. Salsa a ziaschaduna carne.
text: first, finely chop some fennel flowers, then a hard-boiled egg and rosemary. mix everything together and it will be delicious.

title: XCI. Savore camelino optimo.
text: to make a very flavorful almond confection, grind almonds and marzipan together, then add raisins, cinnamon, and cloves. add a little flour and marzipan, all ground into a powder, and moisten with grape must. it is done.

title: XCII. Sartramone overo savore d' ogni carne.
text: to make a good meat or fish sauce, chop and boil the onion, then fry it in pork fat. next, add well-beaten eggs and mix in sweet and strong spices, saffron, and cloves. ensure it's quite thick this is a good flavor for any meat.

title: XCIII. Salviata.
text: chop the sage and pound it in a mortar and pestle. make the sauce whisk in eggs and beat well with the sauce. then add the cheese, a ladle or bowl of strained broth, and place it over the heat. add the pounded sage inside and stir frequently until it thickens and is perfectly delicious.

title: XCIV. Torta de pesse.
text: roast three large thornback rays or one large eel. and three ounces of finely chopped parsley, half a pound of raisins, three ounces of ground pine nuts, and three ounces of sweet and strong spices. then wash and dry the ray well, fillet it, and remove all the pulp. grind this pulp coarsely, and also grind some parsley and marjoram leaves, fine oil, and the spices well. from this mixture, make long, ravioli-shaped sausages and fry them in plenty of boiling oil. then take the remaining ray and boil it with some parsley. when it is cooked through, grind it all up, except for the head, add spices and oil, and grind it again. from this mixture, make small ravioli with thin pasta and fry them in oil. dust with spices. this pie is best cooked in an oven.

title: XCV. Torta de herbe.
text: to make a herb tart for twelve people, you will need large molds and a large quantity of herbs that is, chard, parsley, spinach, and mint and two pounds of salted pork fat and eight eggs. mix these herbs well, beating and squeezing them to remove the juice. mix the cheese with the herbs, coarsely chopped, and the pork fat, which you should beat as much as you can. add the eggs and mix all these ingredients together. place the mixture inside two crusts in a baking dish and cover with another crust on top. this tart is often fatty and flavorful with cheese and plenty of herbs. if you are making it for fewer people, adjust the ingredients accordingly.

title: XCVI. Torteleti de enula, etc.
text: to make endive tortelli with broth, for twelve people, you will need two capons or a pound and a half of pork loin, three bundles of fine pasta, three ounces of fine, sweet and strong spices, well mixed and sifted, two measures of endive, twenty eggs, and the pork loin. put the pork loin to simmer with the endive, which should be well cleaned. when both are cooked, mash the pork loin and endive together, but don't use all of the endive. take the amount you have and pound it with the pork loin, adding the spices and eggs within, enough to bind it well, ensuring it doesn't taste too much of endive. combine everything together, making a smooth paste, and then make small tortelli, using sheets of rolled pasta. these tortelli should be well seasoned and flavorful with spices.

title: XCVII. Torta de gambari vantagiata.
text: prepare the prawns, removing the tails and taking out the flesh. then, finely chop some fresh herbs and pound them well. mix this pounded mixture with almond milk and a fine spice blend, raisins, and form a tart with thin pastry crusts. the top should be generously sprinkled with sweet spices and raisins, while the filling should be very smooth.

title: XCVIII. Torta de fongi bona e perfettissima.
text: to make a mushroom tart, you will need whole mushrooms, about a pound, washed well, cut into large pieces, and pressed to remove excess water. rendered and drained pork fat, chopped parsley, and a few mussels to cook with the mushrooms, along with a little water to prevent sticking. once the mushrooms are cooked, drain them in a bowl and mix with a generous amount of cheese and eggs. beat this mixture and place it in a pastry crust, which should be very thin, smooth, and rich in flavor. add mushrooms, a little pork fat, and eggs, and bake well.

title: XCIX. Torta sambugata, etc.
text: elderflower cake for twelve people. take a large bowl and combine two pounds of fresh pork, twelve eggs, three ounces of sugar, ripe elderflower blossoms, well-drained ricotta cheese, the egg and sugar mixture, a generous amount of butter, and elderflower blossoms. mix these ingredients together, place them in a crust, and this cake should be rich and sweet and delicious.

title: C. Torta in balconata per dodeze persone.
text: use the whitest flour you can find. in quantity of three pounds or eleven ounces of sugar and one pound of almonds, thirty-six good walnuts, half a pound of raisins, twenty-five dates, and a half quarter of cloves, and a good quantity of almond milk, and the flour that you have ground with water so that it is well thickened, and a pan greased well with oil. from this flour make a crust with a dusting of sugar and the aforementioned spices, and the walnuts finely chopped, the raisins well washed, and the cloves. spread all these ingredients evenly, then place a crust on top of everything, so that it forms a cake.

title: CI. Torta de faro, etc.
text: to make a barley cake for twelve people, you will need two pounds of barley, two pounds of lard, and a quarter of a jug of sheep s or goat s milk. also, six fresh cheeses, and eggs. use finely ground and well-washed barley and bring it to a boil in water. when it is well-boiled, drain the water forcefully so that it breaks and crumbles. when it is well crumbled, add the well-beaten lard, the cheese well-pounded, and the milk you have, and the eggs, mixing all these ingredients thoroughly. place the mixture between two crusts in a warm dish. this cake should be very rich and it is delicious.

title: CII. Torta de schalogne o de cepolle, etc.
text: if you want to make a cake with these two things, beat the water well with yeast and then beat the lard until smooth and fluffy add the eggs and fresh cheese and saffron and beat together and make the cake.

title: CIII. Torta de caxo e ova senza lardo.
text: chop the meat into small cubes. put it in a bowl with eggs and plenty of butter either cured or fresh, or fatty but without lard and add seasoning. make thin crusts and bake the tart.

title: CIV. Torta communa e bona, etc.
text: first, pound the pork loin until it's well-mashed, then place it in a bowl. add fresh cheese and mix well. include sweet and strong spices, ground pine nuts, raisins, and saffron. moisten with egg. for three pounds of meat, use five ounces of cheese.

title: CV. Torta d' agli, etc.
text: peel and crush the beets and boil them. when cooked, drain them in cold water and mash. add saffron, fresh cheese, chopped lard, sweet and strong spices, and temper with eggs and dried fruit. then, make the tart.

title: CVI. Torta de late.
text: grate the cheese and egg yolks. add herbs and beat with the eggs. dilute with milk and make the crust as previously described.

title: CVII. Torta de zuche seche.
text: sauté the squash and mash it well. then, season the lard generously, place it in a bowl next, add three portions of cheese, pepper, and saffron, mix into a paste and thin with eggs, then bake into a tart.

title: CVIII. Torta de faxolli freschi.
text: boil the beans and cook them with pork belly. then mash the beans in a mortar and chop the pork belly with a knife. add the best spices you have and plenty of cheese, at least half or a third of the amount of the chopped ingredients. add aged lard and form the tart it will be perfect.

title: CIX. Torta de fave fresche optima bona.
text: cake of fresh fava beans, manfredo style shell the fava beans and cook them in good milk. then mash them, and add cooked pork belly, chopped with a knife. mix the fava beans and meat together, adding sweet and strong spices, saffron, and place in a bowl. add pieces of good fresh cheese and make a thick paste. then shape the cake and place it in the milk, within the paste, and on top, add slices of sweet, rich cheese.

title: CX. Torta francescha bona e optima.
text: grind the pork leg meat, ensuring it's a mix of lean and fatty portions, very finely with a knife. blend in sweet and strong spices, then temper with eggs and form it into a pie. sprinkle with saffron and bake thoroughly.

title: CXI. Torta manfreda bona e vantagiata.
text: mix chicken livers and kidneys with a knife, then season with pepper. rinse them and let them freeze, then take them out, let them cool, then add eggs and make a crust, then place them in a pan and fry gently.

title: CXII. Torta parmesana bona.
text: parmesan cake for twenty-five people. take eight pounds of pork loin and twelve fresh caks, and six bunches of parsley and twenty-seven and a half pounds of sweet spices, and six chickens and four capons. take the pork loin, trim it well, and when it s cooked, beat it with that quantity of mint and parsley. take six fresh caks and twenty-four eggs, as many as you have, and salted lard as much as needed, well beaten, and spices and saffron in abundance. from these ingredients, make a good, well-seasoned paste. remove two fresh caks and egg whites and pound them together, making eight white ravioli with pasta crusts. take two fresh caks, one bunch of parsley, and mint, and pound them together, making twelve green ravioli. take four caks and slice them beautifully across. take the chickens and dismantle them, making one member into two, and fry them in salted lard, well

title: CXIII. Torta ungaresca per xii persone.
text: take one plump capon and one large pork loin, two large onions, and half a pound of sweet, fine spices. also take three pounds of fresh butter, unsalted, and as much flour as three loaves, the best you can get. cut the capon and pork loin into small pieces, and the two onions into small pieces. place these ingredients in a bowl with plenty of fresh broth, along with the sweet spices, saffron, and a little salt. when well-simmered, add a cup of water and let it cook until tender. remove the flour and dissolve it with fresh, salted water. beat it vigorously, and when well-beaten, take a well-tinned wooden mold. grease it well with the fresh lard you have. add the pastry and knead it, then roll it out thinly with a rolling pin, making it very thin. have two people roll it out into very thin sheets with lard, and continue until you have eighteen sheets. then

title: CXIV. Torta de Romania.
text: to make romanian cake for twelve people, remove the chickens and 4 fresh or dried cheeses, 12 eggs, 3 pounds of raisins, 1 pound of currants, ½ ounce of cinnamon, ½ ounce of ginger, ½ quarter of cloves, ½ of saffron, 2 ounces of pine nuts, 4 ounces of sweet spices, well ground take these chickens, well washed and cleaned, and set them to fry in rendered lard, strained. the first time you add them, use the sweet spices, and take the fresh cheese that you have and make small ravioli as many as you can, and boil them in water. when they are cooked, powder them with finely ground spices, and when the chickens are fried, add a little water, and when they are cooked, add a strained cheese and 8 egg yolks, cinnamon and red ginger add the cloves and pine nuts, raisins well washed, and spices

title:
CXV. Tortelli a modo de fritelle bianche
per quaressema bone.
text: to make white tortelli for twelve people, you will need one pound of almonds and a quarter pound of walnuts, and half a pound of sugar. grind the almonds finely and the walnuts finely, and pound them together with sugar as you go. from this mixture, form small fritters. take flour and saffron and mix them with water until the dough is soft and smooth, then wrap it inside the tortelli and fry them in good oil, dusting them with powdered sugar. serve immediately with the other dishes.

title:
CXVI. Tortelli a modo de fritelle bianche
per quaressema bone e perfettissime.
text: take a good amount of cooked squash, the same amount of peeled and ground almonds, a generous amount of chopped herbs, a good amount of oil, and spices. combine these ingredients into a paste, form small tortelli, frizelli, and other shapes, then fry them in oil and sprinkle with powdered sugar. it is done.

title: CXVII. Tredura.
text: to make tredura, take the white part of the leeks and simmer them in broth. then, chop them well with a knife and fry them with the fat from the meat you ve roasted. add bread and grated cheese and moisten with hot water. add a piece of meat and chop the bread and meat together with a knife. then add beaten eggs and saffron, beat them together and pour over the fried leeks with spices. it will be delicious.

title: CXVIII. Vivanda da fare bon stomacho.
text: peel and core the quince and grind them. add almond milk and blend with the quince. cook over low heat. when cooked, add a little sweet spice and sugar to taste.

title: CXIX. Vivanda ditta limonia.
text: to prepare this dish for twelve people, you will need six plump chickens, seven capons, three ounces of fine spices, three ounces of almonds, three ounces of fine sugar, twenty-five dates, and twelve oranges that are well juicy, and half a pound of plums. first, boil the poultry you have. when it is cooked, add one pound of rendered lard, well-strained, and fry the poultry. once fried, add this powdered mixture of the aforementioned spices and sugar, and the almonds, which you have washed and ground well, and tempered with the broth from the capons, which should be thin and well-strained. add this mixture to a pot to simmer. before it boils, add some of the spices, then the plums, well-washed, and then the dates, well-washed, or half of them. then add saffron, tempered. when the dish is boiling, place the capons and oranges inside, along with a

title: CXX. Vino cocto.
text: to make spiced wine, take the finest red wine you can find and good honey. simmer them together with a little cinnamon flower, and boil until the volume reduces to a third. for four cups of wine, use one cup of honey.

title: CXXI. Zuche.
text: to make good zucchini fritters, dry the coins and cook them well in oil, not too much peel and grate the almonds and put them inside the zucchini, then make them white, or whisk them and add raisins.

title: CXXII. Polastri afenochiati vantazati.
text: roast squabs for twelve people. twelve squabs and six capons prepared like squabs. chop, remove the squabs and sauté them in lard. cook well and drain, removing the beards that is, the roots of fennel and parsley, well washed and sautéed with the squabs and three ounces of fine spices and a little of the said spices to sauté with the squabs and when they are well sautéed, remove from the lard in quantity if there's too much, add water and vinegar enough that they simmer below. when cooked, take 18 egg yolks and remove their livers, well-pounded, and spices of saffron, a quantity of verjuice and vinegar, and remove the cooked beards then the squabs and discard them, placing this on top to simmer. this dish should be rich and

title:
CXXIII. Polastri afenochiati
per uno altro modo.
text: roast the chickens and pluck them, then boil them. don't overcook them and fry them in lard. add almonds, fennel flower, and celery, mixing everything together with the chicken broth. then serve them in bowls and season them with sugar.

title: CXXIV. Pollastri assabecho molto buoni.
text: boil the chickens and cut them in half, then fry them in lard. add raisins and season with verjuice, vinegar, and chicken broth. fry an onion and mash it, then mix it with the flavorful sauce. add spices, excluding saffron, and a little galangal, ensuring it s tangy but not too sour.

title: CXXV. A ffare cervellade bressane.
text: prepare twenty-five pounds of pork, ensuring it contains no neck or loin, but rather the meat from the legs or shoulders, or twenty pounds of fat from the base of the legs, more or less, according to your preference. pound it well with a knife, then add fifteen ounces of candia cheese and fifteen ounces of sardinian salt, or two pounds of sea salt and six ounces of pink peppercorns. grind the salt and cheese well and incorporate them into the pounded meat. prepare the casings and let them sit for two days in salt. the colder and clearer the weather, the better. then, smoke them. alternatively, add saffron and spices to the pounded meat, as much as you like, for good reason.

title: CXXVI. Torta lavagnexe per xii persone.
text: you should prepare fresh or aged polastri and eighteen eggs, and a pound and a half of lard, a pinch of saffron, a generous amount of parsley, a little mint, and a little sage. return the poussins to the pot and boil them until thoroughly cooked, then shred them. return the cheese, well washed and coarsely grated, and the lard, which you should chop as finely as you can. return the eggs and add them to the mixture, ensuring it's neither too stiff nor too runny. return the saffron, dilute it, and add it to the mixture. you can add anything else between two layers of dough and bake it in the oven to make a tart. make a rich green crust from the aforementioned herbs, without spices it is very good, optimal, and perfect.

title:
CXXVII. A chonfetare mandole fresche e
persiche fresche e noce fresche vogleno
essere zovenette, né dure, né tenere, etc.
text: gather walnuts, peaches, and almonds four almonds. they should be soaked in water and the water changed frequently, ensuring it is sweet, each day. then boil them in water the walnuts should boil for half an hour, the peaches and almonds when they begin to soften, boil for half a quarter of an hour. then place them to dry in the shade and wind in a basket or on a sloping surface for three days. the peaches and almonds for two days, then add spices of cloves, cinnamon, and ginger. boil them in honey for the space of six hail marys, then remove them from the honey and boil them in another honey until the honey is reduced. then add spices on top, fine, and place in a small earthenware jar in the sun for fifteen days, well sealed. the peaches should be made in the same way, except they should be boiled in the first honey until they are cooked it need not be changed. be mindful that the almonds should not

title: CXXVIII. A ffare bozolati da monege.
text: beat the eggs very well with a little salt, using as many eggs as you desire. then, with this flour, make a mark with your fingers, and knead it with the beaten eggs without adding any water. if you want to add apples, use one good apple for every ten eggs. if you want to add sugar, use one ounce of sugar for every ten eggs. they need to be very smooth and made quickly, and remember they must be baked immediately, because they spoil quickly if exposed to wind or sun. bake them in a hot oven that doesn't produce bubbles as you are baking them, continue working and watch that the earth isn't stuck clean it well if it is.

title: CXXIX. A chonfettare zuche per dui modi.
text: peel and remove the seeds from the small zucchini. cut them into two pieces and boil them in water until tender. have nine glass jars ready and transfer the zucchini from one jar to the next, moving it quickly through the first, then the second, then the third, and so on, until it reaches the ninth jar, ensuring the zucchini cools completely in the water. drain the zucchini and let it air dry in a cool, breezy place, away from direct sunlight, for three days. then, boil it briefly in a syrup. strain the syrup and add it to the zucchini, ensuring it is well coated. if you want them to be more refined, boil some sugar with the syrup. remember, when you make these zucchini, they should be cooked. place them in a clean glass bowl and let them sit in the air until all the syrup has evaporated, then store them where you like. they will keep the syrup for about fifteen days keep them away from the sun. alternatively,

title: CXXX. A ffare ranciata bona e delicata.
text: peel the lemon and use the pieces you desire, grinding them finely. simmer them in water for fifteen days, then let them drain for three days. next, place them in honey, which you will boil for three days. after that, boil it briefly and change the water. then, add the honey and the spices but first, the spices should be put in and the water skimmed. boil until the honey is well cooked, then let it sit in the air for a few days, away from the sun.

title:
CXXXI. A ffare la ranziata batuta
per altro modo.
text: make it like the one above, i think that the apple should not be changed and be very well chopped with a knife, then cooked in the apple. keep in mind that it should be cooked enough that the apple is almost hard and a little fire and seasoned, and cooked together with the apple, and it s done.

title:
CXXXII. Confetti de melle apio o de pome
paradiso se le voy fare subito chomo è 
gratate le poy fare come ti pare.
text: peel and grate the quince, being careful that no pips fall into the grated mixture, and let it soak for two days. keep the juice that comes from the quince with the quince itself pass the grated apples and for every three pounds of apples, add three pounds of sugar, and let them stand for two days, the apples with the sugar. then boil them, stirring constantly with spices until the apples are cooked. remember that the spices should be added when the preserve is almost ready, like the cloves. spread it out on a table or a wet stone and shape it with a thick fire, less than half an inch. then let it cool and cut it into small pieces like chess pieces, and place them in a jar with bay leaves at the bottom, and then from the other hand, layer soil on top and if you want to place spices between the layers, it will be very good. keep in mind that it needs to boil for at least an hour

title:
CXXXIII. A ffare codogniato bono
vantagiato.
text: peel and boil the codgnas until they fall apart take a perforated bowl or a grater, and grate them finely so that you extract all the goodness, being careful that the kernels do not fall into the grated pulp. keep this grated pulp in the air for 3 days before adding it to the apples, then for every pound of grated codgnas, you will need 3 pounds of apples. boil together until the apples are cooked, with fine spices. if you want it for the sick, add a little sugar, for every 3 pounds of codgnat, use 11 ounces of sugar instead of spices. when it is thick, spread it out on a wet table, and work it like pasta dough, roughly the thickness of a half-inch, and shape it like chess pieces, placing them in a small earthenware pot with spices and bay leaves that is, the one not for the sick, boil for two hours, stirring constantly

title:
CXXXIV. A ffare una sana e bona vivanda
de iola.
text: take as much yolk as an egg, and two slices of pork belly, and cook them well, browning the belly and crushing it well with a knife, then into the mortar. also, make some polenta from the cornmeal, cooked and pounded. add some good cheese and 6 or 7 eggs, make a paste, and fry in a pan with some butter. it will make a good, wholesome dish. if you add a clove of garlic, it will be a dish fit for an emperor. if you can't get fresh pork belly, use veal brains, or beef brains, which are good. keep in mind that the dish should be of a fine flavor sugar won't spoil it, etc.

title: CXXXV. Vivanda bona.
text: take flour, eggs, form a dough and grate it take spices and grind them in a mortar. then, with your hands, shape it into long, finger-length strips. close them well, sprinkle with spice and grated cheese on top, and bake.

title: K1. Quomodo fiet oleum de nucibus (Q1)
text: take a dish full of nuts and cherries, and an egg. scald milk with salt. and an egg should be scalded with water. and let them together in a hot mortar and pound them well, and write down the oil.

title: K2. Quomodo fiet oleum de amigdalis (Q2)
text: you must take a pound of chicory and let it in water. to the chicory, add water and dry them on a cloth. and pound them in a mortar. and write on a cloth. then oil is good for all food.

title:
K3. Quomodo fit butirum de amigdalis
(Q3)
text: take a handful of cream and make it into water. and let it be in a small pot and make it warm, like a broth. and let it be with saffron well writhed and salt. and vinegar to taste and make it all hot until it thickens. then time it until it is very thick. let it be in a cloth together as a pouch and hang it up until it is watery, which is sick. and then take it out and make it of buttered dough.

title: K4. Quomodo conficiuntur amigdala in pastello.
text: make thick milk from almonds and make a pot of dough. let it have four parts milk and mix the dough with it. and salt it and bake it in a hot oven.

title:
K5. Quomodo fit lac acetuosum de amigdalis
(Q4)
text: then you must take almond milk and make of it thick milk and add thereto vinegar or wine and sweeten. heat it until it thickens. that is as good as sour whey milk.

title:
K6. Quomodo temperetur salsum dominorum

et quam diu durat. (Q5)
text: to make a good spice mixture, use nutmeg and mace. cardamom, pepper, cinnamon, and ginger. mix all equally. let the cinnamon be as much as all the others. and add two spoonfuls of broth as much as all the others. then pound them all together. grind with strong vinegar and salt. that is a fine sauce, and it is good for half a year.

title:
K7. Quomodo condiantur assature in salso
supradicto. (Q6)
text: to prepare a hen dish, one must first plump the hen well. in a pan, heat over embers without fire. and one must take broth from deer or roast, well grease and roast them well. and cut them well broad. and then, when the sauce is called, that wild broth, add a little salt and that may be added three times. thus one must keep good deer broth. goose and duck. of one cuts them thickly. those are the best sauces with hen.

title: K8. Item de aliis salsis. (Q7)
text: one must take syrup and let it settle, honey and malted barley mixed with good vinegar. then it is ready for the day.

title: K9. Item de aliis. (Q8)
text: grind almonds and let them be divided into thirty parts of honey and wine. divide anise and cinnamon likewise and grind them together. add a little vinegar and one loaf of bread. that is good for three men.

title: K10. Quomodo condiantur pisces in salso sibi adoptato.
text: one must take fish, and herring, and all kinds of fish and steak. dress them well and drip with oil where first there is salt. then season them well, being well roasted. take off the oil then, and stir with vinegar and write a small cloth. this sauce one calls indian sauce. it is good for all kinds of fish.

title: K11. De salso minimi ualoris. (Q9)
text: take onions and cut them small. and add a little parsley and juice there, a bit of salt and let it stand. then add four parts of vinegar. this sauce shall be good always.

title: K12. De salso ualente ad quosdam pisciculos. (Q10)
text: peas and cloves should be chopped evenly and ground with vinegar and salt. this sauce is good for roasted meat and game.

title: K13. De salso ualente ad tres dies et non amplius. (Q11)
text: you must take mint and parsley and cinnamon. and pepper. all together. and grind them with vinegar. all together. then this sauce is good for three days.

title: K14. De salso ad carnes recentas apto. (Q12)
text: you must constantly mix cloves with wineberries and salt. then it is good sauce for goose and green bacon and roasted meat.

title:
K15. Quomodo temperetur cibus qui uocatur
hwit moos (Q14)
text: you must take sweet milk and well-kneaded wheat bread. and beat eggs well and well-kneaded saffron. let that boil until it thickens. then let it cool on nine discs. cast three pats of butter on it and sprinkle with a powder of cinnamon. that is white moss.

title: K16. De cibo qui uocatur kaliis. (Q15)
text: one must take sweet milk and cut there, in crusts, of wheat bread as much as dice. and boil that in a pan. and let there be added to it eggs, beaten well. that is called kalis.

title:
K17. Quomodo conficiatur pastellum de medullis
ceruorum.
text: simmer venison and cut it into pieces. then call it. make a dough of wheat flour and cold water. let it rest with salt, pepper, and cinnamon. add marrow from the bones and make a pastry. bake in a hot oven.

title: K18. De pullis simpliciter temperandis. (Q19)
text: take a fatty hen and sew it with fat. then cool it and let it lie. and well, in a pan. these hens are good to eat warm.

title:
K19. Quomodo temperentur pulli cum diuersis
speciebus.
text: cut a hen into small pieces and boil them in water. grind pepper, cinnamon, saffron, and wheat bread. boil the liver and bacon until melted, then add vinegar and salt to taste.

title: K20. De cibo qui dicitur kloten en honær. (Q21)
text: take a fat hen whole, and another fresh hen. split the latter well small. add to that bacon, trimmed well as peas, and ground cumin, saffron, and wine. add swine's grease and salt to taste. add blossoms of egg, so that they are evenly thick batter. these are formed into balls, one hour.

title:
K21. De cibo qui uocatur honær inder iæghæt.
(Q22)
text: roast a hen and cut it into pieces. grind cloves and add to it, and let it simmer with wine, salt, and well-beaten egg yolks and butter. the hen should be well boiled. this is a hen baked in an eggshell.

title: K22. De cibo qui dicitur spæk honer. (Q24)
text: one must season a hen with whole salt, fat and bacon, finely chopped as peas, and vinegar. and salt to taste. that is called bacon hen.

title:
K23. Item aliud temperamentum pullorum.
(Q25)
text: first, cut a hen into pieces and grind pepper, cinnamon, and cardamom evenly. then take the whites of eggs, quite hard-boiled. cut them finely and let them form a whole flower. add saffron and vinegar and make the mixture thick with egg blossoms. add salt to taste.

title: K24. Quomodo condiatur pullus in pastello. (Q26)
text: one must take a fatty hen, cut and sweep it clean. mix with salt and fat, and salt and herbs. wrap the hen in dough and bake in an oven as with bread. thus one does with all fish pastries and fowl and other meats.

title: K25. De cibo qui dicitur koken wan honer. (Q27)
text: make a pot of dough. and cut a hen there, that is, two. and put there two slices of fat, well ground, as much peas pepper and cumin and egg blossoms, well beaten with saffron. and then cover the pot and let bake in an oven. that is what the cook does when.

title: Chewetes on fysshe day.
text: take turbot, haddock, and good codlings. clean and cut them into pieces. season with salt, pepper, and ginger. put them in a dish. add a good quantity of butter, a little white wine, and parsley. bake until done.

title: In qua luna sit vindemiandum.
text: one must harvest the grapes when the moon is in cancer, leo, or libra, or scorpio, capricorn, or aquarius. however, one must hasten when it is waning, and perform the harvest underground.

title:
Qualiter vindemiatores debeant
vindemiare.
text: those who handle larger baskets should carefully select the grapes, and if any are sour or dry, they should be removed. it is also necessary for the pressers to remember to choose the leaves, for crushed leaves with the grapes produce a harsher wine and are easily spoiled. sour and dry grapes, however, cause the greatest harm.

title: Qualiter debeant uve calcari.
text: grapes placed in the press must be immediately pressed by those appointed to do so, and when they have thoroughly crushed every grape, they should raise the bunches and kernels, and draw so that much liquid flows out from under the press. when they have pressed late and raised the bunches high, and made them soft, warm, and not very moist, then support them under wood and poles. for when they are warm and soft, they become easily and fluidly yielded. but if they are pressed very moist, it is necessary to break the kernels that have been pressed with their composition. those entering and crushing in the press must be very clean in their feet and not eat anything in the press, nor drink, nor go in and out frequently. and if it is necessary to go out, let them go out with clean feet. it is also necessary that those who press should be clothed and girded, because of the sweat that will come upon them. there must also be a good smell around the

title: De uvis acerbis et vini expurgatione.
text: separate all unripe or otherwise spoiled grapes from the rest. the must from these grapes should be treated as follows rainwater should be boiled down to half its volume, and then one-tenth of this boiled water should be added to the wine. then, boil the wine again until one-tenth of it has evaporated. some people, however, do not do this, but mix water with the grapes themselves, adding one-third to the future must, and then they cook the must after the grapes have been crushed, until one-tenth of it has evaporated.

title: De curatione vini pluvia agitati.
text: if many rainy days occur and the grapes in the vineyard, whether still present or after the harvest, become too wet, we will crush them out of necessity. but if you discover the must to be weaker than it should be, taste will tell you when the wine is put into a cask, that after the first boiling, it should be immediately transferred to another cask. for everything watery remains at the bottom because of its weight add to the wine three measures of cotilas to ten. some, however, making the wine better, cook it until a twentieth part of it has been consumed, adding a hundredth part of gypsum. the people of lade leave the wine over the fire until a fifth part of it has been consumed, and then use the fourth.

title:
Qualiter vinum (mustum) mittendum
sit in dolia.
text: before adding anything, the vats must be washed thoroughly with pure salted water and smoked with fire. they should not be filled too full, nor left too empty. one must observe when the fermenting must causes an increase, so that it does not overflow, and the foam rises to the brim. at this point, it is necessary to stir constantly. the must will settle in the vats for about five days, and with hands and paddles, remove the foam and anything else superfluous. all the dregs should be carried away from the cellar and thrown far away, because if they remain nearby, they breed mold and produce a bad odor, both of which spoil the wine. it is essential to consider a good scent for the presses and vats, especially in wine cellars.

title:
De racemis electis et qualiter
ex ipsis vinum sit faciendum.
text: after pouring out the must, the grape clusters must be immediately ejected from the press and put into vats, where they are to be crushed with water. this drink, however, country folk call a poor brew. the remaining grape clusters provide sufficient food for animals. however, it is necessary to press the grape clusters soon after they are removed from the press and to turn them underneath the press, and to rinse them with salty or seawater and to fumigate them with thyme. for if they remain moist in the press, they are entirely turned sour. and from this, the fruit, when trodden later, is spoiled and produces lees, which is a sign of turned wine.

title:
Qualiter vinum (aliter mustum)
non superebuliat.
text: decorate the rim of the jug with a garland of mint or parsley or marjoram. some people also smear the insides of the jars around the edges with rennet cheese, for it will retain the boiling must.

title:
Qualiter vinum (mustum)
cito purgetur.
text: pour a sweet grape must into a small earthenware jar, add vinegar, and after three days it will be pure.

title:
Qualiter mustum possit haberi
per totum annum.
text: before the cluster is heated, let the juice that spontaneously drips from it, which some call the pressing, be put into a pitch-lined vessel, either inside and out, or partially full, and carefully sealed with gypsum, for the juice will remain very sweet for a long time. it will be preserved even more if, after being enclosed in leather, it is placed in a well for several days, and because it will not boil over, it will always be juice. if anyone also quietly presses the grapes so that they are not squeezed, this juice will have permanence. others put it into old vessels, having held very old, sharp wine. others, as has been said, line the vessel inside and out with pitch and place it in a well so that only the edges protrude above this is also excellently demonstrated by experience. others bury the vessel in damp sand. others, digging into the ground with grape seeds, trample the damp earth three times. others put the juice into an

title:
Qualiter debet cognosci si mustum
habeat aquam.
text: put raw pears into the must, and if it has water, they will be submerged. if not, they will float. if they sink to the bottom, it has water.

title: Quo loco debeat poni vinum.
text: the wine should be placed in a stronger spot beneath the slope. it should be exposed to the west and south with certain walls facing those directions. the remaining wines should be placed indoors, and higher windows should be covered facing north and east.

title: Que uve quale vinum faciant.
text: dark grapes make stronger wine. pale grapes make a middling wine. red grapes make a purer and more delightful wine. new wine is very cold, but old wine is very hot, very strong, and pleasantly fragrant. what was watery, time consumes.

title: De apertione doliorum.
text: one must preserve the amphorae, observing the rising of the stars, because at that time the wine moves. and it is not necessary to skim the wine at that time. and if you open the amphora during the day, it is necessary to shade it so that its brightness does not fall upon the wine. but if, through great necessity and frequent urging, you open the amphora, it is necessary to oversee it under the light of the moon.

title: De transvasatione vini.
text: one must transfer wine in northern winds and by no means in southern ones. and it should be weaker in spring and stronger in summer. but wines which are born in dry places after the winter solstice. therefore, when wine is transferred under the full moon, vinegar is made. it is necessary to know that when wine is separated from the sediment, it becomes more refined and weaker. therefore, one must ensure that it is warmed in winter and cooled in summer. it is necessary to transfer wine when the moon is waxing and underground. some say that the wine should be transferred on the first or second day of the moon before it appears to people. when we transfer wine from the amphorae into small vessels, we must observe the rising of the stars. the sediment is then moved in the rising and especially in the bloom of roses. when the vine is flourishing, wise people consult, and especially isidore, that when the amphora is opened, the wine that is

title: Quo tempore vina sint gustanda.
text: some people taste wine as the northern winds depart, for then it is unchanging and clear. others, experienced wine tasters, taste wine when the south wind blows more strongly. for the south wind more readily stirs the wine and reveals what it is and what it could have been. when the stomach is fasting, one should not taste wine, for the taste is harsh then, after much eating and drinking. rather, one should taste it when having eaten little and digested well, and not when it is eaten with salty food or something that alters the taste. some people, wishing to deceive tasters, have a new jar in which they pour the best, oldest, and well-chosen wine, and in it they place the wine they wish to sell. more maliciously still, some offer nuts and cheese to those wishing to taste the wine, so that they may eat and the taste of the wine is better falsified. we have said these things not because we do them, but

title:
De probatione vini veteris et musti 
utrum aquam habeat.
text: when it is necessary to commend wine or must to servants or a buyer, it is also necessary for the buyer to taste the wine to see if it is pure. some people put bad fruit in the vessel, but a pear is better. others put a locust, others a cicada, and if the liquid remains clear, the wine is pure if they sink, it has water. some people coat reeds with oil that is, greek reeds that grow in the water or linen, or papyrus, or hay, or other crushed herbs, anointing them with oil and putting them in the wine, and then pulling out the reeds or other things placed there, in this way they test the wine. but if it has water, the drops will collect in the oil. others, doing it more simply, put the wine into a new pot in which some residue remains, and let it stand for days. the pot drips out a mixture of water. others, heating the wine, put

title: Qualiter aqua a vino possit separari.
text: pour moist alum into a pot, then with wine. cover the pot's mouth with an oiled sponge, tilting it so that nothing escapes, and only water will drain out.

title:
Quibus temporibus omne vinum 
facilius eversetur.
text: turn the wine frequently around during the pleiades' setting, at the winter solstice, amidst blossoming vineyards, and at the summer solstice. also, during the dog days of summer, which commonly are called sultry days, and generally around all the annual winds, in the heat and in the frost, and during long rains, or because of a violent wind, or a harsh thunderstorm, or when roses are in bloom, or during a violent lightning strike.

title:
Qualiter possit provideri vino 
contra tonitrua.
text: iron placed around a barrel is beneficial against thunder and lightning. some indeed place laurel branches above it to repel these passions.

title:
Qualiter possit provideri ne vinum 
evertatur.
text: pour the heated wine in, stirring it, and prevent it from boiling too much, and from producing a larger froth. add sweet almonds and keep it standing. remove the seeds from dried grapes and, having added sand, cook them in must or boiled wine to make a rich and lasting wine. some also choose dried grapes that have fallen naturally in the vineyard and use them separately. plaster added to the initial wine makes it harsher. but as time passes, the harshness evaporates, it makes it lasting, and prevents the wines from souring.

title: De vino versato.
text: fenugreek with burnt salt if it is ground and mixed with wine, the wines which have turned away from their good flavor, separated and poured into a good wine flavor, will remain. some, however, with pine wood embers made or from roots kindling, extinguish it and do not allow the wine to turn. others plunge iron into the wine and extinguish it. some add burnt cedar fruit and burnt chickens into the wine and make it permanent. others mix with wine ash from burnt vine branches and fennel seed, grinding and reducing it to a mass. some pour wines that have turned into freshly tarred vessels and transfer them to another house. if they are damaged by heat, they reduce them in cool places. if, however, from dampness and cold, they transfer them to warm and dry places. others, however, burn flax seed or oak wood and add it to the wine. others mix milk

title: Ad vinum versatum et putridum.
text: take tart cherries in a good quantity and put them whole into a vessel. add wine where it is poured, and thus the wine will begin to boil, and so allow it to simmer for three days, or until it ceases to boil. during this boiling, the wine will be cleansed of sediment very well. when you see the wine clear, place it in another vessel it is tasted.

title:
Ad vinum album in rubeum 
vertendum.
text: once you have transferred the white wine from its harvest into a vessel and the wine has rested for a day, allowing it to settle in a dark tub, pour the black grape skins over it. leave it there for a day or two, and then press it out, making it very clear and deeply red.

title: Ad vinum bene clarificandum.
text: if, however, the wine, after being pressed, cannot be clarified, take strong poles and mix it vigorously in its own must, so that all the wine remains on top of the must and the must beneath the wine, and thus leave it. for the wine itself will begin to boil strongly and the must will rise, and the wine will settle, and thus leave it for a day and more if necessary. and afterwards, draw off the wine, very clear.

title: Ad versatum vinum.
text: if, however, you have mixed it with wine and tempered it with honey in a good quantity, and you have placed this tempered mixture in a vessel where the wine has been poured, and after sealing it with a stopper, you have vigorously stirred the wine with the aforementioned honey, and afterward let it stand, it will clarify because of the honey. for honey, which is cloudy, causes it to settle to the bottom. some, indeed, when making it excellently, at the time of harvest, put a large quantity of fresh, unpressed bunches of grapes in a vessel with the wine, so that the bunches may be the mother of the wine itself. for the grapes restore the wine to its proper goodness and flavor after some time. however, this must be known before anything else is done to the wine, the wine must be decanted and separated from its dregs. some, however, cast away the wine that has been poured in the harvest, from which the fresh black must has

title:
De confectione quae facit vinum 
durabile.
text: to make a wonderful, lasting wine preparation called panarea. take aloes, frankincense, amomum, each two ounces honey, four ounces spice nard, two ounces leaves, four ounces myrrh, two ounces and cassia, one ounce. bind all these ingredients in a cloth and put one snail shell into each amphora. after wine has been poured in and is already clarified, dissolve the cloth and let the powder settle in the wine. then stir the camomile root for three days. some people make another preparation, namely, adding four ounces of saffron, which gives the wine a good color. three ounces of grated male frankincense give the wine a harsh taste. a handful of leaves gives the wine a good scent. mix each of these three, ground, and add them to each amphora, with three snail shells, along with the wine, so that it does not boil over but remains settled

title:
Scriptura quedam que non 
patitur vinum everti.
text: it is impossible to overturn wine if these divine words are inscribed on a vase or in amphorae. taste and see how sweet the lord christ is. a blessing will result if, while writing this on an apple, you place it within a jar of wine through immersion.

title:
De signis pronosticis vini 
an duratura sit bonitas eius.
text: after pouring the wine into barrels, after some time it must be transferred to another vessel gently. in that vessel, the sediment is left behind, and the vessel is carefully sealed, and then one must observe frequently, tasting it, lest any change occur in the sediment, producing bubbles or a white mold that forms beneath the lees or strange shapes or certain talcs. for then the wine is to be feared as spoiled. but if nothing of that sort is produced, one should believe the wine to be lasting. some, however, piercing a reed straight down to the bottom above the sediment, and sealing the top opening of the reed with the thumb, afterward withdrawing the thumb, draw forth the aroma of the lower part by smell, then sniffing, they draw the part of the sediment to the quality, and according to the quality to the aroma, believing it to be the future wine. others, gently bubbling and cooling a little of the wine, taste it and believe that whatever they find in taste will

title:
Ad meliorandum debile vinum et 
malum (qualiter vino possit a muffa
liberari).
text: if the wine has mold or another bad taste, take a white vine with its roots and pour it into a barrel underground, its roots so that they come to the hole of the barrel straight above, so that they remain there for three days, and it will lose that bad taste and smell. if the wine vessel has a bad smell from dryness, wash it first carefully with water so that the vessel remains infused, then take a single juniper berry and put it through one hole of the barrel or barrel so that it makes smoke, and cover it above so that the smoke does not go out all day, and afterwards wipe the inside of the barrel with a cloth. and when it is well dry, put there the wine as much as you wish this removes the dryness and the bad smell of the barrel. if after this has been done the wine is not strong but weak, and you have thrown into the vessel where the wine is bunches of grapes not pressed in a good quantity, according to how

title: Ad preparandam vegetem ut bona sit.
text: if you wish to prepare a savory vegetable preserve, so that it smells well and the wine which is put into it does not spill out, but is well preserved, the vegetables should be washed well, and allowed to dry thoroughly, and rubbed well with a clean cloth and cleaned, then ripe fruit should be taken, well-ripened, without leaves, with which the vegetables are thoroughly infused and soaked, and then allowed to dry. afterward, with the aforementioned fruit, it should be soaked and rubbed as predicted. and let this be done three times. after the vegetables have been well infused with the juice of the said fruit, and have become well blackened from it and dried, they should be rubbed well with a clean cloth and the must should be poured in it will then be good and lasting, truly well.

title:
De muffa et mala putredine 
extrahenda.
text: take three flexible twigs from a vine, about the length of a finger, and tie them with string. suspend them in a jar within the wine, so that the wine does not touch, and the jar is well sealed. it is said that whatever is foul or rotten in the wine is collected entirely by these twigs and purged. alternatively, take one good and healthy walnut for every measure and throw it into the jar within the wine. all foul odors will be collected by it, so that when you taste the wine and find it good in its flavor, remove the walnuts you placed in, and you will find them so rotten and infected with a bad smell that you will marvel.

title: De vino quod volvitur et turbatur.
text: when the wine is transformed, take for every corbe, two egg whites and five ounces of sea salt. grind the salt finely and mix the salt powder with the egg whites thoroughly. add a little water and mix it in, and then add more water and mix again, and skim frequently, and thus add water 4 or 2 times, and skim frequently, and then put it into the vegetable and mix it well. then extract 3 or 4 portions through the lower opening and put it back into the vegetable, and then add one portion of water, and seal the vegetable, and let it rest for 3 days.

title:
De emendatione vini versati 
et turbati.
text: to make almond wine, ten measures of wine, one pound of alum, five pounds of tartaric powder, one ounce of salt. first, grind all these ingredients separately. then, beat the salt with the white of three eggs for a long time, and afterwards add the tartaric powder and beat well. finally, add the alum. afterwards, change the wine and wash the vessel. place the mixture in and shake with a pestle for an hour. the same is done with white wine, but instead of the boiled wine, add four ounces of crushed alum for every four measures of wine, six grains of cloves, three of cinnamon, two of nutmeg, two of mace, and two of cardamom. grind these spices. for a measure, take six peach stones and pound one ounce of common salt, two ounces of cheese. pound these ingredients together, namely the spices separately and with the peach stones. then pour the wine into another vessel, not filled to the measure of a palm

title:
Vt vinum conservetur quando 
mutatur.
text: when the wine is changed in january or in the first week of april whichever is better fill a vessel well with wine. and if there are 20 corbies, boil them and for each corbie boiling, put in common salt as much as a handful can hold and return them to the vessel, and seal it well so that all the wine heats thoroughly.

title: Ad faciendum vinum dulce.
text: take white grapes, also separate them and put them in a pot over the fire, as they boil, stir them with a spatula until they become like thick honey and set aside. afterwards, take grape juice and put it into another pot, 30 pounds of it. add 3 pounds of sugar and 3 pounds of dates, well crushed so that the pulp is extracted, and boil all together until a third has evaporated. strain through a cloth and mix with the aforementioned preparation, incorporating everything well. when you wish to add it to wine, if it is a hundred gallons, add 3 sextarius of this preparation however, boil that preparation with some of the wine and when it is lukewarm, mix with a stick and bottle it.

title:
Ad faciendum de vino plano 
melius quam de monte.
text: take 6 pounds of quince, 5 pounds of figs, pitted 4 pounds of dried roses 2 pounds of cedar seeds 2 pounds of bay berries. put all these ingredients together and place them in strained wine, so that they boil with it simultaneously, and let the quantity of wine be, for the aforementioned ingredients, 100 and a half. and when it has ceased boiling, remove the wine and place it in another vessel, and put the sediment on top of the wine it will then be good and useful.
ingredients: dried roses cedar seeds bay berries

title: Ut vinum non acescat.
text: take fresh sea kale roots and chop them coarsely, placing them into a pot as much as your hand can hold.

title: Ad extrahendum acetum.
text: make one loaf of bread from spelt flour, place it inside a warm earthenware pot over embers, and draw it out with vinegar.

title: Ut vinum non fiat acetum.
text: take wormwood seeds and five-finger grass, pound them together, and put them in when the wine is boiling.

title: Ut uva nascatur sine granis.
text: once the vine is planted, detach it without iron and afterward plant it, and if it sprouts, grapes will grow without seeds.

title: Ad faciendum uvam tinctam.
text: remove the marrow from the vine and in a place where the marrow takes on the color you desire, let it be made like a grape of a similar color.

title: Ut ficus citius maturentur.
text: if you wish that figs ripen more quickly, cover beneath the roots of them with sheep's horns, place them there and they will ripen more quickly. similarly, if figs are touched from above with oil, they will ripen quickly.

title: Ad faciendum cannamellum.
text: take a cabbage head and two large collard greens. cut them and be careful they are not ruined. sprout their heads and backs and through the middle. they are to be boiled and filled with good honey, and the boiled area should be well closed. and thus plant them in watery places.

title:
Per dare ad intender qual carne merita andare arrosto
et quale allesso.
text: large beef and cow meat should be braised veal meat, that is, the fore chest is good boiled, the loin roasted, and the shanks in meatballs. castrated male meat is all good boiled, except for the shoulder, which is good roasted, and also the shank. pork meat is not healthy in any way the ridge is to be roasted when fresh with onions, and the rest for salting or as you like. goat meat is all good boiled and roasted but the hindquarters are better roasted. similarly, so is lamb. goat meat is good in january with garlic. of deer meat, the front part is good in a rich broth, the loins can be roasted, and the shanks are good in a dry pie or in meatballs. similarly, the meat of the roe deer is good. wild boar meat should be in a spicy stew, or in a sauce, or in a rich broth. hare meat is

title: Per cocer capponi, fasani et altri volatili.
text: various birds herons, swans, ducks, cranes, wild geese, egrets are best roasted, stuffed with garlic or onions, and other good things. peacocks, pheasants, partridges, guinea fowl, wild chickens, snipes, quails, thrushes, blackbirds, and all other good birds are also good roasted. roast chickens are excellent. squabs are good boiled, but roasting them is even better. wild pigeons are good roasted, but they are better boiled with pepper and sage. a cockerel is good boiled, and when it is very fat, it is best roasted the same applies to hens.

title: Per haver ogni carne bella allesso.
text: to have beautifully boiled meat, you must divide it into pieces as you like, and soak it in cold water for about an hour. then wash it well with warm water, and again with cold water. place it over the fire in a large pot where it has room to move, so it remains whiter. add salt as needed, and skim it well, especially at the beginning. if the salt isn t pure, dissolve it in a little warm water, which will quickly clear it, turning it into brine. then, once strained, you can add it to the pot gently, so the sediment doesn t settle on the bottom. if the meat is old and tough, especially capon and hen, dip it several times in boiling water and cool it in cold water in this way it will be more beautiful and cook more quickly.

title: Per fare ogni bello arrosto.
text: to make a beautiful roast of chickens, capons, goats, or any other meat worthy of roasting first, if it's a large piece of meat, blanch it, except if it s young veal, and then lard it, as they do with roasts. if it s a capon, chicken, goat, or any other meat worthy of roasting, make sure it's clean and polished, then put it in boiling water, and immediately remove it to cold water. this will make it more beautiful and easier to glaze. then lard it, that is, with chopped lard and other suitable fragrant ingredients, according to your lord s taste. inside, if you like, put in some good herbs with dried plums, maraschino cherries, and sloe berries, or, in season, sorrel, and other similar things. then place it neatly on the spit and put it over the fire, giving it a moderate heat at first. for a beautiful and good

title: Per fare peperata de salvaticina.
text: to make good peppered venison, hare, wild boar, or other game, take as much water as reddish wine, and wash the meat well within it. then strain this washing, adding as much salt as you deem necessary and put the meat to cook in this water and wine. when it s cooked, take it out. if you want to make two plates, remove a pound and a half of dried raisins and grind them very finely. remove the same amount of bread cut into slices, well toasted over the grill, and soaked in good vinegar, and grind it together with the dried raisins. if you can have some blood, or the game s tripe, it would be optimal to grind them with these ingredients. these should be well ground and tempered with the meat broth, a little of the sapa that is, wine cooked in must and the vinegar in which the bread was soaked. then pass this mixture through a sieve into a bowl, adding

title: Per fare brodo lardieri de salvaticina.
text: to make a rich meat broth first wash the meat in good white wine mixed with an equal amount of water, and strain the washing liquid, using it to cook the meat. add a generous amount of lard, cut into small pieces like dice, and also a good quantity of roughly chopped sage. when the meat is nearly cooked, add some good spices, as mentioned above. to thicken the broth slightly, remove two or three egg yolks and an equal number of slices of bread well toasted over the fire, but not too charred or burnt, just dried, and grind them into a powder. then, take a little broth and mix these ingredients together, and return them to the broth. if you have blood or the giblets of the meat, pound them well and add them to cook in the broth it will be much better. note that if you want to make dishes with this broth, the meat should be cut into large pieces of a pound or half a pound. and if you want

title: Per fare civero de salvaticina.
text: to make meat civero first, cook the meat in water mixed with an equal amount of vinegar, and when it's cooked, strain the broth. once drained, fry it in good lard. if you want to make two plates of this civero, remove one pound of dried raisins and half a pound of unpeeled almonds, and grind them well. then, remove one pound of bread cut into slices and dried over the fire, but not too toasted, and soak it in a little red wine. grind it with the aforementioned ingredients, then thin it out with the broth from the meat, and pass it through a sieve into a saucepan. place it over low heat, away from the fire, and let it simmer for about half an hour. then add ginger and cinnamon, sweet or strong according to the common taste, or your lord s preference. next, take an onion and cook it in a saucepan with good lard, finely chopped. once the onion is

title: Per far pastello secco de cervo o capriolo.
text: to make meat pasties of venison or roe deer first, cut the meat into pieces about the size of two fists, and let them sit in a brine made with equal parts vinegar and salt, as needed. then take them out and place them in a spot where the liquid from the brine drains off and the meat dries slightly. afterwards, remove pepper and powdered cinnamon together, seasoning with salt according to the amount of meat. take good lard and make lardons, and wrap them around the aforementioned pieces of meat, well-larding the meat along its length. then take healthy cloves and plant many of them on all sides of the meat, which should also be well wrapped in the aforementioned pastry. then take good flour and make a crust slightly thicker than that of lasagna. and for each piece of meat, make its covering of such crust and bake it in the oven at a moderate heat until well cooked and these pasties can be preserved for fifteen days and even a month.

title:
Per fare pastelli de carne de vitello, o cappone, o qualunqua

altra carne, o de ucelli.
text: first, take lean meat in the quantity you like and pound it well with a knife. then, add some good veal fat and mix it thoroughly with the meat, adding spices according to common taste or the patron's preference. next, make your pastry crusts as is customary for pies and place them in the oven to bake. once cooked, remove two egg yolks, a little good vinegar, a bit of rich broth, and a pinch of saffron, and beat these ingredients together. pour this mixture into the pie. if you don't know how to make crusts, cook them in a pan as you would make cakes. in the pie, you can place one or two chickens or pigeons, or a capon, or any other whole bird, or cut into pieces.

title: Per fare una crostata de pippioni o de pollastri etc.
text: first, boil the beef until it s nearly cooked then cut it into small pieces and fry it with good lard. next, make a thick pastry crust in a pan, like that used for pastries, and fill it with the meat. add dried plums or cherries, then a little rich broth, and eight eggs, beating everything together well. chop parsley, marjoram, and mint finely with a knife then add all these herbs to the pan. place it over the embers, so the pot begins to stick, stirring constantly with the pot. then pour this broth over the crust. bake it over the fire as you would a pie, and when it seems cooked, serve it. make the crust sweet or savory, according to common taste, or as the host prefers.

title:
Per fare un suffritto de carne, o de pippioni,
o de pollastri, o capretto.
text: first, chill the meat very well and cut it into quarters, or smaller pieces, and place it in a pot to fry with good lard, turning it frequently with a wooden spoon. when the meat is almost cooked, drain most of the fat from the pot. then, add some good verjuice, two egg yolks, a little good broth, and fine spices, and mix these ingredients together with enough saffron to turn them yellow. place everything in the pot with the meat and let it simmer a little longer until everything seems cooked. then, remove a little finely chopped parsley and place it together with the said sautéed mixture on a dish and serve. this sauté can be sweet or sour, according to the common taste or that of the patron.

title: Per fare un pastello in una pignatta.
text: first, prepare some good veal and fat, and chop it finely, placing it in a pot. if you wish, add chicken or quail to the pot with the meat and fat. then, set the pot away from the heat source over embers. when it begins to boil, skim it well. next, add a little grape purée and a few chopped fried onions with some good lard, adding them to the pot along with the lard. when it seems nearly cooked, season with spices and verjuice. if you like, add one or two beaten egg yolks. when the dish is cooked, serve it.

title: Per far un mirrause catalano.
text: first, remove pigeons, chickens, or capons and prepare them as for roasting. roast them on a spit and when they are half-cooked, take them off and divide them into quarters. then, divide each quarter into four pieces and place them in a serving dish. next, remove almonds toasted under warm ashes, wipe them clean with a cloth, being careful not to rub them too hard, and grind them. add two or three slices of slightly toasted bread and three or four egg yolks, and grind everything together with the almonds. season with a little good vinegar and broth, then pass the mixture through a sieve. pour this over the meat in the serving dish, adding plenty of spices, especially cinnamon, ginger, and sugar. then, place the dish over the embers and simmer for about an hour, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon. when cooked, serve this roasted dish on plates or in bowls, whichever is more suitable.

title:
Per fare pavoni vestiti con tutte le sue penne che cocto parà
vivo
et butte foco pel becco.
text: to prepare peacocks that appear to be alive first, to stun the peacock, insert a feather over its head, or truly bleed it under the throat, as with a kid. then, split it open under the body, that is, from the neck to the tail, cutting only the skin and carefully peel it off so as not to damage the feathers or the skin. and when you have skinned the body, turn the skin inside from the neck to near the head. then cut off the said head, leaving it attached to the skin of the neck and similarly, make the legs remain attached to the skin of the thighs. then arrange it very well roasted, and fill it with good things and good spices, remove whole cloves and plant them in the breast, place it on a spit and let it cook until dry around the neck, place a wet cloth so that the fire does not dry it too much and continually wet the said cloth. when it is cooked, take it

title: Per aconciare bene una porchetta.
text: prepare the pork loin, ensuring it's thoroughly peeled and clean. then, split it lengthwise along the spine and remove the innards. wash it very well. next, remove the kidneys from the pork loin and chop them finely with a knife, along with fresh herbs, garlic, a little good lard, grated cheese, a few eggs, pounded pepper, and a pinch of saffron. mix all these ingredients together and stuff them into the pork loin, folding it over like a tench, inserting the filling into slits. then, skewer it and tie it securely, and place it to roast on a spit or a grill. cook it slowly, making sure the meat and the filling are both well-cooked. make a brine with vinegar, pepper, and saffron, and add a few sprigs of lavender, sage, or rosemary baste the pork frequently with this brine. this method can also be used for geese, ducks,

title: [Per fare pollastri allessi con agresto].
text: to prepare chicken with cranberries, they should be cooked with a little salted meat. when they are half-cooked, remove the cranberries, cut them in half and discard the seeds. add them to continue cooking with the chicken. when cooked, add a little chopped parsley and mint, and a pinch of powdered pepper and saffron combine all these ingredients with the chicken and some broth in a serving dish, and bring to the table.

title: [Per fare pollastro arrosto.]
text: to roast a chicken, cook it until it's done. then remove the juice of oranges, or good verjuice with rosewater, sugar, and cinnamon, and place the chicken in a serving dish. afterwards, pour this mixture over it and serve.

title: Per fare polpette di carne de vitello o de altra bona carne.
text: first, remove lean meat from the leg and cut it into long, thin slices, pounding them well on a cutting board with the back of a knife. season with salt and pounded fennel and spread it over the meat slices. then, take parsley, marjoram, and good lard, pound these ingredients together with a little good spice, and spread them evenly over the slices. roll them up and roast on a spit, but don't let them dry out too much over the fire.

title: Per fare coppiette al modo romano.
text: cut the meat into large pieces, roughly the size of an egg, but don't separate them, as the pieces should remain attached to each other. season them lightly with salt and savory, that is, coriander seeds or pounded fennel, and coat the pieces well. then place them on a spit to roast, inserting thin slices of fatback between each piece to keep the smaller cuts tender.

title: Per fare mortadelle di carne de vitello.
text: take lean meat from the leg and pound it with a little lard or good veal fat, as you would pound meat for sausages. then add finely chopped parsley and marjoram, a red egg, and a little grated cheese, plus as much seasoning and saffron as you like mix all these ingredients with the meat. then wrap the mixture in a pork, castrated boar, or other good-quality animal casing, forming pieces about the size of an egg. place them on a spit and roast until cooked through, but not overdone.

title: Per fare tomacelli.
