text: make a dough with flour, salt water, and sugar. knead it until it s not too stiff, and roll it out thinly, like lasagna sheets. spread the dough on a board, and using a round wooden cutter or a glass, cut out circles. fry them in good oil, being careful not to let them tear. this way, the fritters will puff up and look full, and they will be lovely.

title: Frictelle in un altro modo.
text: make a composition in that manner and form as described above, in the chapter on making fritters of fennel, using fennel when it is in bloom. if you wish, leave all of the fennel fronds intact, or alternatively, if you prefer, you can separate the small sprigs or branches one by one, or two by two, as you like, incorporating and folding the fennel well into the aforementioned composition. fry it in good lard or in half oil and half butter.

title: Pastinache grosse.
text: drain them very well, and remove the core, that hard bit in the middle. blanch them, and once cooked, flour them generously, then fry them in oil.

title: Frictata.
text: beat the eggs very well, then add a little water and a little milk to make it softer, along with a little grated cheese. cook it in good butter to make it richer. and note that to make it good, it shouldn't be turned over or overcooked. if you want to make it green, you will take similarly the things mentioned above, adding the juice of these herbs, that is, borage, parsley in good quantity, borage, mint, marjoram, and sage in smaller quantity, squeezing out the juice. then, remove the herbs very well with a mortar and pestle. and to make it another way, a frittata with herbs, you will take the herbs mentioned above and finely chop them, frying them a little in good butter or oil, mixing them with the eggs and the other ingredients mentioned, and cook the frittata carefully so that it is well set and not overcooked.

title: Ova frictellate.
text: heat a little oil in a pan, until it s warm. crack fresh eggs into the pan and cook them well until dry. while they're frying, continuously baste them with the hot oil when the tops are set and white, they are cooked, and you don t want to overcook them.

title: Ova sperdute.
text: bring water to a boil and gently drop in very fresh eggs. once they are poached and tender, remove them from the water and place them on sugar, rosewater, sweet spices, and a little orange or lemon juice. if you wish, add a sprinkle of grated lemon zest and sweet spices on top.

title: Ova sperdute in lacte o vino dolce.
text: proceed similarly as described in the previous chapter, except do not add any cheese on top.

title: Ova piene.
text: boil fresh eggs in plenty of water until hard-boiled. once cooked, peel them carefully and cut them in half, removing all the yolks. set aside some of the yolks, being careful not to break the whites. grind a portion of these yolks with a little dried currants, a little old mace, and one fresh. add finely chopped parsley, marjoram, and mint, along with one or two egg whites, or more, according to the quantity you wish to prepare, and season with sweet or savory spices as you prefer. combine all ingredients thoroughly, then color the mixture yellow with saffron, and place the remaining egg whites on top. fry them in very hot oil. to enhance their flavor, take some of the reserved yolks and combine them with a few dried currants. grind them together very well, then temper them with a little sorrel and a little sapa. strain the mixture through a sieve, adding a little ginger, a few cloves

title: Ova sopra la graticula.
text: beat two fresh eggs very well, and heat a small frying pan until it s very hot. pour the beaten eggs into the pan, spreading them evenly across the bottom to create a very thin omelet, like paper. when it seems well cooked, fold it into quarters, forming a square. place it on a grill, breaking in as many fresh eggs as you think will fit on top. cook over a moderate heat, as you would a cake, sprinkling with sugar and cinnamon. when the eggs appear set, remove from the grill and serve as they are, in their square shape.

title: Ova nel speto.
text: heat the spit very well and skewer the eggs on it, lengthwise or across as you prefer, and turn them over the fire like a roast. and when they seem cooked, take them off and serve them at the table.

title: Ova in patelletta.
text: melt a generous amount of butter in copper molds and let it warm slightly. prepare the yolks of fresh eggs, separating them from the whites if you prefer. cook them gently, sprinkling with sugar and cinnamon. temper the heat from below and above so they aren't overcooked. then, drizzle a little orange juice or rosewater over them.

title: Ova in cenere calda.
text: place fresh eggs in warm ashes, turning them frequently with care, ensuring they receive heat evenly from all sides. when they are sweating vigorously, remove them as they are cooked.

title: Ova tuffate con la sua cortece.
text: place fresh eggs in cold water and bring to a boil for the length of a rosary or a little longer, then remove them.

title: Ova frictellate a la fiorentina.
text: have fresh eggs and crack them one by one into a pan with very hot oil. as soon as you put them in the oil, gather them together with a spatula or spoon, shaping them into circles as much as possible, and turn them frequently while cooking, so that the outside is slightly colored, and the inside is not hard or overcooked, but rather soft and tender.

title: Ova sperdute in la brascia accesa.
text: crack eggs directly into a hot, live pan and stir with a stick until they break. let them cook, and when they appear done, remove them from the pan. sprinkle with a little vinegar and parsley.

title: Ova frictellate piene.
text: make fried eggs in the florentine style as described above, ensuring they are not overcooked. on one side of each egg, create a small pocket. carefully remove all the runny yolk from within these pockets. then, take a little grated pecorino cheese that is well-aged and fatty, along with a small amount of finely chopped mint and parsley, plus a few raisins and a pinch of pepper, and one or two raw egg yolks, or more, depending on the quantity you wish to make. mix all these ingredients together and stuff the eggs into the pockets you created. fry them again until the filling is cooked through, turning them frequently. to finish, drizzle with a little orange juice or lemon juice, and a touch of ginger.

title: Ova informa de raffioli.
text: make a pasta like lasagna, neither too thin nor too tender, and break fresh eggs into it, sprinkling it with sugar and sweet spices, along with a little salt. one by one, bind these eggs into the pasta as you would ravioli, and either boil or fry them as you prefer. but they will be better fried. similarly, prepare the eggs into the shape of small cakes, incorporating the ingredients mentioned above and adding a little lemon juice if you like, baking these cakes like a tart or frying them, but ensuring the eggs are not overcooked, because eggs become harder and worse the more they are cooked. finally, it should be generally noted that every fish to be boiled or fried should be scaled and scraped outside, then opened and the insides removed, washed very well. and the fish you want to roast should not be scaled or scraped or opened, except for the mackerel, which must be opened and all its insides removed, and similarly with the sea bass, a small

title: In che modo è meglio cocer lo storione.
text: cook the sturgeon, slightly aged, chopped or blanched, and not fresh. to achieve perfection, use a good white wine or vinegar mixed with pure water, equal parts of each, and enough salt. you will prepare it very well by simmering it for as long as you would beef or veal, according to its size, cutting it into large, substantial pieces as you deem best. however, if you desire it cooked whole for greater splendor, ensure you have large, capacious vessels to cook it whole, as my lord does, because a whole fish is always better than in pieces or otherwise.

title: Sapor di storione.
text: to give the sturgeon a very white and ginger flavor, or with good, white garlic, or with mustard, according to the seasons and appetites and these flavors you will prepare as described above in their chapters.

title: [Ombrina.]
text: the umbrina should be prepared and cooked in the manner of sturgeon, except that it should be boiled less, because it cooks more quickly, and you will give it the flavor i described for the sturgeon.

title: [Dentice.]
text: the fish should be dressed while very fresh it doesn't need to be seasoned with as much wine or vinegar as mentioned above. note that wine or vinegar tightens and preserves the fish, and also enhances its flavor when eaten, more so than simple salted water.

title: Uno varolo grosso.
text: cook it similarly as described when it weighs less than four or five pounds, fry it in good oil, or roast it on a grill, remembering as already stated that it should not be scratched or opened. make a brine with vinegar, oil, and plenty of salt and with a sprig of lavender or rosemary in hand, baste the fish with this brine frequently, turning it often over the grill, cooking it very well until it is thoroughly done. note that every fish, above all, must be well cooked, because by its nature it is moist, and if not well cooked, it is unhealthy.

title: Corvo grosso.
text: roast or fry it similarly to how the woodcock was prepared it should be small. if fried, a green sauce with a little garlic and plenty of ginger is best. you can also add mustard if you like.

title: Orata.
text: if the bream is large, simmer it and let it cool thoroughly. if it is small, fry or roast it in the usual way.

title: Rombo.
text: simmer it, and because it is very delicate and easily breaks, cook it in a basket, or tie it onto a cutting board. this will allow you to remove it whole when it is cooked, so that it does not break and it needs to be boiled thoroughly in clear water. note that all fish generally require simmering in clear water, and it is necessary to understand and know the quality of fish, as some are firmer and tougher than others, and some are more tender and softer. therefore, they should be cooked more or less according to need, but all require slow, gentle simmering in clear water until they are well cooked.

title: Soglie.
text: they should be fried, and sprinkled with a little salt, orange juice, or verjuice, and finely chopped parsley.

title: Palamita.
text: to prepare the mackerel or the bottom fish, as is done with sturgeon, giving them the same seasonings. and if small, fry both, as they cannot be roasted because they lack scales. and if you wish to fry larger ones, slice them into pieces crosswise, about the thickness of a finger or half a finger, and fry them until crisp. then pour over them plenty of orange juice with strong, good spices, and a little chopped parsley if you like.

title: Fraolino.
text: it will be good boiled, roasted, or fried, large or small its flavor is green sauce.

title: Triglie.
text: roast them with good care, and do not open them but simply wash them frequently with the aforementioned brine. if you wish to preserve them for eight or ten days, arrange them neatly on a plate or other vessel, and cover them completely with the same brine. this is how you can preserve them.

title: Salpa.
text: to be good when fried, clean it thoroughly. remove all the innards, as it contains a great deal of tripe and when you want to roast it, make the hole as small as possible.

title: Goze.
text: cook it gently, as its nature and quality are best when simmered, rather than otherwise.

title: Scorfeno.
text: when it grows up, it wants to be boiled. and when it's small, it wants to be fried.

title: [Occhiali.]
text: glasses are better fried or roasted than stewed.

title: [Sorgo.]
text: sorghum is good fried or roasted, however you like it.

title: Morena.
text: first, have it skinned or peeled with hot water, and discard the head and a piece of the tail. fry it well and serve with a green sauce flavored with garlic.

title: Maccarella.
text: they are meant to be fried, and are also good with pepper and parsley.

title: Cefalo.
text: this fish, by its nature and quality, is best roasted, but when it is very large, it should be boiled the flavor of the roast is salty, and that of the boiled is mild.

title: La passera.
text: it will be delicious seasoned with a little parsley. it is also good fried, drizzling it with orange juice.

title: Bestino.
text: simmer in a mixture of wine or vinegar and water, and for a strong flavor, add a little very potent garlic. be aware that this dish is very quick to prepare, more suitable for laborers than for refined palates.

title: Pesce cane.
text: simmer gently, as mentioned in the other chapter. then, with a strong garlic sauce mixed also with a little very hot mustard, fry a few together with these patties but handle it well as much as you can, it will never be good, because of its nature it is melancholy.

title: [Anguilla.]
text: to roast a large eel, skin and clean it very thoroughly. then, thread it onto a spit and cook it well over a low heat, as it is desired to be cooked more than other fish. to prepare it better, cut it into large pieces, about a hand's breadth or slightly more. small eels can be fried in oil. alternatively, you can stew both large and small eels, simmering them with fragrant herbs like parsley, sage, and a few bay leaves, along with some pepper and a little lemon juice.

title: Nocce.
text: to be added like freshwater clams, and its flavor will be that of vinegar.

title: Gamarelli marini.
text: simmer them similarly with fennel and add vinegar to taste.

title: [Ostriche.]
text: oysters are cooked over a hot grill and when they open, they are done and can be eaten. if you wish to prepare them differently, pierce them outside of their shell and fry them briefly in oil, then place them over vinegar and strong spices.

title: [Lampuga.]
text: fry the corvina with orange juice drizzled over it. it is also good roasted, first hollowing it out through the ear opening using a fork and the gutting tool mentioned earlier its flavor will be enhanced by green sauce. it is also very good pan-fried, and in this way it develops a white flavor.

title: Cappe.
text: have a dry skillet, and place the scallops over the heat. when they open, they are cooked therefore, as soon as you see them open, place a little lemon zest on top, along with pepper and finely chopped parsley. turn them once or twice with the skillet. you can also cook them over a hot iron plate or on embers, and when they open, they are cooked. but note that they should be kept, before you cook them, for a day or a night in well-salted water, so that it purges the sand they contain.

title: Merluzo.
text: simmer it, and you will give it a white mustard flavor.

title: Luccio d'acqua dolce.
text: cook it until it's large, first removing the inner core, but without scraping the outside, as you want the scales to come off when it's cooked and with it, you can add white sauce, garlic sauce, or mustard. and if the pike-perch is small, fry it.

title: Trutte grosse.
text: skin and fillet the trout very well, cutting it crosswise into pieces about the size of your hand. arrange these pieces in a pot or other vessel, ensuring the cut side faces up. season them generously with salt. once you ve done this with all the fish you intend to cook, add water carefully, ensuring the salt doesn't wash away, and add a little vinegar so the broth covers the fish by about two inches. bring to a boil, skimming off any foam that rises to the surface. once the foaming stops, reduce the heat to low and let it simmer gently until the fish is cooked through. remove from the heat and place on a clean board to drain, sprinkling it with sweet spices. this trout will have a wonderfully fragrant flavor thanks to the ginger. when the trout is small, skin and fillet it very well, cutting it lengthwise along the spine on both sides. season the cuts and the body generously with salt. let it sit on a cutting board with a weight

title: Tenche.
text: here are three good ways to prepare it. the first is when it is large, and you will enhance its flavor with a broth containing sorrel, spices, and finely chopped parsley and with a little of the same broth from the perch. the second way is to reverse it if it is large, scrape and clean it very well, splitting it from head to tail along the spine. remove all the insides and crush the ribs well on both sides. then take its roe, fat, and liver, and if you don't have perch, those of other fish will be good. have parsley and other fragrant herbs, beat them very well together with these livers and roe and fat, adding a little chopped garlic, that is, in small pieces, a little pepper, saffron, and salt, a little oil also, dried damascene plums or sour cherries or cherries or raisins or currants with some shelled pine nuts also, one or two fresh eggs, depending on

title: Persiche.
text: when it is large, it should be cleaned by removing the insides, without scraping anything out being very fresh, boil it in pure water when you cannot put a little vinegar with the water. once cooked, you will prepare it as you would the pike. and when it is small, it should be scraped and fried in oil. it is also good roasted, basting it with brine.

title: Lampreda.
text: soak it in water and scrape off the slime on top, but do not damage or break the skin, and test it with your tongue and teeth. at the bottom of the belly, where its sex is, you will make a small hole through which you can insert the tip of your finger, and with a knife or a sharp wooden skewer, you will lift up its entrails through that hole so that you can take them with your hand wrapped in a piece of cloth and pull them out gently, ensuring they come out whole and unbroken, because the lamprey has nothing bad in its body, except for these entrails. you will collect all its blood very well, which is used to flavor it, and in its mouth, you will put half a nutmeg, and in all the small holes near the head, you will put a clove. in this way, you will place the lamprey in a clay pot large enough to hold it, and inside you will put half an ounce of

title: Barbo.
text: cook it as you like, but it is not considered good fish and its eggs are dangerous to eat, especially in may.

title: Temolo.
text: temolo is an excellent fish, and cook it as you like, for it is good in any way, but it is best fried.

title: Cancro marino.
text: roast it in the way that eel is, that is, between pieces, placing a sage leaf or bay leaf.

title: Gambari.
text: simmer them by adding a little water and vinegar, using an equal amount of each, and plenty of salt. don't add too much liquid, as they will release their own. bring to a vigorous boil until they foam and the foam rises to the surface two or three times, as described. then they should be done, but to be sure, taste them and you won't be disappointed.

title: Gamari pieni.
text: cook the cockles as described in the previous chapter and, with the tip of your knife, open them carefully on the right side, cutting along the legs and emptying them of everything inside, including the contents of the tail and the flanks. grind the tail and flank contents with almonds and a few raisins. when the mixture resembles an egg's consistency, add an egg yolk or more, depending on the quantity you want to make. also add a little cheese, a little parsley, and marjoram, finely chopped. with this mixture, stuff the cockles and fry them in good oil over low heat until they are as dry as possible. if it's lent, do not add egg or cheese. if you want to vary the stuffing, use ground almonds with sugar and rosewater, and stuff the flanks, or half of the cockles from one batch and the other half from another.

title: Lione de mare.
text: season the mouths and the hole beneath the tail well with flour, so that its goodness doesn't escape, and place it dry in a hot oven, or over a well-cleaned and swept hearth, arranging the embers in a circle around it, far enough away so they don't touch. this is done so that it cooks better and faster. turn it often to prevent burning. alternatively, if you like, you can braise it with water and vinegar, like partridges, boiling it a little longer, as it is larger and tougher than other partridges. and for its flavor, add vinegar.

title: Laguste.
text: roast them over the embers as described above, cooking them in the manner of a lion.

title: Scarde.
text: cook it as you please, as there is no fat and it s fish that doesn t require special treatment.

title: Carpani.
text: boil them when they are large, and you can also roast them. fry them when they are small.

title: [Salmone.]
text: salmon is a very agreeable fish and is best prepared by salting it, but it would also be good cooked in any other way.

title: Lasche.
text: they should be fried in olive oil so they don t burn, and to enhance their flavor, serve with green sauce or verjus.

title: Lactarini.
text: they should be fried, and to enhance their flavor, serve them with green sauce, or green verjuice.

title: Roviglioni.
text: fry gently, and from that obtain the flavor described in the previous chapter.

title: Uselie
text: it is naturally best served chilled, but it is also good boiled and roasted.

title: Tordo marino.
text: make it soften if it's large, and if it's small, fry it. to enhance the flavor, serve it with mustard.

title: Agoni d'acqua dolce.
text: they are good with parsley, butter, and spices similarly, they are good fried with orange juice or sorrel on top.

title: Sardelle.
text: fry them, and then roast them if you like. serve them with a sauce of oranges or lemons mixed with a little oil.

title: [Polpi.]
text: cook the octopus as you like.

title: Granci.
text: make them in the way described for the quince in its chapter, and with them, you will give it a vinegar flavor.

title: [Anguilla.]
text: regarding eel, it has been discussed elsewhere sufficiently, but for remembrance, when you place the pieces of eel onto the spit one by one, always place a sage leaf or a bay leaf between each piece, turning the spit as much as possible. often you will moisten it with a salt water as described above. and when the pieces seem nearly cooked, have a little flour, or a little grated bread mixed with a little cinnamon and salt, and sprinkle it directly over the eel to create a crust around it, which will give it a good flavor. and when it is small, you can boil it with water and wine, herbs, and spices, as mentioned in the previous chapter.

title: Carpioni.
text: have a brine prepared in the way they do for other salted fish, and as soon as you get the carp, immediately put it in that brine, leaving it there for two days in the same brine, and then fry it in plenty of good oil, ensuring it is well cooked and in this way you will be able to preserve these carp for twenty days, and even for a month and longer, by refrying them, two or three times. but note that the more times you fry them, the more they lose substance and become worse this method of refrying is only to make them last longer. if it is large, you will need to blanch it, and fry the smaller ones, being careful to avoid the spine in the head, which is poisonous.

title: Calamari.
text: wash the calamari thoroughly. the smaller they are, the better. a good washing will plump them up, as they say about tench. and even better if you know how. fry them in good oil, sprinkling them with orange juice and some good spices. then, if they are large, simmer them, cutting them into pieces like veal or beef tripe, with a little broth. ensure they are well cooked, and add chopped parsley and more spices. alternatively, if the calamari are large, prepare them this way first wash them with a little white wine, a little grape must, and a little sapa, pressing out the dark liquid together with these ingredients this liquid is what gives the flavor. take an ounce of toasted almonds, scorched with hot ashes, and grind them very well with a little toasted bread, or not, as you prefer, mixing them together. combine all these ingredients with the calamari washing mentioned above pass everything through a sieve. simmer the

title: Gelatina di pesce.
text: you will need water, wine, and vinegar, and to ensure it is preserved and lasts longer, use little water and plenty of spices. to know which fish is best and most substantial for making broth for jelly, i tell you that the perch and pike are the best, and the fatter and larger they are, the better. note that this type of fish should not be scraped, but only opened, and it must be very fresh, cooking it gently over low heat in a little broth so that it is only just covered, and this so that the broth absorbs more substance. when you think the fish is well cooked, remove it and peel it completely, setting it aside, but return its skin to the broth to boil for a quarter of an hour. when you think it has boiled sufficiently, strain the broth very well, observing all the order and method described in the chapter on meat jelly, both to make it clear and beautiful as in every other thing, remembering that this should have and

title:
Per far gelatina di carne o di pesce de duo o tre colori in
un vaso.
text: to prepare it, use white vinegar or verjuice, and with it, put in two parts water. you will need about a pound of skinned and thoroughly cleaned calf's testicles or kid, cut across, removing the bones that is, the leg joints and washing them very well in cold water. then, put them to boil in this mixture of vinegar and water, boiling it as dry as possible, adding to it some well-cleaned and chopped ginger, and a few crushed grains of paradise. when the feet seem cooked, take them out and let the broth without them boil for a while longer. then, have ready ten fresh white eggs, more or less, according to the quantity you want to make, observing all the instructions for clarifying and making the jelly, as mentioned in the chapter on meat jelly. have your plates prepared with capons or chickens, or whatever you want to put in the jelly, and place this elegantly prepared broth on top, putting the plates in a

title: Gelatina in un canestro.
text: prepare a flavorful broth and set it aside. have a new basket or woven container ready and line it neatly with poultry or other meat, as you would arrange it on a plate. have another clean, spacious bowl in which the basket will fit. place it inside the bowl, pouring the broth over the meat, and set the whole thing in a cool place to chill and set. once it is thoroughly chilled, use a knife and warm it slightly. run the knife around the inside of the basket to help remove it from the bowl more easily, carefully wiping the basket clean all around with a white cloth or in another way. this will allow you to transport the jelly within the basket wherever you like. you can also make this jelly in a mold if you prefer. during lent, you can prepare it in the same way, using fresh, healthy fish that looks lively and appealing.

title: A conoscer el bono schinale.
text: slice it crosswise into half-finger-width pieces or thereabouts and trim them well. cook them over a grill, turning frequently and basting continuously with a mixture of oil and vinegar, using equal parts of each. be careful not to overcook them, as they are done when the heat of the fire has penetrated them evenly then drizzle them with the aforementioned oil and vinegar and serve. to tell when it is cooked and good, slice it and, finding it well-colored and reddish, it will be a good sign. but be careful that it is not too old and does not have a rancid smell.

title: Per far el caviaro d'ova di storione et etiamdio cocerlo.
text: lightly toast slices of bread until they are slightly golden, and thinly slice the caviar, similar in size to the bread but a bit thinner. arrange the caviar slices over the bread. using the back of a knife or a suitable fork, expose the slices to heat until the caviar hardens and forms a slightly browned crust. alternatively, wash the caviar thoroughly in lukewarm water to reduce the saltiness. finely chop some fresh herbs, grate some white bread crumbs, and finely chop and lightly sauté a little onion. add a glass of water and mix all these ingredients together with the caviar, then make one or more omelets, frying them as you would egg omelets. to prepare the caviar, use sturgeon eggs from the season when the sturgeon are at their best. remove all the internal membranes from the eggs, rinsing them with good white vinegar or good white wine. spread the eggs on a table and let them dry. then, place them in a jar, salting them

title: Uno bono terantello.
text: to remove the salt, soak in water with a little vinegar and plenty of bran, then bring to a simmer. cook gently, but not too vigorously, until done. remove and drain, then soak in vinegar. the fatter it is, the better it will be. it should be from the belly of tuna, firm and dense, not soft.

title: La tonnina.
text: soak it in lukewarm water for six hours, changing the water two or three times, and simmer it briefly, that is, two or three boils, then remove it and place it in vinegar.

title: Anguilla salata.
text: skin the eel and cut it into large pieces by hand, boiling it in water for half an hour then drain the water and place it in fresh cold water, continuing to boil until cooked through. remove from the heat and place in vinegar with parsley.

title: Trutte salate o altro pesce salato de aqua dolce.
text: soak them in lukewarm water for four or five hours, then boil them in water for over an hour, or less, depending on whether they are large or small. you will do the same with any other salted fish. remember that in all cases and with all types of fish, it is always best to pair the older fish with younger meat, as the saying goes old fish, young meat.

title: Butarghe.
text: use very fresh catfish or mullet roe. if you want them to be at their best, use roe that is in season, and be careful not to break the thin membrane surrounding the roe. sprinkle them with finely chopped salt, using discretion so it s not too much or too little, and let them sit like this, turning them over with your finger for about a day. then place them in a colander for a day and a night. once this is done, remove them and expose them to smoke, far enough from the fire that they don't feel any heat at all dry them thoroughly to preserve them, and store them in a wooden box or barrel with plenty of bran. these bottarga are commonly eaten raw. but if you prefer them cooked, warm them under the ashes, or on a hot, clean hearth, turning them over until they are heated through.

title: Carpionar trutte al modo di carpioni.
text: clean the trout very well and hollow them out, pricking them in many places with the tip of a knife from every side. prepare a brine of water and vinegar, using equal parts of each, and adding a generous amount of salt, ensuring it is very well dissolved. place the trout in the brine for half a day or longer. once done, remove them and place them on a board to dry for three or four hours. then, fry them well in good, abundant oil until they are thoroughly cooked but not burnt. these trout can be preserved for a month by frying them again when desired and preparing them like fried fish.

title:
Per fare uno luccio o altro pesce grosso
che sia cotto sano in tre modi.
text: take a large fish, clean it out very thoroughly. tie around the head a band or strip of wet cloth to cover one-third of the fish this is to protect the area that will be poached. then, turning to the tail, scrape the other third of the fish, slicing this part from the tail slightly on each side, as you would when preparing a fish for frying. begin by cooking this tail section, frying it with care so as not to damage the rest. once that s done, you will need a thin board cut to the length and width of the fish, upon which you will carefully secure the fish to prevent it from breaking. then, place the head section, tied with the band, to simmer, tying it as it is, ensuring the broth doesn t touch the fish except as covered by the band. once poached and cooked sufficiently, remove it gently from the board, being careful not to break it. place it on a rack, creating a

title: Ova contrafacte in Quadragesima.
text: use almonds and pine nuts as white as possible. soak the pine nuts thoroughly with a little rosewater so they don t release oil. temper them with good, fresh, and substantial broth of fat tench, or with a little rosewater, and pass them through a straining cloth to make milk. you will need about half a pound of rice, more or less, carefully washed and polished. cook the rice very well in half of the almond milk. take about three ounces of the finest, whitest semolina flour you can find, and work it into the remaining milk until it is completely dissolved. then bring this milk and semolina to a boil, stirring continuously with a wooden spoon and being careful not to let it scorch. once this is done, add the rice and all the milk to the straining cloth and force it through with your hands. the thicker the mixture, the better it will be. don t forget to add plenty of sugar.

title: Riso in miglior modo che quel de sopra.
text: wash the rice with warm water until it s very white and spread it out on a cutting board to drain. then, dry it and boil it with goat s milk or almond milk, cooking it until done. this is because the milk gives it a better consistency than cooking it in water. add salt sparingly so it s not too salty. and if you want it to be good, don t skimp on the sugar, but add it generously.

title: Pastello volativo.
text: make a very large pastry shell, and in the bottom make a hole large enough to fit your fist, or larger if you prefer, and let the sides around be a little higher than usual, and bake it in the oven after coating it with flour. once baked, remove the hole s contents, taking out the flour, and you will have prepared another small pastry, well-cooked and seasoned, shaped to fit the hole underneath. you will place it inside the larger shell, and in the space that remains around the smaller pastry, you will put live birds, as many as it can hold. these little birds should be placed so that they fly out when the dish is brought to the table you will remove the lid as it is served before those seated at the feast, allowing the birds to fly away. this is to provide entertainment and delight for the young people. and so that they are not disappointed, you will have them cut small pieces of the pastry. and as i say,

title: I
text: here's the translation of the latin recipe into modern english concerning wine, it is fitting that our discourse begin with it, since it is to be preferred above all other drinks. for wine strengthens the limbs, aids digestion, alters bad humors, removes sadness and pains, and makes a man cheerful and pleasant. and i say this if it is good and not corrupted, and consumed with moderation. for corrupted wine does the opposite, impedes digestion, spoils food, generates bad blood, and makes a man sad, sluggish, and heavy. therefore, as will be described elsewhere, it is better and more commendable to preserve something in its goodness, lest it be corrupted, than to restore something already corrupted to its former state and this applies to wine since it is more valuable than other drinks, it is more important to work diligently to preserve it in its goodness, and even if it has been corrupted through negligence, to find a way to restore it to

title: III
text: fish recipes now sufficient has been said about meats. it remains to direct the title of our discourse to fish, and first about oysters. 1. -- oysters are boiled in pure water for a short time. afterward, cinnamon, ginger, pepper, and cumin are finely ground together with saffron, and mixed with wine or almond milk and a little water, and brought to a boil in a pan with fried onions. when it begins to boil, add the boiled oysters. serve. 2. -- mackerel or salmon are cut lengthwise and boiled in salted sweet water until sufficiently cooked. once cooked and cooled, they can be preserved in aspic. or in this way sage and parsley are finely chopped and placed in salt vinegar, or finely ground in a mortar and mixed with vinegar, in which the aforementioned fish are preserved. 3. -- moray eels or eels can be boiled or baked in an oven or pastry in this way first, the eel is stripped of its

title: IV
text: recipes from the text 1. blancmanger begin by thoroughly cleaning and rinsing rice in clear water. pound it in a mortar until it resembles flour. then, take well-cooked meat from chicken breasts, thinly slicing it into small pieces, and pound these finely in the mortar. simmer in almond milk, hazelnut milk, or egg milk, adding sugar. next, add the rice flour and simmer briefly, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon to prevent burning. if you desire a yellow color, mix with the previously mentioned milk and saffron. afterwards, sprinkle a dish with powdered sugar, and over that, a little chilled water, otherwise the sugar will melt. around the edge, place peeled almonds mixed with saffron and fried in oil or honey. some people soak the rice in water for an hour then they let it stand to swell afterwards, they add almond milk as described. this can also be made with barley or oats. 2. mistembec

title: V
text: a culinary compendium 1. fruit fool take ripe pears, slightly tart, and prepare them well, removing any excess pulp. grind them very finely, then mix with milk, raw egg yolks, and saffron. add sweet butter and wheat flour if desired. 2. toasted butter to toast butter, first place a scrap of bread in a pan. surround the butter with fresh bread and place over the fire, turning it as it moves away from the heat. as it begins to taste done, sprinkle with wheat flour until it hardens. it is a delightful and good dish and if you wish, you can season it with spices and salt. 3. green soup to make green soup, first boil the greens themselves, finely chopped and washed, in a pot for a short time. then, drain the water and chop in a mortar with the necessary salt. place in a pot or a cyprion bowl and sprinkle with a little vinegar

title: I
text: recipe translations 1. -- to properly prepare white turnips, peel their outer layers, ensuring no leaves remain. when a pot of water is boiling over the fire, place the peeled turnips or turnip tops inside with the aforementioned water, and add a bit of fennel tops. boil only until they are tender. and instead of oil, you may add meat broth. 2. -- regarding greens for green tops, according to the emperor's custom, take healthy turnip greens and place them in a boiling cauldron with meats, and boil well. then, after removing them, place them in cold water. take another broth in a separate vessel, add fennel tops, and boil them. and when it is time to eat, place the aforementioned tops with the broth in the aforementioned vessel and let it simmer slightly. 3. -- during lent, thinly sliced turnip tops. afterward, drain the broth and fry in a pan or skillet with onions and oil. then,

title: III
text: 1. on a grated dish to make a grated dish, take sheep's milk and thin it. beat the milk vigorously with eggs and place lard in a pan near the fire, so that it is very hot. afterwards, with a perforated spoon, sprinkle the milk into the pan throughout. afterwards, when the mixture has cooked sufficiently, remove from the fire, and add sugar on top. 2. on a spanish grated dish in the aforementioned grated dish, add beaten egg whites, cut into strips and it will be called a spanish grated dish. you can color this as you wish. 3. on a porridge to make a porridge with milk when vermicelli or alexandrian grains are present, take milk and bring it to a boil. and when the milk has boiled, pick out the vermicelli and you will be able to place the aforementioned porridge before the milk boils. and lard or fresh drippings, spread upon it,

title: IV
text: here's the english translation of the latin recipe, as requested regarding fish. and first, about galantines for a fish galantine, take good wine and a little foaming vinegar. boil them together and when they have boiled, cut a large fish crosswise with its insides. cook them together with this. when cooked, remove the fish and let the wine remaining boil down until only about a third remains. then add saffron and other good powdered spices with bay leaves. next, remove the fish and clean it from the insides. some people pound the aforementioned insides with the aforementioned wine in a mortar and mix them into a paste. they add more wine to this paste to help it bind. and when this galantine has cooled, place fish scraps inside and let it stand for one day or night, or longer, until it is completely bound. and in this way, the fish can be preserved for a long time. about fish roe for roe,

title: V
text: translations of latin recipes 1. -- concerning composed foods, and first of all, fritters to fritters, add fresh figs with white spices, sugar, and almonds. and make a good fritter and keep. 2. -- also, take fresh figs with fragrant herbs and pistachios together with good spices. and mix with broth so that it remains thick. and thus you will have a good fritter. 3. -- from these two fritters, reserve half or more. from this half of the aforementioned fritters, make ravioli and tarts, savory pastries of various colors, and lasagna with diverse fillings, adding these pistachios. 4. -- also, take greek beans, figs finely chopped, and mix with walnuts and pistachios. place a little in a mortar, arranged, with the aforementioned on top of one solar layer, making other solar layers from almond milk boiled and thickened and others from walnuts with chopped figs and the aforementioned reserved

title:
HERMOLAVS
Barbarus enuoie salut à
Pierre Cara iureconsulte
& facondissime
Orateur.
text: first, water was brought to wash the hands, not as is customary standing, but presented to each person while seated, and the water was rose-colored. then, immediately, came pine nuts on a tablet and rock made of sugar, rosewater, and pine nuts, and after that, tart and marzipan made of sugar, rosewater, and almonds, which we commonly call martian breads. the second course was new asparagus. the third course consisted of the heart, liver, and stomach of birds, seasoned. the fourth course was roasted venison. the fifth course was the heads of calves and oxen boiled with their skins. the sixth course was chickens, pullets, pigeons accompanied with beef tongues, ham of pork, all boiled, seasoned with lemon sauce this is how milanese cooks call it, which venetian cooks call sermiaque. the seventh course was the dormouse, whole, roasted, on each plate in a silver, quadrilateral

title: EXTRAICT DV PRIVILEGE.
text: to open the kitchen ingredients 12 eggs 1 pound of butter 1 pound of sugar 1 pound of fine flour a quarter pound of ground almonds a quarter pound of rosewater a drachm of salt instructions beat the eggs well, then add the sugar and butter, working them together until they are light and fluffy. incorporate the flour and ground almonds, and then add the rosewater and salt. mix everything thoroughly. grease a baking pan and pour in the batter. bake in a moderate oven until golden brown.
ingredients: eggs butter sugar flour ground almonds rosewater

title:
A MONSIEVR IEAN
CVRTIVS Sr. D'OVPIE, VIVEgnis,
Hermée grande & petite, Aaz,
Visschervverdt, Soumaigne, Mont
St. Halin, Tilheur, &c.
text: as a seasoned soldier, accustomed to wielding his arms, i recall the great works i have undertaken, frequenting the kitchens of several princes and princesses. i have been eager to compile a small collection of recipes to present to you, knowing you are a lover of all virtues. however, without making a grand display as the ancient masters used to do i have desired to bring to light several little delicacies unknown to many. here you will find everything well-proportioned by weight and measure, in order to teach those who are not yet experienced in the art of cooking properly and perfectly. and so that i am not reproached for excessive extravagance in my writings, you will also find several recipes for modest fare, where everyone can choose what pleases them. i beseech you not to take offense at this small effort of mine, praying the creator to grant you a long and happy life, and the fulfillment of your good and virtuous desires. your humble servant, lancelot

title: AV LECTEVR
text: here's a translation of the recipe text into modern english reader, you may find it strange that the cooks here have circled around the kitchen without entering the door. to induce you further, i present here the opening of the kitchen, so you can see what will be most agreeable, just as a merchant seeks out different merchandise. thus, each cook can look in this book to see what is most pleasing to them, for you will find here several kinds and ways of preparing meats, only to help and advance them. i excuse myself for any faults you may find, not having the memory as recent as before, praying god grant you a long and happy life. which treats the instruction for preparing a meat dish, and what is ordinarily needed, and for making several kinds of pies.

title:
BRIEF ENSEIGNEment 
pour petit ordinaire de Cuisine.
text: as many ladies willingly take an interest in cooking, often better than some cooks, in several ways and manners therefore, to please the ladies, here will be found a small introduction to know how they should order their affairs, namely what is needed for a meat dish, and what a meat dish is you must calculate for a meat dish ten people, and serve as follows.

title:
Pour le premier & deuxiesme 
seruice.
text: boiled chicken. cream of cauliflower soup. meat pie or hashed pie. beef hash. sheep s foot. roasted suckling pig or duck. fried calf s liver. leg of lamb or salted meat. calf s hash. roasted cow s udder. roasted mutton. beef tripe. sausage in soup. boiled mutton. duck giblets, or another sauté. roasted hare.

title: Pour accoustrer les viandes susdites.
text: when the capon is almost cooked, put in rosemary, marjoram, mace, a salted lemon cut into slices, a measure of white wine or vinegar, and butter, some beef marrow bones, and let them simmer together, with slices of white bread underneath.

title: Potages de choux floris.
text: add to the soup some sausages, a little chicken or pigeon, or mutton stew, and a bit of chopped mint.

title: Heuspot de boeuf.
text: stew beef with herbs and stuffed roots, with minced veal and beef fat combined, finely chopped. add two or three raw eggs, nutmeg, pepper, and ginger, a little salt, mint, and chopped marjoram, all well mixed. fill the roots and stew your heuspot altogether.

title: Foye de veau frit.
text: slice the foie gras and dredge it in white flour. fry it in black butter and top with pepper and orange juice.

title: Heuspot de veau.
text: veal stew, being half-cooked, with marjoram and chopped mint, nutmeg, a handful of genovese basil leaves, butter, a little white wine or vinegar, and butter. simmer well. if you prefer it differently, take egg yolk and beat it with wine and vinegar, without adding any herbs.

title: Tetin de vache.
text: for the calf's head, once cleaned and cooked, place it in a veal cloth and tie it securely, then put it on a spit. for the calf s head sauce, take two or three slices of white bread that are not burned, and soak them in broth with vinegar. mash the bread with four or five egg yolks, and add nutmeg, cinnamon, ginger, saffron, and sugar. boil it all together, then pour it over the roasted calf s head.

title: Saulcisses en potage.
text: take the sausages and brown them in butter. then take four or five peeled apples, cut into small pieces, and four or five onions, sliced into rounds, and brown them in butter. add everything to a pot with the sausages, and add nutmeg, cinnamon, with white or red wine, sugar, and let it simmer like this. as for the rest, like roast, and other things as written above.

title: Pour le deuxiesme seruice.
text: roast partridge. roast small birds. venison stew. roast veal. chicken pie. mutton stew. capon roast. oranges olives. pie in a pot. veal coated in pastry. roast chicken. boiled pigeons. roast kid. mushrooms. another veal coated in pastry. white meat stew. mayence ham. tongue and pie. another kind of veal.

title: Heuspot de venaison.
text: for a stew of venison, whether wild boar or deer, take burnt bread and pass it through a sieve. add nutmeg, pepper, cloves, and powder, sugar, cinnamon, red wine, two or three finely chopped onions, and brown in butter. simmer all together until it is shining.

title: Veau reuestu.
text: take a veal shank, and cut away the skin to leave half a pound of meat. take half a pound of beef fat and chop it finely, mixing it well with the meat. add a little nutmeg, a pinch of ginger, four raw eggs, a little salt, and some finely chopped herbs. then shape the mixture into a small ham shape, and place a small chicken foot at the top to form the ham's handle. insert cloves all over the ham and place it in a baking dish. bake it in the oven or over coals. for the sauce, take white or red wine and add sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, and pepper, along with dried quince and boiled orange peel cut into strips like tripe, and boil everything together. cut a heuspot into pieces and take parsnip or radish roots, cut very finely, and simmer them with mutton. alternatively, use peeled chestnuts instead of the roots in the heuspot.

title: Pigeons bouillis.
text: once the pigeons are cooked, take rich broth, take six yolks of raw eggs, and beat them with white wine, then take a small handful of finely chopped parsley, and put it into the eggs, and when it begins to boil, throw the eggs in, and remove from the heat, fearing they will turn to scrambled eggs. in summer, add wood pigeon or teal.

title: Autre sorte de veau.
text: take a veal shank and boil it until cooked through. for every pound of meat, take half a pound of beef fat and chop it finely. mix everything together, then add nutmeg, a pinch of cinnamon powder, enough sugar to sweeten it, half a pint of cream, four raw eggs, and a little salt. combine well and place in a pie dish, then bake it in the oven or over charcoal. once cooked, cut it into small pieces and serve on a plate with five or six portions, sprinkled with sugar and cinnamon.

title: Autre sorte de veau reuestu.
text: take the meat and prepare it as you made the jambon. shape it into round balls or long pieces like small sausages, and simmer them in a good broth. add a slice of lemon, mint, marjoram, and a little vinegar or wine. simmer well, and serve in this way.

title: Pour le fruict.
text: poached pears. marzipan. sweet orange or cinnamon. apple tart, or other. chestnuts. roasted pears. biscuits. poached prunes. donuts. jam. raw apples. anise. plum tart. candied ginger. sweet rolls. walnuts or hazelnuts. sweet almonds. butter cheese. you choose the fruits according to the season if you want anything else, look at the end of the book.

title:
Pour faire paste de bugnolle
ou friture.
text: take a bowl of cream and heat it in a pan with a little butter. then add sifted flour and make a dough in the pan over the heat, mixing well with a wooden spoon. break four eggs into the dough and beat them thoroughly with the spoon, ensuring the eggs are well incorporated. then, take another four eggs and beat them again until the dough is soft, like a pear in consistency. you need to add enough eggs to make the dough sufficiently soft. next, take some well-churned butter, with the salt discarded, and place the butter in a pan to heat slightly. then, using a silver spoon about the size of an egg cup, take a portion of the dough and drop it into the warm butter. add eighteen or twenty at a time, and turn them frequently with a skimmer, allowing them to cook until they begin to crack. remove them from the pan, and if the dough still seems too wet, return them to the butter until they are cooked

title: De ceste mesme paste.
text: have a mould or syringe with a small iron inside, having two or three holes, or one if you wish, and pass the pastry through a sieve, and cook it in butter like the others.

title: Autrement.
text: take this pastry and roll it out on a board to the width of a hand, about the thickness of a little finger and cut it with a knife into strips like lardons. then drop them into hot butter and cook as you would the others.

title: Autrement.
text: make a sheet of this pastry. weigh out four ounces of melted butter and four ounces of powdered sugar, and beat them together well. take paper that has been well-greased with butter, then with a spoon, place the pastry on the paper like a small loaf, sprinkle with sugar, and bake it in the oven. serve four or five on a plate.

title: D'vne autre sorte.
text: take white bread dough, kneaded until smooth, and form it into a long strip no thicker than half a little finger and the width of a hand, well-greased with melted butter, and sprinkle powdered sugar over it. roll the dough over itself, and cut the dough to the width of two fingers, and flatten the dough with your hand, and place it on greased paper, and sprinkle sugar over it, and place it in the oven to bake. once baked, sprinkle sugar and cinnamon on top, and serve three or four in a dish. as you see how much meat is needed on a meat day, so you must adapt the fish, that is, all blue-water fish are cooked with water, verjuice, salt or vinegar.

title: Carpe en potage.
text: take a well-scaled and cleaned carp, and cut it into four pieces. then take some fried onions in butter, a salted lemon cut into slices, a little nutmeg, a bit of ginger, marjoram, and finely chopped mint. add wine or vinegar, and butter, and simmer well, along with a little beer.

title:
Pour faire brochet a la mode de 
Hongrie.
text: take a pike that is well scaled and cleaned, then take some onions and apples sliced into rounds, and sauté them over butter, ensuring the butter doesn't brown. scatter them over the pike, then add slivered blanched almonds. season with sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, and saffron, a little salt, and simmer well.

title:
Brochet d'vne autre 
sorte.
text: take a well-cleaned pike and boil it with salted water and vinegar. then break it into pieces to remove the bones, and chop the pike very finely, placing it in a small pot or dish. add a finely chopped fresh lemon or lime, nutmeg, a little pepper, and fresh butter, white wine, and a little orange. simmer everything together.

title: Pour faire vn haché de carpe.
text: take a well-cleaned carp, and cut all the fish down to the bone, and chop it very finely with as much fresh salmon as carp, then take two dried bocheaux or hares and wash them well two or three times in hot water, then take the bocheaux' kidneys out, and chop them with the carp and salmon, and sauté them in butter, and put them in a pot, then add nutmeg, pepper, cloves, currants, sugar, red wine, and plums, and stew it well together.

title: Vne autre sorte.
text: take the same fish, minced, and add two egg yolks before the fish is fricasséed. make small balls from this fish, like meatballs, and stew them with a little water and wine, butter, mint, and marjoram, serving seven or eight in a dish.

title: Brochet d'vne autre sorte.
text: take the pike when it is cooked, and remove the skin, placing it in a dish. add a little water and fresh butter, and set it over the heat. then, take five or six yolks of eggs, beaten with a little white wine, and add nutmeg. when it begins to boil, pour the egg mixture over it, and let it remain on the heat a little longer until it sets firmly on top, and serve in that way.

title:
Pour faire des oeufs lombards de 
plusieurs sortes.
text: take a dozen fresh yolks. beat them with a measure of spanish wine, a little butter, and some sugar. put them in a small pot over the heat until they begin to thicken slightly. stir constantly with a spoon until the mixture resembles a thick apple sauce, then serve on a plate.

title: Autrement.
text: take the same eggs, and take slices of white bread toasted over the grill without burning, and spread the eggs on the toasted bread to a thickness of half a finger, then put them in a dish with butter, and malmsey or spanish wine, and heat them very hot, sprinkle with sugar and cinnamon, and serve thus.

title: Pour faire des oeufs fueiltès.
text: beat the eggs well, and make thin sheets like paper, placing seven or eight on a table. then take powdered sugar and cinnamon mixed together, and sprinkle over the sheets. layer the sheets on top of each other, forming a roll. cut the roll into slices about two finger widths thick. dip the slices all around in the beaten eggs, and fry them in butter, turning them five or six times, or more, until you see the leaves open. sprinkle with sugar and cinnamon.

title: Premierement des choux floris.
text: choux of savoy. red cabbage. white cabbage. green cabbage. parsnip roots. celery root. fennel roots. parsley roots. yellow roots. red roots. turnips. salsify roots. peas. broad beans and small beans. leeks. onions. garlic. red chickpeas. artichokes. melon. cucumber. radishes. white and black sea bass. truffle. chestnuts. orange apple. pomegranate apple. fresh lemon. salted lemon. olive. cappers of genoa. cappers of barbary. cappers of malix. cappers of genuf. green leek. swiss chard or lombardy spinach. lamb s lettuce. borage leaves. bugloss leaves. anise. cat'

title:
Les herbes qu'il faut
pour faire des verdes
votes.
text: valerian. mint. scarlet runner beans. button mushrooms. melon. napoleon pastry. wood sorrel. violet leaves. tansy.

title:
Les herbes pour les huspots
ordinaires.
text: rosemary. marjoram. basil. oregano. bay leaf. sage. parsley. myrtle. hyssop. savory.

title:
Herbes qu'il faut pour
la salade.
text: lettuce or lamb's lettuce. dragon lettuce. rocket. mint. butter lettuce. alencon cress. borage leaves. bugloss leaves. bugloss flowers. borage flowers. these are the herbs commonly needed in the kitchen.

title: Pour faire blanc menger.
text: take a capon or hen that has been killed two or three days, and put it to cook. once cooked, remove the breast and cut it into small pieces, then pound them in a mortar. add two or three tablespoons of cow's milk, then add seven pounds and ten ounces of cow's milk and one pound of very fine rice flour, and thoroughly mix the flour with the capon meat. combine everything with the milk mentioned above. then add one and a half pounds of sugar, which should be very white. put it in a saucepan over the fire, and stir constantly with a wooden spoon. after boiling for a quarter of an hour, add eight ounces of rosewater, a little salt, and let it simmer for another quarter of an hour. then remove from the heat and pour it into a dish, cups, or square molds.

title: Pour faire blanc menger bastard.
text: take half a pound of peeled almonds and grind them very finely. then take a jug of white wine and warm it well, then pass the almonds with the wine and let it cool. next, take five ounces of rice flour and a little chicken meat, like the other, and beat it until it s white, like the almond mixture. add half a pound of sugar, three ounces of rosewater, a pinch of salt, and let it simmer like the other white mixture.

title: Pour faire tourtes de blanc manger.
text: take eight ounces of white meat, three yolks of eggs, a little melted butter, and mix all together well. make a pastry with fine flour, eggs, and butter, a little water, and ensure the pastry isn't too stiff. then beat the pastry well for a quarter of an hour. next, make thin and delicate crusts, and place two on top of each other, brushing melted butter between them. put these two crusts into a tart pan, then add the white meat on top. take four more crusts and butter between them as before, and cover the tart. cut the top crust decoratively and prepare the tart according to the art, then let it bake as usual.

title:
Pour faire tourtes de veau à 
la creme.
text: prepare twelve ounces of veal and cook it. then take half a pound of beef fat and chop everything together. beat three raw eggs, four ounces of sugar, half an ounce of cinnamon, a nutmeg, a little salt, and half a spoonful of cream, mixing everything well. then make your pie as you wish.

title:
Pour faire tourtes de 
Portugal.
text: take meat and fat, finely chopped, and add four ounces of sugar, half an ounce of cinnamon, a mace, a little salt instead of cream, a spoonful of mulberries, two raw eggs, and mix everything well together. place the mixture into the pastry crust. then, take candied fruits, sliced into small pieces, and scatter them over the meat filling. cover the pie and cut vents in the top crust. once baked, sprinkle with colored sugar and mace, and serve.

title: Pour faire tourtes cremoneze verdes.
text: take spinach and boil it, then chop it finely. add a handful of mint, finely chopped, two ounces of good grated parmesan cheese, four ounces of melted butter, three ounces of sugar, two ounces of candied citron peel, two raw eggs, a pinch of cinnamon, and two nutmegs. prepare tarts as the others, sprinkle with sugar, and serve.

title: Pour faire tourtes de ius d'herbes.
text: take a handful of parsley and a handful of your favorite herbs, and mix them well, adding a little nutmeg. then, pass these herbs through a sieve with a spoonful of cream, adding four raw eggs, four ounces of sugar, half an ounce of cinnamon, and a little salt. next, make a crust of pastry dough and place it in a heated oven. pour the cream mixture inside and bake like a flan.

title: Pour faire tourtes badraye.
text: prepare mashed potatoes or fried potatoes. then add three ounces of good, rich cheese, cut into small pieces. next, add a handful of chervil, finely chopped and sautéed in butter, and mix everything together. make a rich pastry for the pie and bake it thoroughly. sprinkle with sugar and cinnamon on top, and note that the top crust should be cut to your liking.

title: Pour faire tourtes de poires de coing.
text: take candied quince slices, then a twelfth part of dates, well cleaned and cut into slices. next, take four yolks of eggs and beat them with a spoonful of muscatel or spanish wine, and add two ounces of sugar, a pinch of cinnamon, a nutmeg, and mix everything together with four ounces of melted butter. for the topping, cut the pastry with a cutting wheel and make it like a lattice, and bake it.

title: Pour faire tourtes geneues verdes.
text: take two generous handfuls of spinach, a handful of mint, and chop everything together finely, then press out the water. next, take three ounces of grated parmesan, mix it with the chopped herbs, and spread the mixture evenly over the pastry to a thickness of one finger. then, take half a pound of fresh cream cheese and beat it well with three raw eggs, half a teaspoon of olive oil, a little pepper, and ginger, blending everything thoroughly. take a spoonful, and add a piece of white cheese, sprinkling it over the herbs spoonful by spoonful, three fingers apart. create a delicate crust, pricking it with small holes using a finger. drizzle a little olive oil on top, and bake as you would other pastries.

title: Pour faire tourtes geneues blanches.
text: take soft white cheese and dress it as above, then add two ounces of grated cheese. next, take nine or ten chopped onions and sauté them in olive oil, adding saffron and pepper, ensuring they are seasoned like the others.

title: Pour faire tourtes de febues.
text: take cooked green beans, and peel them, and pound them, and put in two raw eggs, a pinch of cinnamon, a little chopped mint, three ounces of sugar, four ounces of melted butter, and make them into patties like the others.

title: Pour faire tourtes de naueaux.
text: take young eels and roast them over the fire. once cooked, cut them into small, long slices like you would chop tripe. then, combine four ounces of rich, mild cheese with three beaten raw eggs, a pinch of cinnamon, two ounces of sugar, a little pepper, four ounces of melted butter, and a splash of rosewater. make them into tarts as you would others and serve.

title: Pour faire tourtes de ris.
text: take a small dish of rice that is cooked and well thickened, then take three raw eggs, four ounces of melted butter, two ounces of sugar, a pinch of cinnamon, and a little rosewater, and proceed as with the others.

title: Pour faire tourtes de Biscay.
text: take grated white bread, two handfuls, then take four raw eggs, eight chopped apples sautéed in butter, three ounces of sugar, half an ounce of cinnamon, two ounces of currants, and mix everything well together. spread it all on a greased paper and shape it like a pie. top with candied fruit, cut into small slices, and sprinkle generously with sugar.

title: Pour faire tourtes de pommes.
text: take a dozen apples. chop and sauté them in butter with three ounces of sugar, a pinch of cinnamon, and four egg yolks. add a little ground anise, and bake in a rich pastry crust.

title: Pour faire tourtes d'amandes.
text: take half a pound of peeled and pounded almonds, quince preserves, a dozen dried dates well cleaned inside and finely chopped with the quince, and half an ounce of cinnamon, three ounces of sugar, two yolks of eggs, and mix everything together. make it into a pie like the others.

title: Pour faire tourte de fonge.
text: take well-cooked mushrooms and chop them like tripe, then sauté them in butter. next, combine four ounces of grated cheese, a small handful of mint and marjoram, all finely chopped, and mix everything together. make a pie and drizzle with melted butter.

title:
Pour faire tourte de melon a la
Romaine.
text: take a melon that is not too ripe, and clean it well inside and out, then chop it finely. next, take four ounces of good, rich cheese, two ounces of sugar, a pinch of cinnamon, and a pinch of nutmeg, and make a pie as you would any other. when baked, sprinkle sugar on top, and candied fruit for color.

title:
Pour faire tourte blanche
a la Romaine.
text: take a pound of white cheese. then take the whites of six eggs and beat them thoroughly until they foam like snow, and let them rest a little without beating. then take the foam from the top and add it to the cheese, then beat the egg whites again until they foam as before, and spread them over the cheese. repeat this two or three times, then add two ounces of melted butter, a little grated ginger, and a little chopped basil. form into a tart and bake as usual.

title:
Pour faire tourte d'orge mondè
à la Romaine.
text: take pearl barley and cook it in a rich broth. when it is well cooked, grind it in a stone mortar, after draining the water thoroughly. then add two ounces of grated parmesan cheese, three egg yolks, and three ounces of sugar, a pinch of cinnamon, and a little salt. spread this mixture over the barley. for the topping, make a pastry crust cut into strips the width of three fingers, and chop the pastry finely, like shredded tripe. sprinkle this over the top and bake. sprinkle with sugar and cinnamon. this method is used to make bolognese sausage and various kinds of pastries, both meat and fish, and other types of jellies.

title: Pour faire saulsisse de Bologne.
text: take six pounds of fatty pork and cut it into slices. put it in a cloth and place it in a press to squeeze out the blood, and leave it in the press for an hour until all the blood is drained. then chop it coarsely, not too finely, and add four ounces of salt, one ounce of pepper, coarsely crushed, and one ounce of cinnamon, finely powdered through a sieve, and mix everything together with the salt, then add it to the meat. take eight ounces of spanish wine and mix it well with your hands for half an hour, ensuring it is thoroughly incorporated into the meat. then take beef casings according to the size you want your sausages to be, and fill them with the meat as tightly as you can. have a large needle in hand to pierce the casing constantly, so that there is no air inside and the meat is well packed. then tie the casing securely at the top and bottom to the length you desire for the sausages. next, have a

title: Pour faire mortadelle.
text: take six pounds of meat, and put in it two ounces of pepper, half an ounce of mace, one ounce of powdered cinnamon, four ounces of grated parmesan cheese, then mix well with the meat, and fill the casings, making sausages as you want them large or small. note that they must be eaten hot with some flowering cabbage or other vegetables.

title: Pour faire Ceruelade fin.
text: take six pounds of meat from the upper part, but let it be a little fatter, then take half an ounce of pepper, and half an ounce of cinnamon, and half an ounce of nutmeg, a little saffron, half as much spanish wine as the others, then make sausages as the others.

title: Saulsisse de Bologne de poisson.
text: take three pounds of fresh salmon, two pounds of carp meat, one pound of smoked salmon, and chop everything well together. then take one ounce of coarsely ground pepper, half an ounce of cinnamon powder, three ounces of salt, half a cup of spanish wine, and three yolks of eggs, and mix everything well together, and make sausages like the others.

title: Pour faire gelee.
text: take a pot of white wine and heat it well, then add three-quarters of sugar, one ounce of cinnamon, one ounce of nutmeg, and one ounce of coarsely pounded ginger, and put it into the hot wine. let it sit like this for three or four hours, then strain the wine through a sieve to remove the spices. have linen bags, as used for making ipocras, then add to the wine three spoonfuls of cow's milk, and a small handful of coarsely chopped unpeeled almonds. put the almonds in the bag, then strain the wine through the bag two or three times, until it is clear. add two ounces of good isinglass, well washed, and boil it with a little wine and water until it is completely dissolved. then pour it into the wine, after it has been strained through the bag this will set the jelly. when the jelly is half cold, pour it into dishes and let it cool until it is firm. if

title: Pour faire gelee rouge.
text: take sunflower roots and boil them. add a little of your jelly beforehand, to give them the color you desire.

title: Pour gelee iaulne.
text: color with two threads of saffron when it has passed.

title: Pour gelee grise.
text: bladderwrack, soaked until it is sufficiently pliable.

title: Pour faire gelee noire.
text: take the skins of almonds that are black and burnt, and put them into your clear jelly. after it has drained, let them soak for three or four hours, then strain them through a cloth to remove the almond skins. if you find the jelly is not dark enough, add more skins.

title: Pour faire gelee noire.
text: take peach stones and their kernels, and char them well until black, then crush them finely and soak them in clear jelly, which should be slightly warm, for two or three hours. then strain your jelly through a cloth. if it s not dark enough, you can do the same with almonds.

title: Pour faire gelee verde.
text: bring water to a boil with lemon or orange peel, and make it very sweet, along with ginger. add bladderwrack while the water is still green, and set it to freeze without wine. strain it as you would others. note that if you add wine, it will diminish the green color and turn it grey.

title: Autre verde.
text: take blue and yellow jellies, and mix them together you will have parrot green.

title: Gelee violette.
text: take indigo, and break it into pieces, and soak it in wine that is sufficiently blue, then freeze it as you would others.

title: Autrement en quaresme.
text: take violets and make three or four infusions, until they have a sufficient color, and prepare them as the others.

title: Pour faire gelee passementee.
text: begin by preparing a white iron basin, one foot long and half a foot wide. then take a pint of cow's milk and bring four ounces of hops to a boil until melted. strain it through a sieve and add a little sugar until it's sweet. once it s half-cold, pour it into the white iron basin to a thickness of about a small finger s width, and let it cool completely until firm. when it s thoroughly cold, add red jelly to the same thickness. once it s cold again, add yellow jelly, just like before. after that, add gray jelly, then mix half yellow and half red, and add them as you did the others. next, add clear, colorless jelly and another layer of milk jelly. once everything is completely cold, warm the basin slightly and turn it out onto a board, then cut it into slices on a plate.

title: Pour faire gelee lardee.
text: take red jelly and add to it a layer of gelatin about the thickness of a finger. then, in another bowl, prepare another layer of milk jelly, also about half a finger's thickness, ensuring it is very cold. cut bacon slices as long as the bowl, and arrange them on the red jelly when it has set, spacing them about a finger's width apart, allowing space to insert a finger between each slice. next, take more red jelly, when it s half-set, and pour it over the bacon until they are completely covered. repeat this process three times, ensuring everything is thoroughly chilled. turn the bowl over like the first, and slice two or three portions onto a plate.

title:
Pour faire gelee
de glace.
text: take clear white jelly, being a little cool, you will take a stick split into four, and you will beat your jelly for a long time until it becomes almost entirely cold, and it is full of small bubbles like ice, then you will put it into a dish. when it is very cold, you will pour a little warm water over it, and pour it out immediately so that the jelly is more lively.

title: Pour faire monstachole. [sic]
text: take a measure of peeled almonds and pounded, a measure and a half of white flour, four ounces of cinnamon, half an ounce of nutmeg, a pinch of cloves in powder, ten grains of musk, two measures of sifted white sugar, six egg yolks, two ounces of butter. make a dough with a little rosewater, so the dough is slightly firm, then shape your almond biscuits into hollow forms, as large or small as you desire, and place them on wafers and on parchment paper, then bake them in a moderately warm oven.

title: Pour faire du lard d'Almagne.
text: take a pound of peeled almonds, and grind them very finely, adding a little rosewater, half a pound of sugar mixed with almonds. then put it over the fire in a cauldron or paella pan, and stir it well with a wooden spoon for a long time until the almonds become a pliable paste. mix the almonds constantly with your hands until they are cool. then take half of your almonds and form a cover the size of your hand. note that half of the almonds should be made red with parisian rose petals, until you see that they are red enough to your liking. then take this cover and place it one on top of the other, first the white and the red, and so on until everything is one on top of the other. then flatten the paste with your hand very nicely, so that it sticks together. cut it into slices about half an inch thick, and place it on paper underneath in a slow oven, making sure it is not too hot.

title: Pour faire Marsepain.
text: take the blanched almonds as prepared, and roll out the paste as you would for a tart. then shape the marzipan to the size you desire. next, take some sifted sugar and mix it with orange flower water, beating it together until it is the consistency of an apple sauce. spread a little of this mixture over the marzipan, and smooth it with a sharp knife until the marzipan is completely covered. then place it in the oven on a sheet of paper. when you see it bubbling and forming a glaze, remove it from the oven when it stops bubbling, and sprinkle with ground anise seeds. if you wish to brown it, do so.

title: Pour faire paste de succre.
text: take finely sifted sugar, sifting it through a fine sieve. then have gum arabic, well soaked in rosewater, passed through a sieve as finely as you can. put your gum arabic into a mortar for cooking, or another, and pound it well, always adding a little sugar as you work, until you have a pliable paste. the more it s beaten, the whiter it becomes. from this paste you can form whatever you wish, such as shapes, cutters, flat discs, or cups, as you desire, and place it under a not-too-hot oven. you can also color it as much as you like. be careful that the oven is not so hot that it causes the paste to puff up, as that would be useless, because the paste must remain firm.

title: Pour faire Caneline.
text: take a sheet of this pastry and two ounces of finely sifted cinnamon, and beat your pastry in a mortar for a long time until the cinnamon is thoroughly incorporated with the sugar, then you will make covers very thin, the width of half a quarter. take then sticks the thickness of a finger, and roll the pastry over them as one makes shortbread biscuits, then, once slightly dried, remove it from the stick, and place it on paper, and put it to dry in the oven.

title: Pour faire paste d'orenge.
text: take a sheet of this pastry and a pinch of orange peel powder, dried and well-baked, then beat well with the pastry as you have made the cinnamon pastry, then spread them on shaped forms, large or small as you desire, bake them similarly, bake them until golden as you wish.

title: Pour faire fougeline.
text: to begin with this sweet dough, take four mace blades, finely ground with a little white sugar powder, then beat them well into the dough as with the others, and form it into rolls the size of a large walnut. next, cut them into pieces as large as eggshells, and flatten them with your thumb until they resemble small loaves. place them on wafers and on parchment paper. then, take yolks of eggs well beaten, and brush the small loaves over with them, sprinkling a little cinnamon on top. bake them in a slightly warm oven, allowing them to rise a little.

title: Pour faire Pignolate.
text: take small pears that are well cleaned and singed over the fire, and let them be somewhat dried. then you will prepare a pound of melted sugar with rosewater, and cook it until it is perfect for shaping. next, remove it from the heat and add four ounces of chopped pears, roughly chopped with a knife. throw them into the sugar and mix well with five or six spoonfuls of egg white froth. then, drop them onto wafers in small mounds, two full spoonfuls per mound, and brush the tops with egg yolk. if desired, add a little musk to it it can be done.

title: Pour faire Pistachine.
text: remove the pistachios from the stone and soak them in warm water, ensuring they remain green, then chop them into pieces like small discs. combine them with sugar in the same manner, forming small cakes shaped like discs.

title: Pour faire paste reale.
text: take half a pound of blanched and finely ground almonds, then take the breast of a roast chicken and cut it into small pieces, pounding it in a mortar very firmly. next, take three-quarters of a cup of powdered sugar and two ounces of ground cinnamon, and pound them together well. add a little rosewater, then roll out this dough into small pieces, about two fingers wide and half a finger thick, and score the tops with a knife, then bake them in the oven.

title:
Pour preparer le succre pour
ietter personnages
& fruictage.
